A new analysis technique has been developed for elastic scattering data analysis. In contrast to conventional methods, this approach can effectively handle data with incomplete or missing points without requiring any pre-processing. We demonstrate its capability with an actual scattering experiment involving the $\left. ^{16}\mathrm{O}+^{16}\mathrm{O} \right)$ system, and its outcomes align well with microscopic model predictions. Additionally, this method's feasibility in combining with microscopic models for data interpretation has been explored, offering a significant advancement in the field. We also discovered that using this analysis without a theoretical framework can still provide insights into certain analytical issues. We conducted a preliminary examination of this situation and found that large-volume analysis may offer a way to resolve these disputes. We also found that the target-glint contamination, which was thought to be insignificant by earlier methods, might actually have a substantial effect on results obtained in certain experiments, and could potentially be the origin of noticeable discontinuities in the cross-section at higher energies observed in experiments such as $(18\mathrm{O}+18\mathrm{O})$ and $(20\mathrm{Ne}+20\mathrm{Ne})$. We successfully modeled this contaminate using the glint model, and our results were sent to the NIMA software for further simulation, revealing that in experiments involving $20\mathrm{Ne}+20\mathrm{Ne}$ glint is estimated to account for $7\%$ of the total elastic cross-section at $20\%$ of the kinetic energy threshold. We hope our findings will contribute to future research in the field. The new analysis method, along with all associated code and data, has been made publicly available for use. We also make an appeal to all existing experimental groups to re-analyze their data using this analysis method to see if it can provide a fresh perspective, and to publicly share their analysis code and data for the benefit of the scientific community. A asymptotic expansion method is presented to analyze boundary condition-aided blackbody thermodynamics. This involves developing a novel LGZ-distribution, essential for defining temperature and entropy in the presence of boundary conditions, using entropy as the primary criterion. The proposed LGZ-distribution shares characteristics with the Zimmermann frequency, aiding in handling boundary effects. The paper begins with a discussion on boundary condition implications in quantum and thermal zones, before describing a generalized Zimmermann frequency and entropy based on the LGZ-distribution, accessible via asymptotic expansion methods. Examples of complete and incomplete zones are provided to illustrate the techniques. Furthermore, comparisons with existing literature are made, showcasing the thermodynamic equivalence of the LGZ-distribution and Zimmermann frequency. The work also explores entropy asymptotic expansions for both complete and incomplete zones, yielding insights into entropy behavior. Lastly, the paper discusses an alternative technique for computing LGZ-distribution frequencies, leveraging Zimmermann frequency properties. This approach is illustrated through numerical experiments. The research shows that boundary condition-aided thermodynamics facilitates a seamless transition from bulk to boundary thermodynamics through a mathematical representation. This novel technique is essential for a accurate evaluation of boundary effects in problems with boundary conditions. The LGZ-distribution frequecies are expressed in a way that are suitable for both numerical and analytical computations, providing a valuable tool for analyzing the thermodynamic properties of conducting slabs. The findings also indicate that entropy is a robust metric for identifying distinct thermodynamic phases. Additionally, the research identifies and validates a previously unrecognized phase in the system. The work ultimately contributes to the understanding of zone types by providing a practical frequency enhancement technique. The LGZ-distribution frequency phase transitions are visualized and the Zimmermann frequency is proven to be an essential tool for detecting phase transitions in thermodynamic systems. The research is concluded by outlining future investigations aimed at extending the work to quantum thermodynamics. The final destination of these future studies is to develop a strategy for handling boundary condition-aided quantum thermodynamics. The paper contributes a novel LGZ-distribution frequency to the field of thermal field theories, along with a understanding of its thermodynamic properties. The research introduces a novel phase in the system and identifies five zones, each with distinct thermodynamic properties, while providing insights into zone types and thermodynamic phase transitions. The work ultimately yields a phase diagram detailing the thermodynamic properties of each zone. The research is further extended to bulk systems, enabling a accurate evaluation of boundary effects in problems with boundary conditions, while providing a deeper understanding of bulk system behavior.

A serious issue arises when a user's location history can potentially reveal highly sensitive details about another user, known as privacy loss. Current approaches relying on mutual information have limitations in addressing location dependency, resulting in suboptimal security. To address this, we develop a framework that tracks privacy loss and is applicable to a wide range of scenarios, even conditional independence. By leveraging a novel metric that incorporates Lévy-Khintchine process, our framework provides an accurate representation of privacy loss. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm that approximates privacy loss without requiring a full model specification, which can be applied to various privacy-related problems, such as optimizing a function tailored to specific use cases. The effectiveness of our framework is demonstrated through a comparative analysis of different algorithms across various location-based scenarios. These results illustrate the superiority of our approach in achieving desired security levels with minimal storage overhead. Additionally, we illustrate the applicability of our framework in other privacy-related problems by showcasing a real-world example of an intrusion detection system. This highlights the potential of our framework in other complex problems, such as those involving geolocation tasks in IoT systems. Recent advancements have highlighted the potential of utilizing 3D point clouds for place recognition in autonomous vehicles. Despite the use of more accurate representations like point nets, places are still difficult to recognize and long processing times remain a hindrance. Our contribution presents a novel method combining the Normal Distributed Transform and Descriptors to efficiently recognize locations from 3D point clouds, achieving superior performance with reduced processing time compared to conventional approaches. This novel representation, called NDT descriptor, is used in conjunction with the Normal Distributed Transform to segment and describe three-dimensional point clouds. Our place recognition system leverages a database of predefined locations to match point clouds, with an innovative strategy for merging point clouds via graph optimization to further enhance recognition performance when the initial results are subpar. Our NDT descriptor exhibited exceptional robustness, with precise location identification both close-range and at distance, and significantly accelerates processing times by an average of 227 times. Experimental results demonstrate the substantial improvements brought about by the proposed NDT descriptor over other prominent approaches. Moreover, when integrated with existing merging strategies, our place recognition system exhibits an average 5% improvement in accuracy, with superior performance observed even in scenarios with limited data. Overall, our NDT descriptor represents a significant advancement for real-time place recognition using 3D point clouds. It possesses exceptional precision and is remarkably swift at execution, with its high-quality performance and efficiency making it a suitable choice for various applications in robotics and computer vision. Moreover, its unique capacity to identify locations both close-range and at distance, coupled with its robustness in noisy environments, is an impressive achievement, paving the way for its successful implementation in other applications. Inspired by the work of Dieckert and Wagner (2014, 2015), we investigate the energy consumption of distributed communication problems involving 2-3 stations in different models. The one-way model involves asymptotically optimal solutions for $\lambda$-named and $\lambda$-counting problems with energy complexities proportional to $n\log n$. In the round-robin model, we achieve near-optimal energy consumption for these tasks with constants slightly increased due to round-tripping. Notably, we solve the $k$-element intersection problem with optimal energy efficiency when $k$ is fixed and demonstrate that this task's energy complexity grows linearly with the number of stations. By expanding on the round-trbin protocol of Wagner (2017), we developed a one-way distributed version. Analyzing the one-way edge counting problem, we observed that our algorithm for the round-robin model achieves the previously best known energy upper bound of $2n$. Further refinements to the edge counting algorithm yielded improved upper bounds in both the round-robin and one-way models. In all cases, the energy consumption was either strictly less than $2n$ or essentially equivalent to $2n$. The proposed solutions are efficient not only in terms of energy consumption but also exhibit near-optimal communication distances for many problems. A notable exception is the edge counting problem, for which we discovered that achieving optimal energy efficiency is incompatible with optimal or nearly optimal communication distances in both the one-way and round-robin models. The first general upper bound for the energy consumption in the one-way model was established by Wagner (2017), and we refined this bound using an extremal analysis approach. In the round-robin model, we addressed this problem by considering the continuous energy consumption process and deriving the p-energy complexity as a function of the probability $p$. By applying this concept to the $\lambda$-counting problem, we obtained an upper bound for the energy consumption, which we found to be almost symmetric with respect to $n$ and $\lambda$. By generalizing the counting protocol, we achieved a general upper bound for the energy complexity of the $k$-element intersection problem with stationary $i$ involved. In both the one-way and round-robin models, the upper bound is linear in the number of involved stations $k$. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms demonstrate the near-optimal communication distance property, meaning that the distance achieved with them is either exactly or very closely attained by the optimal solution. To address this limitation, researchers have introduced new techniques for incorporating position-aware features. The proposed position-aware model, P0MXender, uses these techniques and performs well across multiple benchmarks for Hindi-English. The model's design and experiments demonstrate its capability to improve language models for multilingual text. The dynamical nature of hydrogen sulfide's $\ce{S-H}$ bond has led some to predict that H$_3$S would remain liquid at high pressures, maintaining a phononic route to superconductivity. To explore the superconducting potential of this substance, we have employed ab initio calculations to build on prior works. The results show that H$_3$S's transition to superconductivity would be sensitive to isotopic substitution, with a significant isotope effect coefficient ($\beta$) ranging from 0.20-0.50 due to changes in phonon frequencies and zero-point vibrational echoes. Like ethane, H$_3$S features a flat potential energy landscape (PEL) surrounded by vibrational barriers. As the as the PEL's depth is interpreted not solely in terms of structural disorder, we have considered the role of intermolecular interactions to facilitate comparison with ethane's behavior. The application of high pressures in H$_3$S would reduce its PEL's depth, thereby enhancing its high-pressure tolerance and extending the phonon life expectancy at higher kinetic energies. The substance would remain metallic at all pressures, with a constant superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$) yet significant decline in superconducting intensity. The intense hybridization between $s$ and $p$ orbiters in H$_3$S renders its electronic properties substantially different than those in hydrogen molecule ($H_2$), despite the presence of small band gaps. As high pressures would narrow these gaps, we have considered three scenarios to further explore the superconducting phase transition in H$_3$H. The results show that high pressures would significantly slow this transition yet fail to induce a substantial ground state change. The predicted behaviors presented here are a direct result of first-principles calculations based on density functional theory, with corrections drawn from quantum fluctuations in wave-particle duality. For most robots, navigating around obstacles is an essential ability due to the inherent complexity of their environment. Efficient detection and navigation around obstacles around vertical surfaces, such as around beams, is particularly crucial. Current approaches are often hindered by high computational costs, limited sampling methods, and failure to utilize spatial constraints when planning routes around obstacles. To address these limitations, we propose a novel method that leverages spatial constraints to quickly and effectively plan routes around obstacles around beams in complex environments. This approach involves using spatial constraints to create a plausible route around obstacles, thereby drastically reducing the time and effort required for obstacle navigation. Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches, resulting in a substantial reduction of up to 35% in the time and effort required for obstacle navigation. To support the proposed approach, we also provide our source code, a detailed setup manual, and a dataset for training and testing purposes. We introduce a novel learning-based approach to descriptor design for camera recalibration, leveraging both image and camera parameters in an end-to-end process. Our system uses a rotation-invariant learned descriptor to bridge the gap between 2D semantic features and 3D pose, capturing key interactions between image and camera geometry. By optimizing a rotationally-sensitive descriptor, we demonstrate significant improvements in estimating camera position, with an average global cross-validation accuracy surpassing 99%, even in the most challenging scenarios, such as texture-less and distant scenes. Additionally, our method outperforms traditional methods when trained on smaller datasets, offering a versatile solution applicable to various positioning tasks. Our code and training data are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/adiwijaiic/learneddescriptor. Given the simplicity and broad applicability of our model, we anticipate its potential for use in real-world applications. Further investigation into the design of our proposed descriptor is left for future research. As a secondary contribution, we release the newly-created Sudbury Dataset, a collection of 90,000 images paired with ground truth camera transformations in a simulated indoor environment. This dataset facilitates research on learned descriptors and can be accessed at https://github.com/adiwijaiic/simulatedudburydataset. Sudbury Dataset is meant to complement the existing DBO dataset, augmenting it with a substantial increase in data volume. This study introduces a novel LASSO-based approach, known as group LASSO, to broaden the applicability of LASSO in multiuser MIMO systems with limited transmit antennas. By leveraging group LASSO, the problem is decomposed into two distinct direction sets - one focusing on signal and the other on interference. Consequently, group LASSO is capable of handling scenarios with fewer transmit antennas, enabling better reception and signal interpretation, and thus yields higher sum-rates and better interference management. To effectively solve the group LASSO problem, an alternating algorithm is proposed, incorporating basis pursuit in an iterative two-step process, and demonstrating convergence to an optimal solution. Furthermore, group LASSO is illustrated to converge to a optimal solution twice as fast as other methods, and performance is shown to surpass that of other approaches in various simulation scenarios, corroborated by computational results. Finally, group LASSO is shown to yield superior performance to other methods when applied to a 10-user MIMO system, with results indicating a 50% improvement in sum-rate over LASSO and zero-forcing. These findings are consistent across different signal-to-interference ratios (SIR) and load factors. Moreover, group LASSO is observed to manage interference effectively even when interference far exceeds signal strength (SIR ≈ 0.1), and load factors as high as 4 are achievable without compromising sum-rate performance. These results highlight the effectiveness of group LASSO as a robust approach for designing MIMO systems. Lastly, group LASSO's suitability for uplink and downlink scenarios is explored, illustrating its potential as a versatile solution for multiuser MIMO systems. These findings suggest the design of group LASSO-based MIMO systems presents a promising direction for next-generation communication systems. Furthermore, we prove that if a Markov process is irreducible in a stochastic setting, it exhibits exponential convergence towards a unique quasi-stationary distribution. We then establish the connection between quasi-stationary distributions in Markov processes and the solutions to the stochastic generalized Riccati equation in the context of optimal control problems involving linear systems with Markovian disturbance. Finally, we investigate the approximations of quasi-stationary distributions through time-horizon asymptotics in a stochastic generalized Riccati equation, revealing an interesting discrepancy: in the case of linear systems and Markovian disturbance, the time-horizon approximation yields a normal distribution, whereas for certain non-Markovian disturbances it results in a gamma distribution. Additionally, we establish a reverse result showing that a Markov process with a lower bound on its transition rates is not necessarily equivalent to a Markov process with exponential convergence towards a quasi-stationary distribution, thus highlighting a key distinction. Among these models, Type-II two Higgs doublet models remain noteworthy due to their ability to comply with theoretical constraints such as the Zp resonance search by CMS and the muon anomalous magnetic moment puzzle. In this paper, we analyze a vast array of Type-II two Higgs doublet models capable of explaining the b to s decay anomaly while considering multiple constraints, including theoretical and experimental limitations. Our findings reveal a substantial area of models that can fit the b to s decay anomaly under various benchmark orders. Moreover, we show that these models can also comply with theoretical and experimental limitations, thus validating their validity. To further investigate these models, we evaluate their effects on Zp resonance searches by CMS and discuss the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly. Our analysis reveals a significant area of models that can explain both the b to s decay anomaly and the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly simultaneously. Additionally, we found that these models can also comply with direct search constraints, such as the Zp search anomaly at CMS. Our study is the first to thoroughly investigate the connection between the b to s decay anomaly and the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in Type-II two Higgs doublet models. In the analysis, we observed that these models can explain both phenomena simultaneously while complying with theoretical and experimental limitations. Our work provides valuable insights into these models, thus contributing to a deeper understanding of beyond standard model physics. Furthermore, our results may guide upcoming experiments at the LHC in finding new physics beyond the standard model. For translationally invariant materials, a neural network can be trained to identify optimal microstructures by learning from a database of designed and naturally occurring microstructures. However, a question arises about how to handle cases where the microstructures' symmetries do not match. To address this, the algorithm was refined by combining the contributions of multiple experts with distinct symmetry assumptions. Expert 1 assumes guided design, while Expert 2 explores random configurations. Through this combination, the algorithm can automatically detect the differences in symmetry and switch between guided and exploratory designs. By analyzing its performance using thousands of two-dimensional microstructures, the study demonstrates that the refined algorithm achieves higher mechanical strength in comparison to a standard expert. Furthermore, the algorithm was successfully applied to create new, symmetric microstructures with optimized mechanical strength. In conclusion, the developers enrolled a team of experts able to generalize different notions of symmetry, allowing for the development of new, robust materials with specified properties. Ultimately, this could lead to the creation of advanced materials with exceptional performance, crucial in diverse applications, by optimizing their internal structures. A detailed description of the associated Python package, SymMechLearn, is also provided.

This study offers critical proof of the well-posedness for the stationary Navier-Stokes equations within specific function spaces. We show that for $d \geq 3$ and $p = 2$, solutions are unique and depend continuously on initial conditions within the space $\mathcal{B}_{\dot{\gamma}, 2}^{-2}$. Furthermore, for the same parameter values, we demonstrate that the solutions are independent of small perturbations in the sense of attractors, specifically within the space $\mathcal{B}_{\dot{\gamma}, 2}^{0}$. Our results essentially validate certain parts of recent findings by Chen and Vilela (2021). We also extend their work by considering an anisotropic Navier-Stokes model, which exhibits similar properties. This model includes a second-grade fluid effect modeled by a non-conservative d'Alembertian operator. We show that the solutions to this model are well-defined within the same function spaces as before. This work draws upon the theories of maximal $L^q$-solutions and the long-time behavior of solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations, which have been extensively explored in recent literature. Our findings rely heavily on the use of fractional interpolation theories, local and global behavior properties of the solutions to the d'Alembertian equation, the behavior of the solutions at great distances from the origin, and the construction of the global attractors in the studied systems. Our research ultimately provides a more precise understanding of the behavior of the anisotropic Navier-Stokes model, which has been extensively studied in the context of applied mathematical physics. This research outlines an innovative indexing technique tailored for long documents called Long Document Bag Indexing (LDBI). LDBI efficiently extracts crucial terms from documents, omitting the remainder, thus generating a query-based bag comprising terms. For every query term, LDBI determines whether the associated document bag should be included in the ranking process. A novel filtering method minimizes the number of document bags considered, resulting in better ranking performance for long documents. LDBI significantly improves ranking quality for documents exceeding one hundred words in a single pass, surpassing both traditional bag indexing and filtering approaches. Moreover, LDBI achieves notable reductions in storage space requirements compared to traditional indexing methods, exemplified by a 64-bit system, a custom ranking kernel, and the Wikipedia dataset, yielding a storage compression ratio of 291:1. Notably, LDBI's computational complexity in bytes processed is directly proportional to 1/$(n+1)$. Finally, LDBI's overall performance benefits are evident in both pre-computed and on-the-fly indexing scenarios. In comparison to traditional indexing methods, LDBI accelerates ranking processing by 2-20 times for long documents. In the semi-supervised node classification task for Graph Neural Networks, 
labeling methods based on pseudo-labels have demonstrated significant value. 
However, we've found that these methods aren't consistently effective: they 
can both boost or impede performance, depending on specific conditions. 
We investigated the underlying causes by conducting a thorough analysis 
of pseudo-labeling's influence on GNN training. Through adaptive pruning, 
we discovered that pseudo-labels often contain erroneous classifications, 
even with relatively low levels of noise. We further observed that 
pseudo-labels can either enhance or hinder model training, contingent 
on how they're mixed with the true labels in the initial stages of 
training. Building on these findings, we proposed a solution called 
ReWeighted Pseudo Labeling (RPL), which addresses these challenges by 
improving the quality of pseudo-labels and effectively combining them 
with the true labels, thereby facilitating learning from noisy 
data. Comprehensive experiments using six datasets have solidified the 
premium of RPL in semi-supervised node classification, showcasing 
substantial gains over traditional pseudo-labeling methods. The data 
generated during our investigation is currently available for public 
study at: https://github.com/f-feng/Semi-Supervised-GNN-with-RPL. 
We believe our research contributes significantly to the semi-supervised 
GNN field by offering insights and a practical solution to improve 
semi-supervised GNN performance in scenarios involving label noise. 
The proposed method has also been found to be adaptable to other tasks, 
such as multi-task learning, where it may serve as a potential 
solutions to counteract the effects of label noise. We observed 
compplementary benefits when combining RPL with other semi-supervised 
solutions, like mix-up and self-training, suggesting the potential 
for further exploration in the context of semi-supervised learning. 
Overall, our research may serve as a foundation for future work in 
this field, offering insights into how pseudo-labels interact with 
neural networks, as well as effective strategies to effectively 
utilize pseudo-labels in semi-supervised GNN learning. 
The theoretical underpinnings of our research have been documented 
in an accompanying study, titled "The Influence of Pseudo-Labels on 
Neural Networks." The paper detailing our research is available for 
download at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.12791.

This research introduces a novel method of plasma wakefield acceleration based on betatron radiation, offering a high-energy output at an extremely low cost compared to other particle beam accelerators. A key benefit of this approach is its sensitivity to the plasma's longitudinal electric field, making betatron radiation an attractive option for studying plasma beam dynamics and optimizing its performance. However, a key challenge to be overcome is the impact of mismatch between the beam's radial size and the plasma's electric field. To address this issue, this study investigates how radial size mismatch affects a focused proton beam within a plasma column, using computational simulations to analyze the impact of this mismatch on the beam's particle distribution, focusing narrows, and energy loss. These investigations consider various plasma column densities and beam focusing settings to understand and mitigate the impact of radial size mismatch on the beam's performance. Furthermore, this study evaluates the influence of this mismatch on the beam's overall performance and energy output, providing valuable insights for optimizing plasma beam dynamics and the feasibility of this approach. This research develops an approach to undertake model selection and assessment within the context of chain event graph models, a group that includes directed cyclic graphical models, by leveraging product Dirichlet priors. For strongly convex functions, we investigated the speed of convergence for the heavy ball method under different levels of data noise. By utilizing a generalized method for wide area computing described in Vasil'ev et al. 2021, we found that the rate of convergence is determined by the relative strength of the data noise and the damping coefficient. Through our analysis, we established that the optimal combination achieves linear convergence at both extreme levels, with the upper limit achieved with very small and the lower limit attained with very large damping factors. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the optimal coefficient for the damping factor is closely related to the square root of the inverse of the function's strong convexity parameter, multiplied by the square root of the number of iterations. This optimal damping coefficient can also be applied when working with an oracle that returns noisy gradient estimates as well as exact gradients, thereby minimizing communication requirements. As an additional contribution, we provided a precise bound for the expected distance between the method's solution and the true minimizer of a strongly convex function, given a predetermined precision had been reached. Vasil'ev et al. (2021) previously applied the heavy ball method in a network setting to find the global minimizer for strongly convex functions, achieving precision $\varepsilon$ in $O(\log(1+\varepsilon^{-1})$ iterations and an $O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$ distance to the minimizer. Building on their findings, our analysis showed that the optimal iteration complexity can be reduced to $O(\log(1+\varepsilon^{-1}))$ by selecting the damping factor in accordance with the formula $\sqrt{\log(1+\varepsilon^{-1})} / \sqrt{1+\varepsilon}$. This paper defines a new curvature flow equation with a driving term and investigates its well-posedness within the context of the Navier-Stokes free boundary problem. Specifically, it examines the stability of a plane interface in channel flow under the influence of a distributed driving force. Building on the existing body of research, the paper adapts established methods from fluid dynamics to study the dynamics of geometric evolution. Firstly, it establishes the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the associated initial-boundary value problem using a combination of regularisation techniques and the maximum principle. Additionally, it develops a suitable a priori estimate by relating the geometry of the interface to the velocity field of the surrounding fluid. Finally, it proves the long-term stability of the plane interface by demonstrating that as time approaches infinity, its geometry stabilises and it begins to move at a uniform velocity. All of these findings are relevant to the study of fluid-driven surface growth models. Moreover, they have implications for iron nanowires and biological systems, as well as contributions to the fields of fluid mechanics, surface science, and materials engineering. Lastly, it confirms a conjecture made by Chen-neuper et al. regarding the stability of a plane interface under the influence of a driving force. This confirms their conjecture, as reported in their paper titled "Fluid driven surface growth" and provides a more precise understanding of the driving force's effect on the plane interface. Scientists utilize various simulations of plant growth and movement through chemotaxis, where plants adjust their root directions in response to chemical substances, resulting in the formation of symbiotic patterns on their surfaces.  In chemotaxis-based simulations, plants are modeled to grow towards specific chemicals with their roots moving in an adaptive manner.  However, designing control strategies for these plants presents a complex control issue due to their non-linear and time-varying nature, compounded by the need to implement control via the plants' edges, limiting the use of invasive control methods.  Researchers have applied strong invasive control methods, but the need for less intrusive approaches prompted the exploration of using soft control methods, including reinforcement learning.  This study involves the development of a custom robotic system to simulate plant growth and movement through chemotaxis, and the successful application of model-free reinforcement learning for the first time in the adaptive control of plant root directions.  Model identification for bilinear systems revealed initial challenges due to the presence of unidentifiable parameters.  However, analyzing the system via the fundamental matrix helped scientists understand the parameter identification issue and its fundamental causes.  Further experimentation involved implementing the actor-critic algorithm for ALSS, a dynamic adaptive algorithm, to control plant root directions in response to changing chemical substances, resulting in the successful adaptation of root directions.  This innovative method has practical implications in the design of adaptive control strategies for the real-world integration of plants within robotic systems.  Furthermore, this work offers an unique contribution in the application of reinforcement learning for soft invasive control methods, and its applications in the predictive guidance of robotic arms.  This research has been accepted for publication in the journal IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control and is currently available online through the IEEE's Xplore platform with the doI  10.1109/TAC.2023.10.118.  A video detailing the experiment can be viewed at https://youtu.be/ef6d8cP3x3k.

We investigate various types of closed polygon loops on the Gaussian plane. This study focuses on four types of closed polygons: non-intersecting ones, those that enclose a given set of points, those surrounding a randomly generated set of circles, and those trapped inside these circles. We demonstrate that all these cases exhibit the same behavior as a large set of data, which can be characterized by the critical exponent approximately equal to -5/6. This finding agrees with previous research on randomly generated quadrangulations with a single entangled loop. We also show that the distribution of the areas enclosed by these polygons converge to a specific type of stochastic process with a negative mean. This convergence has an equivalent relationship to a specific type of random process, which can also be mapped to the critical exponents of a specific type of interacting particles on the one-dimensional plane. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the distribution of the lengths of the quadrangulations in the critical regime, and this study leads to a new understanding of the critical exponents distribution. Finally, we model certain characteristics of the large quadrangulations using a specific type of fractal tree, which allows us to calculate several critical characteristics, such as the moments of the perimeters. This study leverages the "uniform infinite weighted tree" model. All the research mentioned above extends current knowledge to encompass new types of closed polygon research. The main contribution of this study lies in the derivation of specific mathematical models for the large sets of data characterized by the critical exponent approximately equal to -5/6. As radiomics analysis becomes increasingly extensive with the growth in relevant medical data, developing efficient and standardized image analysis techniques becomes vastly critical. We introduce a high-throughput image analysis pipeline, designed to process images on computing grids like grids used for medical diagnostics. This approach is demonstrated through a case study where we apply our pipeline for radiomics analysis, leveraging grid computing to process over 1,000 digital images within a 24-hour timeframe, and achieving comparable results to more traditional, time-consuming methods. Additionally, the pipeline is adaptable to support the development of diagnostic models based on non-imaging data, and allows users to incorporate external knowledge for data pre-processing and feature extraction. This technique has the potential to streamline radiomics analysis and enable new diagnostic models, promoting the development of efficient and standardized image analysis techniques. Furthermore, the open-source code for our pipeline is available online for further modification and improvement.

This research proposes a new concept based on the observation that dark energy and dark matter may be interconnected, represented by a shift from de Sitter to FRW-like universe models. We introduce a basic framework and outline the general structure of the proposed model, aiming to provide a initial foundation for further exploration. We discuss possible connections to cosmic inflation and outline how the model could be extended to unify dark energy and dark matter, comparing it to existing models like Quintessence. We also examine the potential constraints on the proposed model by considering the scattering of gravitons, calculating the scattering length to predict the time interval between universe slice separations. With the proposed model, we predict a separation of approximately $10^{18}$ meters in a near-future experiment like the James Webb Space Telescope. We develop a Gaussian model for course pruning by incorporating side information derived from enrollment data. Each course has a set of characteristics, and students with similar course preferences tend to have similar characteristics. We capture the links between courses based on students' preferences for related courses, and the similarities between students based on their course preferences. We model these relationships using a joint Gaussian distribution in the space of course characteristics. We also discuss how to balance model complexity by adjusting the number of related courses considered. The proposed model is applied to understand comprehension and completion patterns at a large university. The model helps analysts make informed decisions about course pruning by evaluating the importance of each course based on its characteristics. We conduct statistical analysis on a comprehensive dataset of 290 universities from the National Center for Education Statistics, revealing significant and consistent patterns. For example, universities with heavy science departments tend to prune physics courses last, and universities with diverse student demographics tend to prune less-enrolled courses first. Our analysis highlights the value of this approach for higher education leaders and researchers. We also demonstrate the model's applicability to other areas by examining texture types in the MNIST dataset. We find that the proposed model surpasses the conventional PCA method in identifying meaningful characteristics for image classification. This leads to interesting insights, such as the distinction between man-made and natural textures among the eight considered, as well as individual characteristics within each texture category. We hope that our model, analysis, and insights will contribute to a deeper understanding of course pruning patterns at universities. We plan to make the source code publicly available for easy replication of our results. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/quantifiedthoughts/GaussianModelForCoursePruning. Additionally, our model has the potential to be expanded to other areas, and we envision its applications to understand features in other relevant domains. We discuss the potential applications and future directions in the discussion section. Ultimately, our model provides a framework for making informed decisions about course pruning by providing crucial insights for university administrators, researchers, and decision-makers. We discuss implications and concerns regarding the use of student enrollment data in course pruning at universities. We conclude by highlighting the promising directions for further investigation.

Our analysis reveals that this algorithm shares identical limit points with traditional SGD and achieves a faster learning rate by using more informative data samples. To understand the algorithm's convergence, we established a universal bound, taking into account both the model's complexity and the data's distribution into consideration. Unlike conventional bounds, this one does not demand knowledge of the underlying logistic function, instead using an upper limit of the logistic function's derivative, referred to as the "curvature of the logistic function" (CAL). It is this "curvature of the logistic function" that guides the algorithm, making it the key component in CA-SGD. By substituting the characteristic of the logistic function as its derivative being less than 0.25 times 0.125 times pi squared, we established a more specific bound, with the constant 0.25 being a conservative approximation, whereas in practice, the constant is less than 0.25. To further illustrate its efficacy, we demonstrated that this "curvature of the logistic function" can be used to refine the logistic regression issue, with the constant being adjustable. Our numerical log-likelihood convergence experiments on various logistic regression instances verify that the proposed CA-SGD method is efficient and robust. More specifically, when comparing it with conventional SGD, we found that CA-SGD can reduce required iterations by as much as 30% while producing a significantly lower log-likelihood value, one order of magnitude lower than the baseline SGD method. To maximize their effectiveness, these arrays are equipped with real-time calibration systems that can correct distortions in observed data. The benefits of incorporating such real-time calibration in these arrays will be analyzed, focusing on how it influences the variability of antenna gains. The calibration process itself introduces uncertainty in the gains, consisting of a common and an individual component. The effectiveness of various sky-based and data-driven methods in minimizing this uncertainty will be evaluated. The impact of real-time calibration on the overall gain variability will be assessed under the assumption that the antenna gains change independently. The outcomes suggest that, assuming independent changes in antenna gains, sky-based methods are the most efficient in minimizing the gains' overall variability. On the other hand, data-driven methods have the advantage of being adaptable to changes in the gains. To illustrate the practical application of this theory, the redundant LMT camera system will be used as a case study. The findings show that, without any antenna failure, sky-based real-time calibration can decrease the gains' overall variability by 30%, 70%, and 80% for configurations with 57, 78, and 87 elements, respectively. Conversely, data-driven methods may reduce the gains' overall variability by 10%, 20%, and 30% when compared to the baseline in the same scenarios. The research suggests that, depending on the specific array configuration and antenna failure rate, either sky-based, data-driven, or uncalibrated systems may produce the lowest overall variability in gains. CGAN is utilized to generate portfolio weights by learning the best investment portfolio to attain a given return for any specified risk level. The ACGAN approach is shown to produce well-optimized portfolios in terms of return versus risk performance, outdoing the traditional Markowitz method. It also offers enhanced portfolio diversification, achieved through machine learning's ability to bypass market assumptions. Moreover, CGAN's generative capability allows it to produce portfolio weights for previously unobserved risk-return profiles, extending the feasible set of portfolios. In addition to using ACGAN, the research also presents a new method called LCGAN, which integrates Markowitz's portfolio optimization principles into its generative model. This integration is done by adding a loss function component that matches generative and discriminative models, thereby reducing the risk of overfitting in the ACGAN approach. LCGAN is shown to have improved performance with large datasets, however, it may have reduced generative performance for smaller datasets. Overall, the results indicate that ACGAN (and LCGAN) is a highly effective tool for portfolio selection. With its ability to generate optimal portfolio weights for any specified risk-return profile, it can extend the feasible set of portfolios and may also lead to better investment decisions in the feasible set. Furthermore, the application of ACGAN (and LCGAN) could be extended to other portfolio optimization paradigms, offering enhanced portfolio diversification and return versus risk performance. Recent developments in tensor analysis have significantly influenced the study of weighted hypergraphs.  The introduction of the tensor join has streamlined calculations of spectral properties, while new techniques for adding tensors have facilitated the creation of meaningful indicators.  In particular, hypergraph partitioning and tensor join have made it possible to obtain explicit formulas for the eigenvalues of the Laplacian tensor, as well as those of the degree tensor.  The tensor join has also enabled the efficient computation of mean values and standard deviations for various indicators, such as the walk tensor, the Laplacian tensor, and the connection tensor, all of which are relevant to statistical analysis of weighted hypergraphs.  The proposed methods have been verified with experiments and are presented in a usable form, ready for applications in real-world problems.  Beyond the mentioned indicators, the approach can be adapted to other tensors and computed in other types of networks, including simple graphs, given the versatility of the tensor join.  The study highlights the potential of tensor analysis for understanding the structural characteristics of networks and offers a concrete example of its usefulness.  The provided R code for the implementation of the method is available at https://github.com/alejo10/empirical_tensor_analysis.  A corresponding MATLAB version of the code can be found at https://github.com/AlisoNaM/matlab_tensor_analysis.  The work was supported by the grants #161858 from the Argentina's Conicyt agency and  197157 by the Mexico's CONACYT agency.

This study focuses on how Church encodings contribute to the expressiveness of simply typed lambda-calculus, showcasing that they can be removed in systems with a natural numbers type, yet present in systems without a natural numbers type. We also examine a technique to convert Church encodings into data types and provide a method to represent Church encodings using lambda-typing, a typing system introduced in a prior research paper. This representation reveals a method to encode booleans, arithmetic functions, and finite lists within lambda-typing, thereby demonstrating the deletion of Church encodings in systems including a natural numbers type. In contrast, we offer examples illustrating that church encodings can only be encoded in systems lacking a numbers type, and further encode them in a reduced lambda-calculus model, called the lambda graph calculus. This model further reduces to the standard lambda-calculus. Encodings in lambda-graph calculus offer an alternative method of encoding booleans, arithmetic functions, and finite lists, comparing favourably with data types. We conclude that Church encodings are, in fact, an expression of type dependency through explicit Lambda-typing references to type variables. We expand on this concept with data types containing unknown dimensions, an idea developed for a different purpose in a separate research paper, and demonstrate its relevance in lambda-graph calculus. In addition, we present a method of encoding in normalisation for lambda-graph calculus. This method involves a reduction similar to data types, yet differs in case analysis, allowing reduction to occur across multiple level dependencies. We further offer a comprehensive study of lambda-graph calculus using the existing typing method of data types, and show that data types define limits to lambda-graph calculus, limiting it to single level dependence. We conclude that in systems including a natural numbers type, data types restrict lambda-graph calculus, limiting it in favour of single level dependence. This concept expands our current comprehension of data types in this context. The research further compares and contrasts lambda-graph calculus with existing models for normalisation in lambda-calculus, such as the singular recursion theory model of lambda calculus developed by Krivine. We re-introduce the typing method of data types in the context of lambda-graph calculus, and show that data types in lambda-graph calculus enforce a form of positivity, restricting certain forms of lambda calculus reduction. This study presents a novel, database-independent framework for generating executable code from formal specifications within the framework of while languages. Initially, it translates the specifications into executable code under the assumption that database contents are available, then it generates a set of queries to fill in the missing information, and finally it modifies the code to handle the unknown database values. Our approach can be applied to any language that adheres to the standard functional-imperative paradigm. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a virtually flawless execution in the vast majority of cases where database contents are known, and roughly 85-90% of the time when it has to generate the database values. Notably, all cases where database values had to be generated resulted in error-free execution. This achievement is a significant breakthrough, as it was previously established that executable code generation can produce errors even when database contents are known. We gathered six images of Andromeda XXV in three fields with a total of 34 square degrees covered, and our observations resulted in an effective surface density of 16.7 arcmin-2. After integrating our data and utilizing a noise estimation formula, our final surface density was determined to be 13.5 arcmin-2. This led to the detection of 20 stars, five of which were identified as probable Andromeda XXV members. Based on color-magnitude diagrams, we were unable to detect any stars belonging to the galaxy's red giant branch. This was followed by the application of an innovative technique to measure the galaxy's mass-to-light ratio, which we found to be significantly lower than that of other dwarf galaxies. The suggested framework integrates two core elements: a machine learning network with a high level of generalization and an innovative sequence design that is not mutually exclusive. In a typical scenario, a low-resolution image is passed through the network, which produces multiple high-resolution duplicates using the sequence. These copies are merged into a single, enhanced version of the original image. The sequence's non-orthogonal nature creates conflicting demands on a detector, which in turn enhances the performance of the superresolution process. The system's effectiveness was tested using a dataset of facial images and compared to a controlled system, which employs orthogonal sequences, yielding notable improvements in image quality. The results show that the suggested system achieves significant enhancements in image quality while maintaining its stability and robustness. The implementation of the sequence's non-orthogonal nature has a positive impact on the following parameters: the stability and consistency of the SR process, the efficacy of the learning and training process, the accuracy of the numerical representation of the face, and the overall performance of the system in terms of its speed. The system's functionality and the effectiveness of its implementation are demonstrated in the field of facial recognition technology. The suggested system has the potential to be adapted and successfully integrated in various other applications and domains. This paper revisits the 2019 Dialogue State Tracking challenge and compares various pre-trained language models with a baseline slot-filling model. We improve this baseline by incorporating an attentional confusion network encoder in the decoder section of a transformer-based dialogue state tracking model, leading to an enhanced performance. Furthermore, to examine pre-trained language model performance across different levels of annotation, we employ Wikibeda's annotation dataset, in addition to the original DSTC datasets. Results indicate that the attentional encoder enhancement is most pronounced with less detailed annotation. Moreover, the proposed attentional encoder enhances the overall Dialogue State Tracking performance, bringing it closer to state-of-the art performance. Finally, pre-trained language models from various sources, such as RoBERTa, XLM, and ULM-FiT, are evaluated and we observe that the proposed attentional encoder outperforms these models by incorporating it into the baseline slot-filling model. We hypothesize that the reason our attentional encoder model excels is due to its ability to reduce the adverse effects of word dropout during training. Therefore, we recommend using this attentional encoder to boost Dialogue State Tracking performance. The proposed code is publicly available at https://github.com/DuNguyen/2019-DSTC10. Overall, our objective is to provide a straightforward code implementation to facilitate pre-trained language models' integration in the dialogue state tracking task, ultimately improving performance. We hope this work will serve as a building block for future developments in dialogue state tracking. With our enhancements considered, we still acknowledge that the proposed model falls short of the current state-of-the-art performance in the DSTC10 evaluation, and we thus encourage the community to build upon our findings. Most current continual learning research focuses on training neural networks from a blank slate, but in reality, real-world applications involve using pre-trained models that generate initial predictions. This study is the first to investigate how incremental learning techniques perform when incorporating these pre-trained models. By examining the effectiveness of various approaches--including the Nearest Mean Classifier, Sudarshan's approach, Kingma's approach, and Sudarshan-Kingma approach--our results reveal that the Nearest Mean Classifier surpasses state-of-the-art performance, with only minimal deterioration compared to maintaining a blank slate. Notably, our findings also indicate that incorporating memory-based methods enhances the effectiveness of neural networks trained end-to-end. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates that the Nearest Mean Classifier exhibits comparable or superior performance relative to established continual learning methods, including Sudarshan's approach, Mason et al.'s approach, and Sudarshan-Kingma approach, in tasks involving remote sensing, medical, and cognitive engineering datasets. Importantly, our research shows that the Nearest Mean Classifier, a relatively straightforward approach, achieves comparable or superior performance relative to established continual learning methods, including Sudarshan's approach, Mason et al.'s approach, and Sudarshan-Kingma approach, in tasks involving various pre-trained models and datasets. Importantly, our results suggest that the Nearest Mean Classifier may serve as a reliable alternative to more complex continual learning methods, with potential reductions of 37%, 28%, and 33% in the number of parameters, FLOPs, and training epochs, respectively, while still achieving high accuracy. Overall, our research highlights the practical utility of the Nearest Mean Classifier as a simple, effective, and efficient approach to incorporating pre-trained models into incremental learning frameworks. This research investigates how individual and cultural differences influence AI models' capacity to identify hate speech on social media, demonstrating that these models operate within cultural frameworks that shape their perception of language. We develop a new theoretical framework, the socio-cultural agency filter, to explain this phenomenon and enhance hate speech detection. We combine this concept with value-sensitive design principles to illustrate how AI systems, including those used to hate speech detection, should be constructed with explicit cultural considerations in mind. The re-design of the AI system, as proposed in this study, aims to reduce false positives, which can harm non-majority group members. Furthermore, our research highlights the need for more detailed user representation in AI models, given their reliance on group-based generalizations in their decision-making processes. We suggest that AI developers, policymakers, and platform regulators should work together to establish guidelines for the cultural consideration of these technologies. Our study contributes to the field of value-sensitive design by defining the cultural factors that should be taken into consideration in AI system development. We also shed light on the practice of cultural consideration in AI system development, a field that to date has received insufficient attention. The study relies on data from the 2020 DOVE challenge, which compares the performance of 35 hate speech detection models on three data sets. We analyzed participant survey responses, with 19 participants providing detailed insights into their cultural context and the decisions made by their algorithms. We conducted 12 qualitative interviews with participants, exploring their perceptions of their models' cultural biases and the factors that influenced their performance during the competition. We discovered that socio-cultural context repeatedly emerged as a critical factor contributing to the performance of these AI models. We observed that these models were designed to operate within cultural contexts, with their algorithms making decisions rooted in these groups. We found that AI developers did not intentionally incorporate cultural factors when working on these systems, but rather, the participating systems were influenced by their operators' cultural backgrounds, which shaped their performance. We also established that these systems were perceived by their developers as reflecting the cultural norms of their operators. Consequently, we propose that AI systems should be developed with the explicit cultural considerations of their operators in mind. The study's results call for more detailed user representation in these systems. We conclude that this goal can be achieved through value-sensitive design methods that take cultural factors into account. The cultural consideration of these systems, a practice that to date has received insufficient attention, is an essential step towards reducing the cultural biases present in these systems. Collective oscillations in coupled network dynamics are widespread, also occurring in biological networks such as firefly light sync and coupled heart cells. We investigated electrically coupled oscillations in two-dimensional networks of stochastic gap junction coupling, where individual connections are represented by random variables. Varying the degree distributions in these networks revealed a transition from in-phase oscillations to out-of-phase oscillations. Notably, when the distribution's mean remained constant at 10, but the standard deviation (sigma) was varied from 0 to 3, the standard deviation significantly impacted the frequency and amplitude of the oscillations. A parameter representing network synchronizability showed that increased standard deviation leads to decreased synchrony. To understand these results, we considered two idealized networks with identical degree distributions as the original network and obtained similar outcomes, leading to the conclusion that degree distribution affects network behavior, but the impact is primarily through the expected values of the degrees. We further observed that when the standard deviation is zero, the standard error is also zero, indicating limited opportunities for improved synchrony in such networks. However, the standard deviation does not entirely account for out-of-phase oscillations. Notably, as sigma increases from 0 to 3, the average and maximum frequencies of the degrees in the network increase. A plot of the average and maximum frequencies against each other for different networks shows a positive correlation. These observations confirm that network behavior in gap junction coupled oscillations is complex and can be leveraged to develop advanced tools for data analysis and interpretation. To address these challenges, we propose a method to quickly determine the degree distribution from a given network, providing an alternative approach for data analysis and confirming that our method is as effective as a statistical analysis of the degrees in the network, both resulting in similar outcomes. Furthermore, applying our approach enabled the comparison of degree distributions in in-phase and out-of-phase networks, revealing differences in the degree distribution parameters for out-of-phase networks, particularly a higher average frequency and lower standard deviation, indicating that network behavior can be predicted based on degree distribution alone. We verified these findings by developing networks with the predicted degree distributions and observing in-phase and out-of-phase oscillations. Consequently, our approach offers a valuable tool for data analysis, understanding, and interpretation of gap junction coupled networks and can be extended to various applications in neuroscience and other fields. The inner bound for channels, traditionally derived from common source outer bounds and single-letter representations of individual components, often fails to accurately capture the structure of interference processes. By considering these interference processes as joint random variables instead of separate components, a novel inner bound has been developed, yielding substantial gains in capacity when applied to interference channels, (2,2) interference channels, interference channels with state and, recently, compound channels. As a result, this paper suggests that achieving a structurally superior inner bound should be a primary objective in channel modeling, positioning the belief propagation approach as an attractive method for uncovering such structures. Furthermore, a case study detailed in the paper highlights how this approach can outperform leading channel models, including the single-letter sum-product channel model, by accurately capturing the interference structure of a specified interference channel without, in the process, increasing its complexity. We conclude that a structurally superior inner bound may also lead to enhanced performance in channel coding techniques. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to the advancement of a new paradigm in channel modeling, centered on the design of a structurally superior inner bound. We also hope that this approach can be used as a tool for evaluating the efficacy of channel coding schemes and their future proofs. Additionally, our study shows that multi-variable predictors significantly surpass single-variable predictors in predicting violent and property crime rates, and that incorporating spatial dependence can help address issues of missing data and data imbalance. Nesterov's acceleration technique has been effectively applied to a variety of first-order optimization methods, including stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Although acceleration benefits are well-documented for methods using fixed step-sizes, their advent with adaptive step-sizes, notably the light-bold condition, is more recent. Research demonstrates that for the light-bold condition, Nesterov acceleration yields an optimal convergence rate, similar to its fixed-step-size counterpart. Notably, previous studies show that acceleration is unbeneficial when employing step-size conditions outside the light-bold range. Nonetheless, these findings leave unanswered questions: (i) Are Nesterov acceleration and nesterov acceleration with the light-bold condition interchangeable when the light-bold range is narrowed? (ii) Are acceleration and light-bold conditioning mutually dependent in their effects on convergence rates? Investigation reveals that both conditions, whether applied alone or in conjunction, contribute equally towards achieving optimal convergence rates, thus forming interchangeable components within an optimization method. Moreover, an adaptive procedure for deciding between accelerated and non-accelerated steps is developed, showcasing its efficacy through successful replication of results from a previously similar study on quadratic problems. Lastly, acceleration is applied to SGD in a dataset consisting of image classification scenarios, illustrating its practical benefits. Our findings suggest that acceleration has widespread implications for first-order optimization methods, encompassing both fixed and adaptive step-sizes. Ultimately, these findings present an move towards a unified understanding of acceleration in first-order optimization methods. We examine a bosonic oscillator connected to heat sources composed of fermions with a large number of degrees of freedom, which converges to a nonlinear self-oscillating system under a classical approximation. This nonlinear system is characterized by a "stiffness" value of θ and "damping" value of γ, both measured in ω0 basis, with specific heat bath parameters varying as 1/N, while the system's initial oscillator state depends on N before equilibration occurred. Two main conditions are required for linearization: (a) the system's parameters (θ, γ) must remain unchanged as N varies; (b) initially, the oscillator must be in an eigenstate with n-th power related to N, which becomes the equilibrium state of the combined system. When linearization conditions are met, the oscillator's dynamics follows a damped harmonic motion governed by the parameters θ, γ, and ω0. This linearization facilitates the creation of a fermion-boson entanglement measure, which reaches its maximum (n*γ/ω0)*θ in this harmonic regime. When the oscillator is initially prepared in any of the N-dependent eigenstate (n), which have mean photon values (<κ_n>)*N independent of N, the system transitions to a steady-state where the oscillator's mean photon values (<κ_n>)*N also depend on N, leading to the self-oscillation phenomenon in the large N limit. This phenomenon is further characterized by the introduction of non-conservative, dissipative system's motion governed by the effective equation of motion of a particle moving under a force influenced by θ and damping by γ. Nonetheless, developing a comprehensive grasp diversity library for intricate objects remains an impossible task due to the significant number of potential grasping configurations. In response, our proposal, DexGraspNet, synthesizes diverse grasps utilizing a conditional grafting network, thereby alleviating the need for exhaustive manual collection. In evaluations across 84 complex objects, DexGraspNet generated a considerable number of stable and diverse grasps exceeding those achieved by leading existing methods. Our proposed approach demonstrated particular superiority in object classification through grasp diversity, where it consistently surpassed the other baseline methods. Furthermore, to optimize grasping in real-world scenarios, DexGraspNet's synthesized grasps consistently yielded higher success rates in planning than both human-crafted and machine-learning-based prior approaches. Our research offers substantial advancements in both grasp diversity and robustness, addressing long-standing challenges in dexterous manipulation. A novel linearly separable sampling method, referred to as rCASPR, is presented and assessed in comparison to traditional linear sampling and sinusoidal sampling patterns. With its capability to replicate complex periodic patterns through simple one-dimensional mappings, rCASPR efficiently emulates linear frequency-encoding technology. Initially, a spatially uniform CSPR pattern is generated and point-sensitivity is optimized via a radial distribution. By comparing rCASPR, linear sampling, and sinusoidal sampling in a system mimicking an approximate linear frequency-encoding process, CSPR-based reconstructions demonstrated better contrast and a more similar point-sensitivity profile to the ideal linear system compared to the others. As a result, rCASPR can effectively substitute periodic patterns in linearly-separated imaging techniques such as linear frequency-encoding, compressed scheduling and sampling, and periodic pattern-reconstruction techniques in X-ray computed tomography. Moreover, rCASPR can create non-periodic patterns for non-contrast-preserving reconstruction objectives and offer customisable sampling patterns. Consequently, rCASPR offers enhanced image contrast and a more similar point-sensitivity profile to the ideal linear system compared to the others. Expert models, with their valuable experience, can facilitate knowledge transfer to less skilled models through various techniques like distillation. Nonetheless, distillation often results in expansive student models that mirror their teacher models in scope. This may lead teachers to relinquish their valuable knowledge to equivalent models, negating the purpose of transfer. Additionally, such large student models prove costly to deploy and are often unfeasible on devices with limited resources.

This problem can be addressed by reducing the complexity of the student model, making it more responsive to inputs. Channel pruning, by eliminating unessential channels, achieves this by transforming the student model into a more compact version. This research investigates the relationship between distillation loss and channel pruning, showing that: (1) an optimized pruning strategy depends heavily on the distillation loss, (2) using a loss-based guided pruning strategy bridges the gap between teacher and student models, and (3) this method leads to better model convergence.

To validate these claims, we conducted an experimental analysis on the ResNet-50 model, incorporating the pruning strategy into the pre-activation version, and found that: (1) an optimized pruning strategy enhances top-1 accuracy at smaller model sizes, (2) an accurately set pruning density further boosts accuracy, and (3) this method leads to a more efficient distribution of computational resources across the model.

Finally, this method was successfully applied to the EfficientNet family of models, achieving the impressive BERT-L large model level of top-1 accuracy with up to 90% fewer FLOPs on the ResNet-50 scale. We open-sourced the model pruning tool, available at: https://github.com/ziplab/PruneOnDistill. This technology has the potential to greatly expand the applications of expert models, enabling them to efficiently transfer knowledge to a variety of models, be they cloud-based or edge-based. In a study on 820 $\mu$b Pb-Pb collisions using the Pythia 8 Monte Carlo generator, a comparison was made between the transverse momentum dependence of two flow phenomena, triangular flow $v_3(p_{T})$ and elliptic flow $v_2(p_{T})$, from both charged hadrons and identified protons and pi mesons.  This comparison revealed that $v_3(p_{T})$ from identified protons and pi mesons is very similar to $v_2(p_{T})$ from the same, indicating that the source of this triangular flow is a single collision event.  Additionally, a plot of $v_3/p_{T}$ versus $p_T$ for identified protons, charged hadrons, and pi mesons showed that these three groups have similar magnitudes but differing directions.  A theoretical explanation was given using a blast wave model with azimuthally symmetric symmetry.  It was found that hadrons acquired this triangular flow through collisions with forward or backward moving nucleons while traveling in the forward or backward directions in the transverse plane.  Since the pi mesons have a shorter average path length than protons, a correlation exists within this model for the ratio $v_3(p_{T,{\rm for}}) / v_3(p_{T,{\rm back}}) = 0.7 = 0.8$, where $p_T$ is greater than 4 GeV/$c$.  Furthermore, a measurement was made of the difference between the flow directions of identified protons and pi mesons as a function of $p_T$, showing that they exhibit opposite flow directions at $p_T$ less than 3 GeV/$c$.  A simulation confirmed this observation by suggesting that nucleon-nucleon collisions involving a transverse momentum greater than 2.5 GeV/$c$ from the forward direction for protons and the backward direction for pi mesons are the primary source.  Therefore, this simulation was able to reproduce the experimental observations that triangular flow is similar to that of elliptic flow for identified particles in terms of both magnitude and dependence on transverse momentum.  Additionally, a blast wave model explanation for this phenomenon was provided along with its comparison with data obtained from central Pb-Pb collisions.  In conclusion, a simulation was performed to study the source of this triangular flow by comparing the flow's magnitude and direction for identified particles and charged hadrons. This research introduces a novel method for combining Federated Learning (FL) and Local Differential Privacy (LDP) to create a secure and private communication system for Decentralized Multi-Agent Networks (DMANS). The proposed approach involves training a global model using user agents' locally processed and privately sent data, and applying LDP to maintain the privacy of individual agents while ensuring the convergence of the aggregation process. A dynamic learning rate-based aggregation strategy is also presented to promote convergence, and is accompanied by analytical proofs of its properties and convergence properties. The proposed method's effectiveness is further demonstrated through simulations of private communication networks, which show that the approach successfully achieves both convergence and data privacy for DMANS applications. Furthermore, the method outperforms existing baselines such as Centralized Learning and Local Learning in terms of convergence, data accuracy, and overall performance. The results indicate that the application of FL with LDP is a suitable solution for addressing the security and privacy challenges faced by modern DMANS applications. A decomposition-based optimization strategy is also identified as a potential tool to improve the performance and convergence rate of the proposed method, and is envisioned to enhance the application potential of the approach when paired with appropriate decomposition techniques. At present, the method faces a trade-off between convergence speed and data accuracy due to the required adjustment of the learning rate, and future research aims to address this and other existing challenges faced by the approach. A Decentralized DMANS communication network was used to test the method, and the results show that the approach successfully met the main performance goals and outperformed the baseline methods in terms of convergence and data accuracy. Notably, the approach achieved a data accuracy that was 10% higher than the baseline methods, and converged at a rate that was 3 times faster. The results also showed that the approach successfully maintained the privacy of the individual agents while ensuring the convergence of the aggregation process. A user interface for the proposed method was developed to facilitate the demonstration of the approach on real-world applications, and the results showed that the approach successfully addressed the main security and privacy challenges faced by the DMANS applications. The proposed method and its associated components, including the code used to implement the approach, are available for public access via the GitHub platform. The approach can be further optimized by applying reinforcement learning-based training techniques to improve its performance and convergence properties when paired with appropriate decomposition strategies. This paper explores aspects of badly approximable numbers in non-integer base systems, driven by research questions stemming from recent findings by Bergwehr, Bergwehr–Veech, and Kuipers–Maier. We demonstrate that the survivor sets of intermediate beta-transformations share key characteristics with the bad lattice points of non-integer base systems. Building on this connection, we establish that the cardinalities of these survivor sets follow a pattern consistent with those in beta-discs and provide a direct proof of a key estimate for the dimensions of bad sets in non-integer base systems. Additionally, our work sheds light on the dynamics of beta-transformations by revealing instances of weakly infinitely infinitely branch points. We also showcase the complex structures within the beta disk's interior by identifying numerous non-trivial injective maps between its boundary and interior points. Finally, through analyzing self-similarities in the beta disk's perimeter, we identify a distinct fractal structure characteristic of non-integer base systems. This research directly addresses a question posed by Kuipers and Maier at the 2007 workshop titled "Transcendence and the dynamics of polynomials". The current study builds on previous work discussed at the workshop, titled "Badly approximable numbers in (function) field contexts" and contributes key insights in this area. Further, it includes a detailed review of related topics and areas of active research. We manage to achieve a level of precision that was initially considered beyond reach, given the significantly more complex nature of the considered base system. Our solutions rely heavily on establishing ties with areas such as the dynamics of polynomials, geometry of numbers, and the theory of Simon's famous deep hole problem. We successfully leverage recent breakthroughs, including the establishment of bad set estimates and directions set estimates by Bergwehr for general beta-transformations, as well as unique insights into the dynamics of beta-transformations provided by Bergwehr--Veech and Kuipers--Maier. We "lower the bar" for the dimensions of bad sets and directions by offering distinct and novel perspectives likely to contribute to the advancement of this area.
