The majority of deep neural networks are now used in image classification tasks, with many of these studies focused on unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). This is because UDA enables a model to resolve issues related to bias and bias transfer when training on data from one source and testing on data from another. Key UDA techniques include adversarial training, batch domain matching, and graph-based methods. Over the past five years, the most successful UDA models have consistently been those that incorporate an adversarial decoder in their architecture. However, an alternative approach developed by our group, known as edge-based unsupervised domain adaptation (EUDA), has shown comparable results without the necessity for an adversarial decoder. Instead, EUDA employs an edge representation that bridges the gap between source and target domains, enabling similar images to be labeled with similar confidence. This confidence similarity is then used for final target-domain image classification. This project presents an expanded version of EUDA that integrates all current leading UDA techniques in a singular framework, resulting in a unified approach known as deepUEDA. The results demonstrate that deepUUDA outperforms its individual components, while also providing insights into how different UDA methods can be employed in different contexts. Based on these findings, deepUUDA is then employed for improving medical image analysis tasks in specific. The code for this project will be made available to the public upon screening by peer review. The peer-screening process will be conducted at https://lenetgy.com/. The project's website can be accessed at https://gyphope.com/. Peer screening is used here as a participatory research method to gather the opinions and suggestions of the community regarding the project before it commences. The screening process yielded 46 responses from which key suggestions were gathered and implemented. The project's data demonstrates how participation can be used to enhance the reliability of AI systems by uncovering any biases in the model. The project's findings highlight how participation can be used to address any biases in the model. The project's contributions are as follows: (1) an expanded version of EUDA known as deepUUDA is presented as an alternative approach to adversarial decoding in UDA; (2) the project demonstrates the efficacy of combining multiple leading UDA techniques, yielding superior results; (3) the project highlights the importance of participation in AI by providing an example of how deepUUDA matches the performance of more complex models while reducing bias; (4) the project's findings shed light on UDA as an underexplored field within the machine learning

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become widely used in applications involving graph-based data but the clarity of their underlying logic poses a challenge when attempting to explain their results. To address this issue, an innovative explanation generator based on Generative Adversarial Networks (Generative Adversal Networks) is introduced, capable of generating explanations for specified input/output pairs using black-box GNN systems. Compared to current explanation generators, PGExplainer exhibits improved accuracy in generating explanations for a larger range of GNN models as well as diverse types of graph data such as social networks, computer code, and chemical structures, among others. Experiments using the GraphNet, ML100k, and Epistemic Uncertainty datasets show that PGExplainer achieves explanations that accurately reflect the interconnections within these graphs. Furthermore, it outperforms other explanation generators by maintaining explanation consistency across various GNN models and graph datasets. We observe that explanations generated by PGExplainer are short and easy to grasp, thereby facilitating the development of new GNNs by allowing them to be trained on explanations rather than labels directly from the output of the explanation generator. Our work is now available online at: <https://github.com/rima123/pgexplainer>. A live demo of the PGExplainer can be accessed at: <https://pgexplainer.github.io/>. Our research is supported by a grant from the National Science Foundation (Award Number: 1922281). A educational video illustrating the PGExplainer can be found at: <https://youtu.be/3O1Z3L4Xb6>. Research is also conducted at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign under the direction of Dr. Leman. All code used to implement the PGExplainer is written in JavaScript, utilizing the TensorFlow.js library for generating explanations based on GNNs. A tutorial highlighting the simplicity of integrating the PGExplainer is provided in the appendix. As the PGExplainer is now a trainable model, it can be easily extended to other domains where explanation generators are applicable, for example in identifying machine learning algorithm biases, detecting computer code plagiarism, and improving technology system reliability by allowing developers to train the explanation generator to generate explanations that can improve user system trust. By being a general explanation generator, it can also explain complex concepts not yet coded in the GNN model. A notable example of its applicability is explaining concepts related to the human immune system. By comparing these improvements to numerical simulations of the cluster's formation, researchers aim to accurately determine the radial brightness of the cluster's X-rays in the 0.5-7 keV energy range. Moreover, these simulations are used to identify whether the cluster's bright South-West region is a physical part of the structure or an illusion created by distortions caused by the disruption of a nearby galaxy merger. To this end, researchers utilize the MCMC algorithm to simulate various stages of the cluster's merger to compare with observations taken in 2016 and 2019. It was discovered that removing the cluster's bright South-West region significantly improves the fit of brightness models to these simulations, suggesting that the South-West region is likely an optical illusion created by the distortion of the disruptor galaxy. However, it remains possible that this South-West region may still be a physical component of the structure due to an unresolved central galaxy or ongoing merger activity. Additionally, researchers found that plume shapes observed in 2016 aligned with simulations of a right-handed system, whereas in 2019, these shapes aligned with left-handed systems. This addition allows for an internal 3D learned storage space within the LMU to be utilized during training, thereby accelerating the speed of deep neural network training. Furthermore, the LMU's ability to execute repeated operations across data tensors is similar to that of a recursive neural network, thereby enhancing the flexibility of its constituent learning modules. Additionally, the LMU's internal storage and duplicated operation components can be configured to mimic the functionality of a graph convolution layer when dealing with graph-related tasks, thereby facilitating the adaptation of inductive learning methods on transductive graph-based tasks with limited labeled data. Experimental evaluations conducted on the MNIST and CIFAR datasets reveal that the LMU can reduce the number of required parameter updates by up to 60%, thereby leading to a 55% decrease in the training time of LeNet Chen et al. (2018) and ResNet He et al. (2016). Moreover, the LMU has successfully achieved comparable accuracy to the Graph Convolutional Neural Network (GCNet) on the link prediction task of the ogbn-proteins dataset. Furthermore, the LMU has demonstrated the potential to surpass the state-of-the-art performance on the link prediction task of the ogbn-progbp dataset under certain conditions. The implementation of the LMU is provided at https://github.com/qinruoyang/learned-memory-unit. Two additional methods, the Self-Patheting Mechanism (SPM) and the Self-Communication Mechanism (SCM), are also proposed to enhance the performance of the LMU. The SPM allows for the communication of multiple communication layers, thereby facilitating the extraction of more robust features. The SCM allows for the adaptation to tasks with limited labeled data by mimicking the self-supervised learning paradigm. Migration can significantly impact language development, and a simple mathematical model is used in this explanation to investigate how it affects languages by creating divisions and separating speaker groups. With the introduction of a few basic parameters, this model effectively illustrates how migration influences speaker migration, language differentiation, and the formation of exclusive speaker groups. However, to fully understand the impact of migration, additional factors must also be taken into account, including the rate of migration, language similarities, and the tendency for speakers to stay within their established groups. Furthermore, this model reveals that moderate migration rates can lead to the splitting of speaker groups and the separation of distinct languages, but only under specific conditions and with the long-term perpetuation of migration. Lastly, this model suggests that migration does not always result in the isolation of speaker groups, but can easily lead to their merging when migration slows down. This is shown to be true across various scenarios and resolves a previous contradiction in existing research regarding the impact of migration on language differentiation. The simplicity and adaptability of this model make it suitable for the study of a wide range of scenarios, from small to very large populations of speakers. By applying this model to specific cases, such as the splitting of the Romance languages and the separation of English from Germanic languages, this explanation provides concrete examples of how migration may have influenced speaker migration, language differentiation, and the formation of exclusive speaker groups. Additionally, the observations from these examples highlight the need to fully consider the interconnectedness of cultures and the intermingling of speakers throughout history. Ultimately, this understanding can shed light on the complex process of language formation and may one day contribute to the development of improved language preservation strategies. Mathematically, the impact of migration on language can be represented using a system of ordinary differential equations that model the growth of exclusive speaker groups and the separation of languages. By analyzing the long-term behavior of these equations, this explanation can accurately predict when migration will lead to the splitting of speaker groups and the separation of languages, given specific values for the parameters. When using these parameters to simulate scenarios, the model can effectively identify patterns in the long-term behavior of these equations that relate to the splitting of speaker groups and the separation of languages. The simplicity and adaptability of these equations make them suitable for a wide range of scenarios, such as the study of population dynamics, the separation of English from Germanic languages, the splitting of the Romance languages, the formation of Scottish English, the formation of African languages, the splitting of English from Germanic languages, the splitting of English from Germanic languages

This paper investigates the theoretical properties of physics-informed neural networks (PFN) to understand the spectral characteristics of their underlying operators. We examined how the choice of neural network architecture, optimization method, and input data localization effect the spectral behavior of PFN. Our analysis highlights the significance of optimizing the operator's dominant eigenfunction in various applications and identifies stochastic gradient descent with momentum as an effective learning approach that can mitigate spectral bias by shifting the weight distribution towards the operator's principal eigenfunctions. Our findings are further validated through numerical experiments. Additionally, we provided a model that addresses observational data, analyzed the challenges associated with using neural networks in high-dimensional problems, and suggested a possible solution to improve the spectral properties of PFN. Finally, we demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed approach in a cross-sectional study aimed at estimating population parameters. Our method accurately captures the inverse relationship between signal-to-noise ratio and the operator's conditioning, as well as the impact of data localization on the operator's spectral properties. Our experiments showed that integrating the inverse of the data localization matrix into the neural network can counteract sampling bias, thus demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, we successfully applied our approach to the problem of inverse transport and found that our model closely approximates the true transport operator even when its eigenfunctions are unknown. Our numerical investigations also revealed that our approach consistently outputs reliable predictions among highly competitive methods. We established an online repository to host the implementation of our models and experimental results at a publicly accessible GitHub page (https://github.com/cu-icaim/advisory-opinion-2022-LA). Our research contributes the first theoretical analysis of PFN, providing the groundwork for the design and evaluation of deep learning models that address inverse problems. Our findings have the potential to inform the development of similar methods, thus advancing the understanding of their performance limitations in the context of inverse problems. Our model can be used directly in the provided repository, specifically in the file named \textit{ablation study/1\_inf\_loc\_exp\_crosscatalytic\_noise\_demo.m}, by adjusting the hyperparameters located at the end of the file. This paper investigates the behavior of solutions to a wave system with friction that has a non-constant damping coefficient, which varies smoothly. Despite this damping coefficient being non-continuous, analytically non-smooth, and displaying compensation characteristics, it leads to energy loss in the system. Consequently, the solution exhibits exponential decay. Using a combination of two Lyapunov functions, we show that its energy decreases over time, providing further evidence of its exponential decay. Furthermore, the method used can easily be adapted to other partial differential equations with certain types of non-continuous damping coefficients. Additionally, the method used can easily be adapted to other partial differential equations with certain types of non-continuous damping coefficients. As an example of this, we study the long-term behavior of the solutions to a wave system in the region near its resonant frequencies, showing that their energy remains bounded and that the solution approaches a random-like state. This behavior aligns with previous findings for similar problems studied by the first author. Meanwhile, for a wave system without resonant frequencies, we show that its solution's energy decays at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{3}{2}+L}$, with $L$ denoting the order of the non-continuous damping coefficient, assuming that $L$ is less than 0.5. This behavior aligns with previous findings for similar problems studied by Joe Wiener. Finally, for a wave system with multiple dimensions and a non-continuous damping coefficient, we show that its solution's energy decays at a rate proportional to $t^{-1}$, showing that its behavior is similar to that of a wave system with a constant damping coefficient, provided that certain conditions are satisfied. These conditions include the fact that the principle damping coefficient acts in the region far from the resonant frequencies, the fact that the principle damping coefficient is large enough, and the fact that the  time considered is large enough. These results generalize the findings of previous works studied by the first author and Joe Wiener. To address this challenge, researchers have been developing more structured approaches to reinforcement learning, such as using decision trees to represent policies. Nevertheless, incorporating rich symbolic expressions to enhance expressiveness and interpretability comes with the challenge of increasing the search space. Our research introduces Deep Relational Expressions, a novel framework that leverages deep learning to search for symbolic expressions with relational components within large state spaces. By applying this framework, we achieved state-of-the-art performance in the recently established symbolic reinforcement learning benchmark games and significantly simplified the processes by introducing a novel metric to measure expression complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrated the practical applicability of our approach in two real-world scenarios, namely traffic light control and robotic grasping. Our findings indicate that the resulting symbolic expressions accurately capture the underlying rules of these tasks and outperform baseline methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/kuo-e/Deep-Relational-Expressions. Ultimately, this work aims to provide actionable insights and practical solutions for agents, which are crucial in various critical applications. Our scheme enhances the development of all-optical diodes and quasi-circulators by introducing a chiral coupling between interresonator links, which generates a comprehensive optical transfer network. Initially, we create a perfect diode by incorporating an uneven detuning in a single-resonator structure to guide light from a source interresonator to an idler interresonator, but this scheme is compromised when the interresonator signal is intensified. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the chiral coupling as a means of connecting and isolating the interresonators. When properly tuned, this scheme allows the flow of signal power while blocking the counter-propagating idler power. Consequently, we expand our concept to a multi-resonator system consisting of N = 5 cavities and design a global optical transfer matrix, enabling the diversion of input signals to specific destinations based on predetermined propagation paths. Furthermore, our multi-channel, chiral-coupled optical transfer network can be utilized to execute a specific optical operation, namely, an XOR logic operation, thereby opening up avenues for the creation of optical computing networks and circuits. Our study yields a highly versatile and adaptable optical tool, capable of executing multiple functions, including actuation of all-optical diodes, quasi-circulators, optical multi-channel logic operators, and optical crossbars. developed a method for automatically translating natural language assertions into

Furthermore, the system is confined to operating within existing infrastructure platforms such as Amazon EC2 and Google Cloud, limiting its versatility. In contrast, the enhanced RCanopus protocol allows users to specify resilient tasks that can be executed across multiple distributed platforms, including those based on peer-to-peer networks and cloud computing. By incorporating client-side tasks that handle input and output data, RCanopus achieves improved robustness against failures. Moreover, RCanopus implements a consensus-based failure detection mechanism that operates at the task level, significantly enhancing its tolerance to transient and persistent failures. The findings showcase the effectiveness of RCanopus in processing diverse tasks across various network and infrastructure settings. updated loss functions and data augmentation, they have yet to integrate an

network to not only localize objects but also determine their detection
probabilities. Leveraging high-confidence and low-confidence priors, as well
as low-confidence and high-confidence posteriors, this proposed model
demonstrates substantial improvements over current methods in object detection
performance with uncertainty estimation. Key benefits include higher
detection accuracy when an uncertainty metric is factored into the object
detection loss, lower false positive rates, and a greater likelihood of
flagging uncertain positives for further human verification. Importantly,
this proposed model surpasses BayesOD in object detection performance while
achieving comparable uncertainty estimation results. Uncertainty estimates on

We designed a compact, plug-and-play device capable of producing high-purity far-forward neutron beams for industrial and medical applications. This device consists of a portable chamber containing liquid-scintillator-detectored detectors and an electric-field generating system. A in-depth study was conducted, incorporating simulated and actual data from the STAR experiment at RHIC. This experimental device uses an air shower mechanism to convert cosmic rays into protons, which are then directed towards the scintillator-based detectors for measurement. A particle identifier was utilized to select neutrons based on energy loss readings. Results showed a notable correlation between detected event triggers and scintillator-based hits. This correlation indicated that the majority of events with connected hits were indeed produced by neutrons. Moreover, trace amounts of events were seen to be linked to gamma rays. Calculations of neutron flux showed variations depending on the angle of observation, a factor influenced significantly by the geometry of the detecting system. This experimental device was found to be effective in generating focused beams of neutrons, and these results have facilitated recent industrial applications. This paper proposes a novel skeleton-based neural network, termed SkyNet, with a pyramidal-like skeleton design. By graduating the channel numbers of its compact middle layers gradually, SkyNet enhances its representation capacity while reducing computational complexity. Specifically, SkyNet utilizes lightweight SkyBlock, a unique block with exclusive filters, to refine its features within the shallow sections. Additionally, SkyNet incorporates SkySpatial, a highly efficient spatial block with efficient convolutional layers, to extract subtle details efficiently. Furthermore, SkyNet incorporates SkyPool, a novel pooling layer with filters, to prolong the feature map length and thereby improve performance. Comprehensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate that SkyNet surpasses other skeletal networks in terms of accuracy while exhibiting a significantly higher inference speed and reduced parameters. Specifically, on the ImageNet dataset, SkyNet achieves an top-1 accuracy of $78.36\%$ with an inference speed of $266.67$ FPS and $25$ MB parameters. In comparison, SkyNet outperforms various skeletal networks such as SnakeBlock $78.34\%$ at $275.36$ FPS and $27$ MB, CoSnake $77.44\%$ at $240.33$ FPS and $30$ MB, Snake $76.94\%$ at $210$ FPS and $35$ MB, and SkyNet-$\mathrm{SNN}$ $79.22\%$ at $248.22$ FPS and $21.66$ MB. Abstract interpretation has long been recognized as a fundamental technique in program analysis, used for precise flow analysis, error detection, and program optimization. The efficiency of abstract interpretation directly affects its applicability to large programs. Speedups in this process would be particularly useful in programming environments. The majority of abstract interpreators employ a first-order approximation of programs, based on their operational semantics. The operational semantics model accurately represents the dynamic behavior of programs but generates extremely complex logical expressions resulting in considerable computation time. To address this, a proposed modification accelerates the abstract interpretation process by substituting these complex logical expressions with simpler ones. The substitution is based on applying basic abstract operators from a finite dictionary. The new method has been structurally validated and demonstrated with three concrete examples, showcasing a 50% performance gain over the traditional first-order approach. The theoretical justification relies on the established relationship between first-order logic and many-valued first-order logics, allowing for equivalent translations. Consequently, the introduction of the abstraction operator framework enables the representation of the substitution effect, effectively reducing the complexity of the abstract logical expression. This results in better efficiency, as illustrated by the examples, or equal efficiency when appropriate choices are made. The theoretical analysis further shows that this method has the capability to handle context-free abstractions, offering a new benchmark for comparison. The integration of higher-order abstractions also presents an opportunity for enhancements, as examined in the conclusion. The abstract interpretation framework has significant implications in program analysis, with many subfields benefiting from its use. The proposed modification has the potential to yield many more substantial applications and should be taken into consideration when first-order logic is applied in program analysis, as it may lead to the development of more effective programs. This new method is then compared with the linear response theory in generating coherent states within a two-level system subject to a coherent drive. Additionally, by modulating the quantum correction terms, it becomes possible to control their magnitude and sign. This method may be further explored in creating other types of coherent states by adjusting the quantum correction terms. Moreover, its applicability in generating multi-photon coherent states demonstrates its promising potential for use. Lastly, an interesting perspective arises regarding the connection between the quantum closure relation and the quantum eraser, suggesting an opportunity for further in-depth analysis and research. While human feedback is necessary for any recommendation system, traditional approaches have centered around text and rating scores.  Recent research aimed to incorporate interactive elements like reviews and that rely on textual context to determine relevance.  Our study deviates from this trend by recognizing that textual features within reviews have a hard time being accurately translated into numerical values, and thus we cannot rely solely on rating-based information to guide interactive learning.  Our proposed solution involves treating review-based features as key drivers of user feedback and combining textual and numerical features equally to inform interaction signals.  Our framework introduces two new concepts: a numerical feature-weighted approach to interaction learning that combines user feedback on items with features from those items, and a feature-weighted approach to item re-ranking that concurrently learns user features and item features while producing top-recommended items. A mesh's computational accuracy depends heavily on the quality of its individual elements. Underpinning mesh generation algorithms are rules ensuring element quality. However, these algorithms often struggle with complex domains, necessitating manual intervention to create a fully meshable subdomain. To address this issue, we propose a new approach for automatically identifying and simplifying sensitive areas by measuring element-star quality. This method involves analyzing the element-star geometric properties to identify regions where mesh generation algorithms fail due to poor element quality. We compare our method with two existing techniques, employing the element-star geometry to assess mesh quality, in both 2D and 3D settings. Testing these methods on several benchmarks demonstrated that two of the methods fail to detect some areas requiring domain simplification, whereas our approach successfully identified all required regions, though not all simplifications were necessary. Additionally, we evaluated the effectiveness of our element-star based domain simplification approach in a 3D setting and compared its impact on mesh generation algorithm performance in both absolute mesh quality and computational time. The results show that domain simplification led to significantly improved mesh quality, increased efficiency, and reduced artificial errors in parallel mesh generation algorithms. To support further research, we have made our high-quality meshes and corresponding C++ mesh generation tools available for public use. This work contributes a novel method for automatic domain simplification in both 2D and 3D mesh generation by leveraging element-star quality analysis. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the beneficial impact of this simplification on mesh generation algorithm performance, resulting in improved mesh quality, decreased computational time, and reduced artificial errors. Our method also enables mesh generation algorithms to effectively tackle challenging domains, overcoming previous limitations driven by element quality restrictions. To ensure reproducibility and facilitation of future research, we have made our mesh generation code and associated dataset comprising over 60 benchmarks, including both basic and complex domain types (2D and 3D), publicly available for use. For 3D domain simplification, we have employed an iterative geometric algorithm adjusting the mesh node locations to improve element quality. We have also validated the effectiveness of our approach by demonstrating its ability to significantly enhance mesh generation algorithm results. Consequently, we have made our mesh generation tools publicly available for use, with the associated repository link provided below in the references. This research contributes a novel method for automatic domain simplification in both 2D and 3D mesh generation based on element-star quality analysis, with public access to the associated mesh generation code and 3D mesh dataset. Knowledge graph link prediction has emerged as a vital application for enhancing knowledge graph completeness by forecasting unobserved links between entities extracted from text through relation extraction.  Recent studies have proven the effectiveness of leveraging context from nearby triangles in this process.  However, conventional methods relying on triangular context for link prediction lack an essential understanding of the underlying relation between the entities involved.  To address this limitation, we propose a novel link predictor, Dubbed Context-Invariant Relation-Aware Link Predictor (Cirap), which incorporates the insights of relations in the knowledge graph by filtering out distracting context and identifying entities' commonalities.  As a result, Cirap can give more significance to the specific relationships between the entities and ignore irrelevant contextual information.  To further refine the quality of the links predicted, Cirap also employs a novel filter mechanism called the Cirap Filter, which uses weakly-supervised labels to eliminate incorrect predictions.  Thoroughly-tested on public datasets, our experiments demonstrate that Cirap can outperform state-of-the-art methods in link prediction accuracy, while the accompanying results show that the relationships predicted by Cirap are in line with the actual patterns observed in the knowledge graph they are meant to enhance.  Additional support for our approach can be found at https://github.com/minminuser/CiRAP.  This research reveals that Cirap's capacity to identify entities' commonalities contributes significantly to its ability to link prediction.  Moreover, the relationships predicted by Cirap can be considered context-independent, which makes them usable across various contexts.  Ultimately, the relationships predicted by Cirap can be considered as interpretable as they align more closely with the actual patterns observed in the knowledge graph they are meant to enhance.  This research underscores the entities' commonalities shared among the knowledge graph relations as a vital application of knowledge graph link prediction.  Moreover, the relationships predicted by Cirap can be considered as actionable insights that may help train other down-stream models and applications to fill knowledge graph gaps.  Finally, the relationships predicted by Cirap can be considered as abstract concepts that may offer new avenues for end-users and developers to better comprehend the underlying knowledge graph mechanisms through interactive visual interfaces.  This research may open doors for new applications of knowledge graph link prediction to provide users with a deeper, more meaningful understanding of the knowledge graph. Agency was defined as an object's ability to act independently, while animacy was seen as a combination of that agency and also the object's responsiveness to its environment. In a series of experiments using both computer-generated scenes and real images of animals and vehicles, we analyzed participants' classifications of these objects on both the agency and animacy spectra. A type B QPO showed frequency variability from 12 to 35 Hz, while a type C QPO showed frequency variability from 5.3 to 7.3 Hz. Furthermore, the authors discovered correlations between the frequency of the type C QPO and the hard colour flux, along with opposing correlations for the amplitude of the type B QPO. These findings suggest a potential connection between the physical characteristics of accretion flows and the generation of QPOs. Moreover, the authors hypothesize that topological defects such as cosmic strings could explain the observed type C QPO frequencies. However, the origin of the very low frequency QPOs (VLF QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients remains unclear, leading the authors to speculate that the very low frequency type C QPOs may be a VLF QPO. Similar to previous studies, the authors propose that the VLF QPO could serve as a direct probe of the characteristics of an inner accretion disc near a black hole. Consequently, the frequency of the VLF QPO has shown a shift to higher values during the hard to soft transition. One of the main challenges in multi-agent reinforcement learning is zero-shot coordination, which involves being able to coordinate with other agents without any prior knowledge of specific situations. Empowerment, a measure that assesses the ability of one agent to influence another, can be a useful tool in overcoming coordination difficulties. However, the existing definition of Empowerment is not suitable for use in ML frameworks due to its analytical nature. In this research, a transfer empowerment metric is introduced to capture the commonalities between different scenarios. Transfer empowerment can be utilized as a target for optimization, resulting in more resilient coordination mechanisms across various situations. Experimental results using the two-killer line formation benchmark confirm that optimizing transfer empowerment yields better outcomes in zero-shot coordination settings compared to traditional policy gradient methods. Additionally, the proposed metric contributes to a deeper understanding of the commonalities between different scenarios in multi-agent reinforcement learning and provides a valuable tool for controlling the level of transfer in multi-agent systems. Although the proposed target is more practical than the original empowerment metric, which requires a computationally infeasible search over policies, it is still challenging to optimize transfer empowerment directly due to its analytical nature. As such, the existing definition is approximated by modeling the agent's communication with its environment using a Gaussian process. By modeling the agent's environment, a more feasible objective function for optimization is derived, resulting in a simpler and more practical target for transfer empowerment. It investigates the properties of this cohomology theory, focusing on its deformations, classifications, and representations, especially examining how a 2-Lie algebra's extensions and central expansions relate to its first cohomology groups. simultaneous extraction of both spatial features and linear and non-linear
image segments. In contrast to traditional methods, our proposal can operate
entirely within the multiplicative domain, thereby improving robustness to both
illumination fluctuations and noisy conditions. Moreover, both feature detection
and matching processes can be synthesized into a single, highly parallel operation

neuron architecture. Experimental evaluations confirm our approach outperforms
conventional techniques in both detection and translation tasks under various

is publicly accessible at https://github.com/utkakansoy/multiplicative-image-feature.

applicability in linear domains. Furthermore, we propose a novel way of

underlying theory, code, and MuFe dataset can be found at https://github.com/utkakansoy/mufe.

The shape of an active region's magnetic field can be better understood with 3D information, but current 2D vector magnetic field maps lack this dimensionality due to their inherent nature of providing surface-normal components of magnetic fields, not vectors themselves. To address this, a new approach has been developed to enhance the accuracy of these maps by taking into consideration the space occupied by magnetic fields parallel to the surface, which is essential for capturing active region shapes' overall structures. Focusing on the most prominent active regions of 2020, an analysis showed that this improvement could lead to a 15% boost in correlation between observed white-light flares and magnetic field strength, ultimately enabling the prediction of these flares based on 3D field shapes. As a result, this technique could eventually enable the forecasting of a significant portion of flares that will be detectable in future space missions such as VERIS and MAGNETO. We investigate the rate of convergence for time-averages in Ergodic Theorems associated with a matrix $A$, specifically when $A$ is a real $2 \times 2$ matrix lacking a spectral gap. We demonstrate that a variant of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, developed by Adams and Guionneau, yields convergence rates comparable to those in a theorem proved by Burghardt. Notably, while von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem provides convergence rates dependent on the sequence of time $n$, progressing to infinity, the variant considers convergence rates dependent on the sequence $\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max}(A^n)}$, where $\lambda_{\max}(A^n)$ represents the maximum eigenvalue of the matrix $A^n$, or a related expression for iterated averages of $A$. This modified Ergodic Theorem, tailored to specific classes of matrices $A$, notably includes cases of matrices $A$ having a spectral gap and those related to quadratic systems. Furthermore, it has also been applied to analyze convergence rates in a sampling method for quadratic integrals over irrational orbits. We also establish that for certain $2 \times 2$ matrices $A$, also of integer entries, for which a growth rate of $A^n$ can be computed as non-constant, the rate of convergence of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem remains inferior to that of an Ergodic Theorem developed by Burghardt. In order to prove these results, we have constructed a set of bounds on the maximum eigenvalue of the matrix $A^n$, or a related expression for iterated averages of $A$, whose characterisation, although found to be acceptable for low-dimensional cases, appears to be inherently restricted to that of matrices $A$ consisting of two-by-two entries. We have also observed that a related theorem proved by Burghardt provides a general expression for the convergence rate of iterated averages of a matrix $A$, or at least an upper bound, applicable to a broader class of matrices $A$. In order to establish a lower bound on the convergence rate of iterated averages of $A$, we have introduced an auxiliary matrix $\tilde{A}$, which can be expressed as $\tilde{A} = (I - B^{-1}AB)^{-1}B^{-1}A$, or, equivalently, $\tilde{A} = A B^{-1} (I - A B^{-1})$, or expressed in Jordan normal form

This paper presents a novel spatio-temporal event detection framework capable of handling arbitrary-sized events. The approach employs a deep neural network consisting of a two-part model, combining a convolutional neural network for extracting spatial features and a recurrent neural network for handling temporal data. Events of any scale can be input into the system, which utilizes predefined masks to maintain a uniform size for spatial features and the same number of channels within the temporal feature map. A proposed self-attention mechanism subsequently aggregates spatial information based on event duration, varying event size, and frequency, thus identifying multiple types of spatio-temporal events in real-time traffic video streams. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our method over existing approaches, showcasing its effectiveness in detecting diverse events. Furthermore, this paper suggests an innovative and efficient strategy for continuously adapting event detectors in the face of changing data distributions. Evaluations involving an actual attention mechanism confirm its efficacy and provide insights on optimizing hyperparameters, such as the number of recurrent network frames. The paper also examines operator performance characteristics, such as latency and throughput, thus offering practical implementation suggestions. Based on experimental findings, it is estimated that our method can process around 30 events per second. Although this may seem relatively low, further optimization of hardware components and operator architectures could significantly improve performance. A critical component in bidding algorithms is risk tolerance, which ensures that proposed graphs accurately represent the problem at hand. By utilizing expert knowledge, we develop a formulated approach that measures risk tolerance and presents adjustable criteria for quantifying desirable network features. This method assesses a graph's modularity and clustering density to model risk tendency. With these definitions reworked into linear terms, we formulate a coordinate descent framework for optimization that incorporates constraints on adjustable network characteristics. The formulation's integration with a gradient descent algorithm using a task-specific loss function leads to the development of our proposed DES algorithm. Experimental evaluations in two fields demonstrate that DES outperforms state-of-the-art methods with a 9% density improvement and a 25% reduction in loss on labeled datasets. Additionally, DES' generated networks on two datasets meet the requirements for density, connectivity, and similarity to training data, thereby facilitating its application to new tasks through inductive learning. DES' density graphs also exhibit a 7% increase in performance over baseline methods on three benchmark datasets. Importantly, DES offers a flexible task assignment mechanism depending on network characteristics, which can be used to achieve improved performance on new tasks with previously seen inputs. DES' potential in demand response systems is also explored through the application of a heating and cooling request task. The outcomes of experiments conducted on 187 requests from 59 customers indicate that DES's proposed networks result in a 9.72% improvement in a key performance indicator as opposed to baseline methods. By extending the number of customers in the system, we found that DES' density networks allow the assignment of a 3.86% higher number of customers compared to baseline methods. Ultimately, DES' network density and performance are shown to be correlated according to a correlation value of 0.60. The code associated with DES is written in the Python programming language and is publicly accessible via the following link: https://github.com/jaidesh132001/DES. This code facilitates the reproduction of experiments and the adjustment of DES algorithm parameters. By utilizing these code components, we found that altering the prior weights on density and risk tolerance allows for a 1.13 correlation value change, thereby highlighting the flexibility of DES algorithm parameters. Similarly, we found that adjusting the number of customers in the demand response experiment leads to a 0.03 correlation value change. Conversely, we found that modifying the loss function associated with a task results in a minimal correlation value change of 0.18. Recent research revealed that the subsystem Wigner negativity of a bipartite Gaussian state can serve as an indicator of quantum correlations absent in local unitary transformations. Consequently, this work investigates whether these correlations are essential for producing Wigner negativity in a subsystem when sharing a non-Gaussian state. To accomplish this, we apply displacement operations as a means of simulating local unitary transformations. Through this simulation, we observe that, under the majority of circumstances, the application of displacements alone is sufficient to produce Wigner negativity in a subsystem. However, there exist exceptional scenarios where these displacements fail to yield negativity, provided that the shared non-Gaussian state possesses certain properties. These properties include possessing at least one conjugate frequency mode or exhibiting an excessive number of excitations. Moreover, our results demonstrate that when using displacements to simulate local unitary transformations, the Wigner negativity in a subsystem can be viewed as an indicator of quantum correlations absent in collective rotations, rather than the traditional unitary transformations. These findings contribute to an enhanced understanding of the subsystem Wigner negativity as an indicator of quantum correlations in bipartite systems. Moreover, our results open the door to utilizing experiments based on photoelectric measurements to assess these correlations. Importantly, our work further elucidates the unique properties of bipartite Gaussian states, whose pure forms do not contain any quantum correlations yet require non-trivial unitary transformations to produce Wigner negativity in a subsystem. To access this phenomenon, our work leverages a combination of displacement and rotation operations while revealing their respective roles in producing Wigner negativity in a subsystem. Furthermore, we show that the application of these operations can induce an excessive excitation in the subsystem responsible for Wigner negativity, an outcome that occurs in bipartite Gaussian states. Importantly, our work derives a condition to determine the ability of the phase-point measurement to detect quantum correlations in bipartite systems, an area of research with potential for resource realization in quantum information processing. In quantum key distribution, the amount of information an unknown quantum state contains is measured by the min-entropy. We show that the average min-entropy of a random number generator restricts the maximum secure transmission rate in the BB84 protocol. Our findings highlight the significance of the random number generator's quality in quantum communication systems. We also examine how the characteristics of the noise affecting the photons sent establish an essential limit for the average min-entropy of the random number generator, thus further underlining the importance of the random number generator's quality in quantum communications. Finally, we discuss how to accurately determine the average min-entropy of a random number generator, taking into account practical considerations. Specifically, we investigate whether it's feasible to determine the average min-entropy from the distribution of individual random bits. Our analysis shows that, while the average min-entropy can be estimated relatively easily, the conditional min-entropy required for secure key exchange is more difficult to determine, primarily due to the extensive resources needed to sample from the probability distribution. Our main tool for examining the average min-entropy is the quantum reverse reconciliation protocol, which enables fast sampling from the probability distribution. In current waveguide QED studies, N-photon scattering matrices have been directly calculated from quantum dot parameters, however, little attention has been given to delayed coherent feedback, a key component in advanced quantum control. We show that incorporating coherent feedback changes the Hamiltonian of the quantum dot, resulting in a new parameterization for N-photon scattering matrices. We derive an exact matrix formula based on the original quantum dot parameters, and reveal that certain interactions become suppressed under coherent feedback, providing increased flexibility in quantum engineering. Our work offers a general method to update scattering matrices in systems with feedback. Furthermore, we apply this formula to investigate the delayed feedback effect on single-photon scattering in a quantum dot, and examine the trade-off between single-photon efficiency and multi-photon purity, and determine the optimal delay time for maximum performance. Our study is also validated by modeling a quantum teleportation protocol with delayed feedback, and show that teleported fidelity can be boosted by incorporating coherent feedback, approaching the ideal quantum teleportation. The results of this research are implemented in a Python package named 'qdot', which provides a efficient way to compute N-photon scattering matrices in waveguide QED systems with feedback. The 'qdot' package is available at https://github.com/chunhuel/qdot. We believe that our study and the 'qdot' package will facilitate the design of quantum devices based on waveguide QED. With the 'qdot' package, users with basic Python knowledge can reproduce our results and design custom quantum devices. Furthermore, 'qdot' provides a range of pre-defined models that can be used to compute scattering matrices, and offer an efficient way to design quantum circuits based on pre-characterized QDs. As a result, 'qdot' offers added value to the existing literature, and provides new insights into the role of delayed coherent feedback in quantum systems. Sub-GeV dark matter interacting with matter other than dark matter is referred to as boosted dark matter. This paper focuses on measuring the spin-dependent interaction of boosted dark matter. Since direct detection experiments are challenging for this type of interaction, we instead examine how it can be determined from constraints placed on the charged lepton electric dipole moment and from nuclear decay data. We discovered that the spin-dependent interaction of boosted dark matter is more sensitive to the model's parameters than a contact interaction. This increased sensitivity could help us learn more about the properties of the dark matter particle. We also found that our results for the electronic electric dipole moment can serve as a crucial constraint for certain parameter values, while nuclear decay data may set a more significant limit for certain other parameter values. This investigation is the first to examine the spin-dependent interaction of boosted dark matter in this way. Additionally, we extended the developed analytical expressions to a specific type of dark matter interaction called vector-fermion mediation. This interaction is particularly relevant because it is linked to a type of dark matter particle called vector-like leptons. This study examines the interplay of frustration and nonlinear effects in ferroions and ferromagnons within the context of classical spin systems. To this end, a comprehensive review of recent findings regarding the nonlinear dynamics of ferroions and ferromagnons is provided, with a notable emphasis on nonlinear wave development, instability of steady states, and topological order. Key topics are discussed, including those where nonlinearities drive topological order, cases where wave structures naturally arise due to system instability, and scenarios where nonlinearities hinder topological order. Ultimately, a comparative analysis is performed to distinguish and free the concepts of nonlinearities and frustrations. Lastly, hypothetical directions for further investigation are outlined. This work is a tribute to L. D. Landau, celebrating his enduring influence in the physics of classical systems over 80 years since his seminal work on spin wave instability.

Research in Ref. 37 demonstrates a significant connection between the spectral analysis of large random Hermitian matrices and the stationary states of unitary quantum dynamics. As a result, the eigenvalue distribution of these matrices can now be studied within a unitary framework. Utilizing this finding, the present work shows that the eigenvalue spectrum of 2x2 random Hermitian matrices spans the entire real line when their band width is sufficiently narrow. Conversely, the eigenvalue spectrum was previously proven to be entirely real when the band width was sufficiently narrow in the tri-diagonal case. Additionally, the present work examines the critical band width instance where the eigenvalue spectrum undergoes a transition from being entirely real to entirely real and complex. Through the use of a self-consistent equation approach, the occurrence of this transition was previously studied in Ref. 25. A more in-depth analysis of this equation is carried out here, resulting in the determination of a critical band width value that differs from the instance identified in Ref. 25. A numerical investigation has also been conducted to validate the eigenvalue distribution. The eigenvalue distribution was then compared with the findings of Refs. 27-34, which relate to the stationary states of unitary quantum dynamics. Consistency between the eigenvalue distribution and the findings of Refs. 27-34 was observed. A connection between the eigenvalue distribution and the dynamics of quantum systems was established, resulting in the determination of stationary-state complexity and entropies for unitary quantum dynamics. An in-depth analysis of this complexity and entropy measure has been carried out. Furthermore, the present work examines the critical complexity and entropy instance where the dynamics of a quantum system transitions from ordered to disordered. Various distinct features of these systems have been identified through this analysis, including an isolated island in the complexity landscape and the dynamics of disentangled quantum systems. An in-depth analysis of these isolated islands and disentangled systems has also been carried out. Finally, the present work investigates the applicability of the eigenvalue distribution findings to the dynamics of quantum systems and identifies general characteristics applicable to all qubits. These characteristics include the occurrence of critical complexity and entropy instances in the dynamics of quantum systems. An additional numerical investigation has been conducted to validate the eigenvalue distribution and the findings of Refs. 27-34. Consistency between the eigenvalue distribution and the findings of Refs. 27-34 has been observed. Ultimately, the present work contributes to a deeper understanding of quantum systems, enabling greater control and efficiency

Machine learning models are being scrutinized for their accountability, one reason being the model's interpretability. Understanding how these models work is crucial for building trust. This research delves into developing a universal interpretation method for deep neural networks across various domains, leveraging a standard gradient-based technique, and applies it to a range of tasks including visual classification, natural language processing, and computer vision. Furthermore, this research touches on explaining model predictions by identifying areas of importance within the input data. Lastly, it attempts to answer a critical question: whether a neural network's decision-making process can be compared to that of a human, by employing both quantitative measures and qualitative assessments to evaluate the reliability and accuracy of the interpretations derived from the models. Extreme events in various fields such as finance and meteorology have been the focal point of recent statistical analysis. This research provides an overview of three Bayesian estimators initially developed to specialize in extreme events. By incorporating expert judgment, these estimators can offer precise estimates of parameters including the extreme portion of data. The primary goal of this paper is to examine how the estimation varies with the tuning parameter m that underlies each of these estimators. The practical utility of these models is assessed through applications to real-world datasets. Specifically, the Estimation using the Generalized Pareto Distribution (EGP) is evaluated by analyzing 95-year records of the Schriever flood gauge located in Alberta, Canada. The Estimation for Extreme Values (EVE) is applied to a 50-year dataset of annual maximum rainfall in Toronto, Ontario. The Estimation based on the Generalized Extreme Value distribution (GEV) is used for the analysis of annual maximum winds at a weather station in Calgary, Alberta. The results reveal that the eigenvalue m plays a crucial role in shaping the estimated posterior distributions of the parameters. Furthermore, the convergence issues can be mitigated by incorporating priors on the parameter space. The estimated posterior distributions demonstrate the potential for each model to accurately capture the uncertainty associated with the parameter of interest. The comparative analysis highlights the importance of model selection to evaluate the relative efficacy of these estimators. The research indicates that the Bayesian estimators can offer valuable insights when expert judgment is incorporated, but model selection may be required to gauge the reliability of the estimates depending on the dataset in question. This dataset comprises 211,979 sentences, each containing information about a particular entertainment topic, and its predecessor, ATOMIC, comprised 342,083 sentences. We outline a major data processing pipeline for the Hi-GAL survey, a key component of the ESA's Gaia legacy project, and examine the initial outcomes of the data reduction pipeline for the Hi-GAL survey maps. The pipeline leverages a blended approach, merging the results of individual Green Bank Filter Bank (GBFB) correlators to generate around 360,000 megapolarisation maps per scanning beam through 11 different GBFB configurations, resulting in approximately 3.9 million maps per survey tile. To produce high-quality, fully sampled maps for each of the 423,729 Hi-GAL survey tiles, we employed an advanced co-adding technique, utilising the 16 unique frequencies provided by the Executive Information System, a custom-made deconvolution algorithm for deblurring and deconvolving the data, and a rigorous quality assessment process to ensure the reliability of our final maps. The data reduction pipeline for the Hi-GAL survey has achieved outstanding results, producing fully sampled, high-quality 466 arcsecond resolution CO 1-0 maps for every Hi-GAL survey tile, accompanied by corresponding CO 0-0, 4-kpc kinematic and spectral maps, all of which boast exceptional precision. The resulting data set features an impressive 3.9 million megapolarisation maps per tile, making the Hi-GAL survey data significantly more sensitive than the Gaia mission' s extragalactic background flux limited map. The data set has been made publicly available through the Gaia archive at www.sussex.ac.uk/astro/dag1/gaiadre/. Furthermore, the pipeline sources for the Hi-GAL survey data reduction are hosted at www.sussex.ac.uk/astro/dag1/gaiadre/software/, accompanied by a comprehensive data visualisation platform at www.uvdata.org.uk/. UVData is an open source, general-purpose data access and visualisation library for supporting the analysis of UV radio interferometry data, including legacy sky mapping missions such as Gaia. UVData boasts extensive re-usability, transparency and reproducibility, coupled with native support for over 30 major radio telescopes worldwide. The data set has undergone rigorous quality assessment, leading to the establishment of a comprehensive, publicly available catalogue providing precise CO emission flux density estimates for nearly 2.8 million Hi-GAL survey sources, up to a flux density threshold of around 30 Jy km s$^{-1}$, based on the final maps. The catalogue was officially released on the Gaia archive

The diverse chemical properties observed in the galactic globular clusters lie at the core of understanding their intricate history. We utilized the latest APoGEE data to examine elemental variations within the metal-abundant globular cluster NGC 4140 by analyzing 2025 high-resolution spectra covering multiple elements. Our findings reveal substantial variations in key light elements such as calcium, scandium, and titanium alongside the already established variations in other elements like iron, chromium, and zinc. Through further analysis, we were able to determine the stellar lifespan required to create the observed patterns. Our results suggest that stars within NGC 4140 underwent multiple episodes of star formation spanning 250 million years. Furthermore, our findings indicate that supernovae played a pivotal role in shaping the galactic cluster's unique chemical profile, particularly in the early stages of star formation. Our observations also reveal the presence of vertically dispersed populations across multiple epochs, stretching back over 7 billion years. These discoveries challenge the established, relatively uniform star formation model of this galactic cluster. Instead, our data suggest that galactic cluster formation involved more intricate and nuanced processes, including the possible merger of smaller star clusters. These new insights have significantly expanded our understanding of galactic cluster formation and evolution. Nonetheless, our study also highlights the scarcity of high-resolution spectroscopic data across the galactic cluster's entire depth, underscoring the significant potential of the galactic bulge's evolution to inform future astronomical research.}].\\

In one-dimensional physical systems, the relationship between error rates and means square displacement is well documented, resembling the speed-accuracy trade-offs proposed by Fitts and by Lashley. We examined this relationship in the context of stochastic walks in discrete spaces with various degrees of constraint. Our findings showed that multiple error rates converge as the discrete space becomes more restrictive. Additionally, we derived a general formula for the speed-accuracy trade-offs in this scenario, validated through numerical simulations. These results were also applied to two specific cases: stochastic walks on a ring with fixed step size, and means square displacement being investigated with probabilistic stepping mechanisms. Further investigation using mean field theory suggested the existence of a critical value beyond which these trade-offs become impossible, while simulations revealed the corresponding time convergence patterns. Lastly, our study involved analyzing speed-accuracy trade-offs for two specific stochastic walks: the Brownian rotor and the trans-dimensional walk, discussing their characteristics and identifying areas for future improvement. These findings shed new light on the speed-accuracy trade-offs, offering insights useful to both theoretical physicists and engineers designing systems and devices. Furthermore, our research demonstrates a viable approach to merging statistical physics and machine learning.  A novel open-source Python package, PhysMod, was developed parallel to this research to facilitate the demonstration of these concepts and the implementation of various stochastic models. The package consists of 24 distinct physical models and 26 optimization techniques, as well as 3 tools for evaluating the performance of these models, all of which are available under the terms of the open-source license. The code can be accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/julien Palmer/PhysMod. 

Key words: speed-accuracy trade-offs, stochastic walks, stochastic differential equations, mean field theory, open-source programming, NumPy and PyALPYt libraries. 

Please refer to the report for the complete list of the author's contributions including the mathematical derivations, the design and the coding of the open-source package PhysMod, as well as the technical and the scientific contributions.

Specifically, we find that the fifth transfer excels at distinguishing the effects of certain operations on polynomial algebras, while the tenth transfer excels at understanding differences involving power operations on these algebras. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that the transfers are particularly potent when analyzing differences involving power operations on polynomial algebras. Moreover, we observe that the transfers can be attenuated by certain operations, but only for specific types of projective spaces and up to a certain degree, which is roughly around 63. Lastly, we find that the transfers are ineffective at distinguishing non-zero differences in several scenarios, including cubic extensions and quadratic extensions, but again, only up to a certain degree, which is roughly around 63. 
This research makes use of state-of-theart techniques in algebraic topology, such as the detection theorem for algebraic transfers, the Lee spectrum, the Hopf induction spectrum, the Adem multiplication table, and the detection theorem for algebraic transfers again, along with a dash of combinatorial number theory.

As part of this study, a specialized hydrogen gas cell was constructed specifically for the experiment. This study proposes a novel scheme that modifies traditional channel codes to insert authentication, using codes with a single error correction. Traditional methods insert authentication by introducing dedicated control packets that are detected and handled outside standard decoding processes. In contrast, our scheme authenticates data transmitted over general channels without needing these control packets, thereby declining a measure of channel capacity known as the authenticator's gain. Under the assumption that these errors do not affect the overall transmission, our scheme effectively serves as a form of public-key encryption. Using specific types of channels, we demonstrate that our scheme can transmit messages at a rate approaching optimal levels as the transmitted length increases, while maintaining a coding rate that vanishes asymptotically. This means that our scheme can transmit authentic data almost as efficiently as channel capacity, while only dedicating a small fraction of capacity for authentication. As an additional contribution, we show that our scheme can be implemented using shorter transmission lengths called authenticating blocks, without necessitating channel state information for authentication. In this variant, we demonstrate that the total transmission length required for authenticating $k$ messages can be made proportional to $k$, while maintaining asymptotically negligible coding rates and authenticating block lengths that both vanish as $k$ increases. This problem was inspired by a 2013 conference paper titled "Authentication in the channel" [IGA13], which posed an asymptotically negligible coding rate when using single-error correction codes. The current study can be viewed as a significant extension of that work, addressing the theoretical challenges mentioned within. In particular, our scheme can be viewed as a form of "almost public-channel encryption," a concept discussed in the mentioned conference paper. The current study can be viewed as a significant extension of that work, addressing the theoretical challenges mentioned, while yielding positive outcomes. A distinct, "public-channel" perspective on this problem is presented in the study's conclusion, where we discuss an alternative scheme that achieves authenticable transmission rates that approach the capacity of a public channel as the transmitted length increases, while requiring the ability to signal channel state information. The Brownian motion of particles in periodically varying potential structures is widely found in natural systems. The underlying transport process can be complex, involving interaction effects that contradict simple diffusion. The current study investigates this phenomenon, focusing on scenarios where the underlying periodic potential is tilted and the force caused by the potential exceeds a certain threshold. A mathematical model employing a Fokker-Planck equation and a mean-field approach represents the transport process. Analytical calculations within the mean-field approximation reveal a superdiffusive behavior, characterized by a superdiffusion exponent of 3/2, both in the presence and absence of particle interactions. The validity of this analysis is confirmed through direct numerical simulations. As the strength of interactions changes, the transport exponent may shift. For instance, if the interaction parameter is set to 1, the transport could be close to normal diffusion, whereas increasing the interaction parameter can lead to a transition towards normal diffusion from initially superdiffusive behavior. The study concludes by outlining a range of potential research areas where this superdiffusive phenomenon may be observed. The superdiffusive behavior could significantly impact these systems, causing their characteristic distances to grow over time, leading to remarkably diverse and irregular observations. A deeper understanding of the superdiffusive behavior, caused by the superdiffusion exponent of 3/2, may reveal more intricate features and functionality in these systems. The superdiffusion may lead to notable delays in the typical time required for particles to reach certain targets over long periods. The identification of these delays may unlock a richer diversity of system responses. The study suggests that superdiffusion may be prevalent in nature, and recognizing this phenomenon may allow for the advancement of data analysis techniques, enabling researchers to identify superdiffusive behavior in diverse scenarios. The recognition of superdiffusion may also unlock a wealth of additional natural occurrences within the relevant scientific disciplines, such as sociology, biology, physics, and chemistry. The study outlines a range of potential research directions for further exploration of superdiffusive phenomena, involving the investigation of target retrieval times, the role of global optimization, the analysis of system responses, and the impact of interactions, both in the presence or absence of specific threshold parameters. Automated document summarization is a well-defined task where a system condenses lengthy documents into concise, abridged versions. The majority of existing summ systems employ neural approaches pre-trained via masked language modeling, such as BERT, to generate summaries in a predict-one-word-at-a-time manner. Nevertheless, these models pose significant computation requirements, making it impractical to employ traditional greedy prediction methods during inference. As a result, they cannot effectively exploit past decoding history or utilize a decoder pre-trained separately. To overcome these limitations, we develop GAE-ISumm, a novel summarization system that pre-trains a generic autoencoder (GAE) separately to encode documents and decode summaries in a sequence-to-sequence fashion. The pre-trained GAE is then fine-tuned via policy gradient methods to improve summary quality. In practice, we hybridize the BERT-based ISumm decoder with the pre-trained GAE and use a sampling-based decoding method to reduce computation costs. Meanwhile, for the family of logistic maps based on the cosine function, the corresponding transfer operators show a decay in correlations at a strictly geometric rate. Furthermore, for certain non-uniformly expanding systems, including a notable example of a countable iteration map, the transfer operators form a dual set of $\ell^p$-H\"older spaces, where $p>0$, leading to the conclusion that these systems support an $\ell^p$-integrable invariant density for all $p\geq0$. Additionally, the invariant density based on a polynomial is uniquely associated with the system in question. Lastly, the tempering effect in the transfer operators of the sine family provides the necessary tools to prove the existence of $C^{\alpha}$-H\"older eigenfunctions, critical in constructing an explicit expression for the spectral measure. This spectral measure has a particular property where its density of eigenvalues grows not faster than a geometric series. Consequently, this leads to the existence of $C^{\alpha}$-H\"older eigenfunctions under the assumption of a Gibbs measure, also enabling the existence of an explicit optimal coupling between iterates and the spectral measure itself. A general covering array with parameters (q1, q2,..., qm; m; t) has the property that for every subset of size t, all possible combinations of unique elements are present within the array's rows. In contrast, a uniform covering array adds the requirement that each element of q1, q2,..., qm appears together with all possible combinations of unique elements within the array's rows. This study investigates the smallest uniform general covering arrays with parameters (q1, q2,..., qm; m; t), focusing particularly on cases with m = 2 and 3, while also exploring asymptotic uniform general covering arrays with parameters (q1, q2,..., m; m; t). Uniform general covering arrays with smallest sizes for m = 2, 3, and general cases with m > 3 are presented, in addition to combinatorial upper bounds for such arrays. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in using multiple targeted treatments for individual patients, based on their unique characteristics. However, identifying which patients benefit from a specific treatment is often challenging due to small sample sizes within subgroups. To address this issue, researchers have developed statistical tools to identify which subgroups experience significant benefits from a treatment, while maintaining a controlled rate of false discoveries. Building upon existing methods, we have developed two novel approaches, using Bayesian estimation and frequentist inference, to detect the average treatment effect in targeted groups. Our proposed methods leverage functional mixing models and enable us to adjust for multiple testing and group correlations. Moreover, we employ minimum statistics to incorporate genomic differential expression into our testing procedures, reducing the rate of false discoveries and improving the ability to replicate findings. Through simulations, we have demonstrated that these methods can detect significant treatment effects in smaller groups, maintain a controlled rate of false discoveries, and perform similarly to existing top-ranked methods. Furthermore, we have illustrated the practical value of these methods in a real-world example, using data from a targeted trial to identify which subgroups of patients with rheumatoid arthritis respond best to different treatments. Our findings have practical implications, as they enable researchers to seamlessly switch between identifying individual subgroups and detecting multiple targeted groups. Moreover, we have developed user-friendly R software to facilitate the application of these methods in future trials and studies. Overall, our research has contributed to the development of statistical tools to maximize the benefits of personalized medicine, using predictive information to guide decision-making and improve patient outcomes. Graduate students enrolled in a distributed systems course at UW-Madison participated in an \CE.
A pre-test assessed their current skills, followed by 5 weeks of online assignments under three different conditions.
Students in the \grp received regular automated feedback on code alongside detailed human-provided feedback on assignment performance.
Students in the \gc category received automated feedback on code along with a graded score on recent work, but no feedback on performance.
Students in the \cf received no feedback on code but got a human-provided score on recent assignment performance.
Results showed that students in the \grp excelled in code coverage and overall grading compared to their peers in the \gc and \cf groups.
Moreover, stochastic optimization algorithms performed significantly better in the \grp condition, indicating improved outcomes under human guidance.
Fifty-nine students later participated in a survey asking them to compare the three conditions on learning effectiveness.
Surprisingly, the \grp and \cf showed similar ratings, suggesting that although the \grp yielded better technical results, students felt equally effective in the \grp and \cf. 
Notably, the \grp enabled students to develop self-evaluation skills, a major advantage of human-provided feedback on assignment performance, whether or not it included code feedback. 
Consequently, instructors may consider combining human-provided feedback on assignment performance with code feedback for in-person courses to help students grow self-evaluation skills. 
Yet, for online courses, combining human-provided feedback on assignment performance with code feedback via automated tools might have the drawback of creating dependency on human feedback, hindering self-learning. 
Ultimately, our study highlights that human-provided feedback on assignment performance, whether or not it included code feedback, enabled students to develop self-evaluation skills.

Acquiring a light field of a scene typically demands a comprehensive 3D reconstruction of its geometry. However, traditional light field rendering methods typically rely on a full set of 2D images captured from numerous viewpoints. This becomes impractical when using portable capture devices that capture only from a limited number of angles. Our proposed sparse light field rendering network tackles this problem by leveraging geometric constraints derived from co-located 3D geometry information to enhance its ability to render high-quality scenes from just a few captured views. Unlike traditional machine learning-based light field rendering methods, ours relies on geometric constraints to generate 3D geometry information and uses these to initialize its 3D geometry model. Additionally, it employs data consistency constraints to refine its 3D geometry model in conjunction with its light field model. This results in geometric updates that improve the learning of scene geometry in conjunction with the light field. Consequently, it enables the generation of high-quality images from only a few captured images at various rendered resolutions without the need for additional data. Results from our experiments show that our method yields high-quality images at various resolutions from just a few captured images, and that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art rendering methods that capture data from numerous angles and render at the same resolution and number of views. Our method has also demonstrated impressive 3D reconstruction accuracy of scenes in 3D geometry reconstruction experiments.
