Characterizing the characteristics of network nodes is crucial for understanding various network phenomena. In particular, the identification of influential nodes in networks has received significant attention in recent years. A new metric called Gromov centrality is proposed, which characterizes how a node behaves as part of a larger network and how it contributes to the formation of a subgroup within that network. By analyzing the similarities and differences between neighborhood topologies with and without a node, the Gromov centrality captures the unique structural properties of a node within a network. In contrast to existing centrality measures, the Gromov centrality is capable of detecting algebraic connections among different types of nodes in homogeneous and complex networks. For example, the Gromov centrality is shown to distinguish between central nodes and peripheral nodes in a social network, between large and small clusters in a cluster-overlapped network, between hubs and careers based on community membership, and between nodes of similar hubmanship but distinct structural properties in a co-authorship network. Additionally, the Gromov centrality is found to outperform existing metrics in predicting income levels and innovative capabilities. Furthermore, the development of a software tool enables researchers to effectively apply the Gromov centrality metric when analyzing large networks. Through its unique focus on algebraic connections among nodes, the Gromov centrality is demonstrated to be a universally applicable metric for network centrality analysis. This can be achieved by approximating the 1-skeleton of the M\"{o}bius strip in 3-dimensional space. Our proof utilizes the 3-dimensional Spanner for projective planes, and it is independent of previously published work. This new embedding has implications for reducing the running time of algorithms related to the metric Baker's problems in minor-free graphs, specifically from exponential O(2^{r/n}) to O(2^{r/3.5n}) time. This improvement is significant for graphs like dipoles, tori, and Heawood graphs, with the running time dropping to O(2^{r/(r+1)}) for dipole and Heawood graphs, and O(2^{r/(r+2)}) for tori. Our method also yields a more efficient solution for Pache's problem in minor-free graphs, with the running time decreasing to O(2^{r/3.5n}) from O(2^{r/(r+1)}) for dipole graphs. Furthermore, we derive faster algorithms based on our embedding for practical graph partitioning problems, such as the Schnyder's labelings, with the running time decreasing to O(2^{r/3.5n}) from O(2^{r/(r+3)}) for 3-dimensional plane embedding and the running time decreasing to O(2^{r/3.5r}) from O(2^{r/(r+4)}) for 4-dimensional plane embedding. All these reductions hold for any real value of r from 1 to infinity. Investigations into electronic structure through variational quantum embedding hold great promise due to its potential for scalable computations. A promising approach in this field is the fermionic-ADAPT-VQE algorithm, which forms the theoretical basis for the qubit-based equivalent, qubit-ADAPT-VQE. Although fermionic-ADAPT-VQE exhibits optimal characteristics, its quantum circuit is inherently flawed due to connected-weight circuits not meeting the quantum principle of unitarity. This limitation results in suboptimal performance. To address this, a hybrid approach combining the fermionic-ADAPT-VQC circuit with the quantum adjoint principle has yielded the quantum adjoint fermionic-ADAPT-VQE, which exhibits an exceptional convergence rate in simulations. This approach further lays the groundwork for the quantum adjoint principle to be implemented in qubit-based ADAPT-VQE, which we have tested and found to yield faster convergence and optimal energy-estimation accuracy on various molecular systems. When compared with qubit-ADAPT-VQE, the quantum adjoint fermionic-ADAPT-VQE displays improved performance, and our approach's integrality allows for the effortless extension of the approach to the mixed electronic-quantum spin model. This may lead to new applications and insights in the study of quantum systems. Furthermore, our approach presents an efficient method for optimizing two-qubit gates. This has led us to propose the QEB-ADAPT-VQE protocol, which achieves faster convergence and optimal energy-estimation on various molecular systems when compared to qubit-ADAPT-VQE. This breakthrough enables the quantum circuit to efficiently achieve optimal performance through accurate parameter estimation, which may contribute to the development of robust and efficient variational quantum algorithms. Moreover, our approach has led to the integration of ADAPT as an optimization principle in the hybrid algorithm, which has led to the proposal of the ground-state hybrid multidimensional quantum embedding approach, which may find practical applications in the investigation of complex molecular systems. These findings have been made available through the open-source integration of the algorithms into the PyAlaMode library. To facilitate future implementations, the energy-estimation methods developed in this study are presented as a set of easily implementable steps that can be leveraged in current quantum computing hardware to achieve optimal performance. By analyzing the energy-estimation behavior, our approach has enabled the analysis of various quantum system behaviors using quantum circuit design. A recent framework known as the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) offers a straightforward approach to learning a compact representation of data by discarding input details and preserving overall characteristics. When used for unsupervised learning on unlabeled data, it can implicitly extract features that differentiate between distinct classes. The key discovery presented in this paper reveals that, even when working with labeled data, the DGD can achieve class separation within its representation space through a specific manipulation that forces the competition between class-specific reconstruction costs. Building upon this discovery, the paper introduces a supervised variant of the DGD that capitalizes on the inherent structure of the labeled data. Comprehensive experiments validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, outperforming existing state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised feature learning methods. Furthermore, the paper successfully demonstrates the application of the DGD to the challenging task of multi-class lung texture classification from imaging scans. The paper's findings are made publicly available through an online data repository containing corresponding code. The research results are further illustrated through a detailed healthcare-based example involving the segmentation and analysis of bronchi. The proposed DGD method is incorporated as the deep feature extractor known as BronchiDecoder. The performance of the model is measured as 0.84, 0.60, and 0.61 for the training, validation, and testing sets respectively. Our proposed approach includes three key components: a generalized multi-objective optimization model, a novel performance metric, and a practical implementation method. The Investment Ratio (IR) metric assesses non-deterministic solutions in multi-objective optimization by evaluating their overall performance relative to an ideal outcome. To verify the feasibility of IR, we developed a practical and efficient randomization method to generate non-deterministic solutions, demonstrating that, on average, these solutions approximate the optimal values for both objective functions. Utilizing SPARAS, a streaming algorithm for multi-objective optimization, we derived general criteria and a specific streaming algorithm for achieving non-deterministic solutions with improved Investment Ratios. The efficiency of our approach was demonstrated through experimental validation on seven public multi-objective datasets, showcasing positive outcomes for several popular performance metrics. Additionally, we established theoretical bounds for the expected Investment Ratios achieved by the developed methods. Further research is encouraged to utilize streaming algorithms in multi-objective optimization, encompassing diverse applications such as survey sampling, experimental design, and data analysis. To facilitate future contributions, we are providing our code under a permissive license at https://github.com/optimization-LAB/Investment-Ratio/tree/master/Streaming-MOO. 

We are confident that our approach can be insightfully utilized in conjunction with prior multi-objective optimization techniques, offering promising possibilities for further investigation. Nonetheless, in the present study, we have deliberately avoided leveraging deterministic solutions derived from non-deterministic streaming algorithms, instead focusing on the theoretical and practical efficacy of streaming algorithms for multi-objective optimization. For instance, it is feasible to modify the Rastrigin function-based streaming algorithm to achieve better Investment Ratios for certain regions of interest. Similarly, by integrating the Partitioning-based algorithm for multi-objective optimization, one may successfully attain a higher Investment Ratio compared to the baseline random search approach, though the current analysis does not encompass these enhancements. We intend to delve deeper into these subjects in upcoming studies.

The capacity of bacteria, including the pathogen \emph{Listeria monocytogenes}, to cause disease in the host is typically restricted by the presence of a functioning immune system. In situations where the host's immune response is impaired, conditions become more conducive for L. \emph{monocytogenes} to thrive, often leading to the development of listeriosis. In pursuit of better understanding how the immune system disablement enables the bacterium's invasion of host tissues, researchers investigated how reduced immunocompetency accelerates \emph{Listeria}'s onset. In this investigation, researchers also examined whether gastric suppressor treatments, which reduce stomach acidity, expedite L. \emph{monocytogenes}' internalisation by host cells and facilitate its spread to distant organs. Crucially, researchers discovered that the disablement of the host's immune response, whether achieved by immunosuppression or gastric suppressor treatment, triggers a swift production of inflammatory cytokines in the host, thus thwarting the bacterium's capacity to cause disease in a timely and efficient manner. In light of these key findings, researchers' assumptions about the role of gastric suppressors in facilitating bacterial invasion are refined, and further research is suggested to explore additional means to control the spread of the bacterium prior to the onset of the host's immune response. Furthermore, these studies' implications on the administration of immunosuppressive or gastric suppressor treatments in patients at risk of developing listeriosis or on individuals with reduced immunocompetency are investigated. In particular, these individuals may either already possess a weakened immune system or have undergone gastric suppressor treatment. The study's results in these situations are confirmed through in silico simulations of patient scenarios. This research investigates the performance of a secure multiuser communication system that incorporates a reconfigurable intelligent surface to manage the channel environment. We investigate the impact of hardware impairments and unknown eavesdropping channel on a two-stage system consisting of a base station connected to a power source and a user equipment with adjustable intelligence capabilities. We aim to optimize the base station's power transmission and the user equipment's surface reflection to achieve the highest possible data transfer rate while maintaining full security through the base station connection. We model the hardware impairments as a combination of factors that cause interference and accuracy degradation, and the reflection ability as a variable influenced by the user equipment's configuration and noise. We convert the optimization problem into a simpler version by substituting variables and using a multi-stage approach. We numerically examine the performance of this system with and without hardware impairments and uncover the significant influence of these impairments on system performance, as well as the trade-offs between power transmission, reflection ability, and configuration settings. We also find that a balance between these factors is crucial for optimal system performance. Additionally, the results show that hardware impairments diminish the impact of eavesdropping channels on the base station connection, thereby offering a built-in security feature. We hope that these findings and our proposed design model can inspire future practical implementations. We also compare our proposed design to a conventional method and observe that it consistently yields the highest data transfer rates while maintaining system stability. In some cases, the proposed design achieves secure transmission even when the eavesdropping channel is known, which is an advantageous feature. We also found that the user equipment's surface reflection has a limited impact on system performance when the eavesdropping channel is unknown, which is an insight for further optimization. The numerical evaluation of our proposed design shows a 30% to 200% improvement in data transfer rates compared to a conventional method, which highlights the potential of the reconfigurable surface and smart power management as key elements of the base station equipment. These findings offer practical guidance for the integration of these technologies into future base station equipment. We identified the trade-offs between hardware impairments, surface reflection, and configuration settings as crucial factors affecting system performance, which is an insight for the practical implementation of our proposed design. Additionally, the results confirm that a two-stage approach is an efficient method for optimizing system performance. Lastly, the results show that the user equipment's surface reflection has a significant influence on system performance, which is an insight for the practical implementation of this technology. This study examines the current status of a particular method for establishing the consistency of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$ and explores its potential applications to far-reaching cardinal characteristics in set theory, particularly those involving the size of power sets. A fundamental element in this inquiry is the concept of a $P$-point, which has been utilized in various consistency proofs, although such an application requires highly restrictive set theory models. We reveal that the significance of $P$-points extends beyond their association with the least weakly compact ordinal, as evidenced by a host of consistent instances where the underlying models are not only failure models for a type of set theory or partial order but also numerous other types. We analyze under which conditions the method for achieving the desired cardinal sizes works, providing a framework that distills the requirements down to just combinatorial properties or the existence of a type of set. Additionally, the relationship between $P$-points and stationarily compact sets is explored through an outcome showing that, if the method is successful in achieving the desired cardinal sizes under a stationarily compact condition, then a stationarily closed $P$-point must exist within that model. We ultimately conclude our investigation by outlining several open questions and potential areas for further research. A significant portion of this work arose from the discussions at the 15th Conference on the Foundations of Mathematics, specifically during Session III on Large Cardinals, Cardinals, Set Theory, and Logic, which led to the compilation of the papers in the proceedings. This method involves a deep neural network that maps a function to its weighted integral average, and in the process, it satisfies an associated ordinary differential equation. This paper provides evidence that a specific form of this ordinary differential equation is a conservation form. Leveraging this formulation, we extend the neural network method to encompass a broader class of functions. Furthermore, our conservation form framework enables the easy adaptation and incorporation of commutativity-like properties. In practice, this is achieved by incorporating additional neural network layers that can manipulate conservation laws. Additionally, the upgraded readout system can take advantage of the full $2\times10^{-5}$ cubic centimeters of the detector's acceptance, yielding a rate of about six events per nanobarn-centimeter, without the limitations of earlier cuts. This research endeavors to apply Event Extraction techniques to texts in Portuguese, a challenging task in any language other than English. To address this, we enhance the FastText library by integrating it with a Graph Convolutional Network, thereby allowing our system to learn semantic representations for the event and its associated arguments. To test our approach, we participate in the Extraction Challenges organized by SemEval-2020, using the ANNIE dataset and focusing on single-argument events. Our participation in the competition reveals the superiority of our proposed solver, named FC-GEI, when compared to other competing systems. Our results demonstrate that our two-stage approach, consisting of training FastText on the training data and then fine-tuning it with a GCN, significantly enhances the accuracy of Event Extraction in Portuguese. Notably, this accuracy increase is substantial when the model is limited and the dataset is reduced. To facilitate further research, we are publicly releasing the code and dataset for our solver, FC-GE. Additionally, we are contributing a new dataset of extracted events related to the Brazilian Real currency. This dataset, named R$3M, comprises 5050 instances of extracted events, each including the event's SemEval ID, the Brazilian currency's ID, the description of the event, and the arguments associated with that event. The R$3M dataset will enable researchers to access full text descriptions and accurate machine-extracted events for analytical purposes. The FC-GE solver is now available at https://github.com/utnloa/FC-GE/tree/master/solvers/FC-GE, and the R$3M dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/utnloa/FC-GE/tree/master/datasets/R$3M. Both the FC-GE solver and the R$3M dataset are provided under the terms of the MIT License. The FC-GEI solver is available at https://github.com/utnloa/FC-GE/tree/master/solvers/FC-GEI. The code was developed using Pytorch, Pytec, and the Pytec library, which are utilized for the training and evaluation processes. The code also utilizes the SpaCy library for the processing of the semantic representations. The results of our FC-GE solver can be accessed at https://evalut.nloa.io. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the full orbit spectral variability in the 2019 explosion of the high-mass X-ray binary 4U1636$-$495 observed near its critical overflow limit. Utilizing high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy and photometry from the NASA Swift, our findings involve detailed modeling of the light curves and temperatures across the entire system. They reveal a soft and hard band light curve discrepancy in the later phases of the explosion due to interstellar medium absorption changes affecting the soft band. However, our research indicates the absence of a distinct bright hard flux enhancement typically observed in earlier explosions, possibly due to interstellar medium absorption reduction in the hard band or a reduced inclination angle. Additionally, our measurements indicate surface gravity enhancements, pointing to significant surface enrichment. Moreover, our observations of the explosion's early and later phases reveal contrasting patterns - the early phases corresponding to average coherence, the later phases exhibiting coherence reduction. Utilizing fast-eddy viscosity from the Murchison Widefield Array to estimate coherence, our research provides the initial evidence for high-mass X-ray binary shock conversion to purely radiative phases post-explosion, consistent with Riemann-type shock conditions. Consequently, our research identifies the 2019 explosion of 4U1636$-$495 as an explosion dominated by the most coherent and highest frequency variability observed across the entire mass range. Ultimately, our research highlights that shock conditions can persist for extended periods, potentially governing coherent behavior in the early and later phases of explosions. It serves as an empirical representation of general shock conditions applicable across all mass ranges. Lastly, our research proposes a distinct explosion class comprising mass range analogs distinct from the typical radiation-dominated explosion category. Future observations could potentially detect coherent signals from these types of explosions using next-generation telescopes. Nonetheless, our research indicates that coherent signals from these types of explosions are likely to be obscured by exponential decay at low frequencies. Ultimately, our research highlights the remarkable uniqueness of the 2019 explosion of 4U1636$-$495 as an extraordinary occurrence within the realm of high-mass X-ray binary explosions.

The non-abelian version of Thompson scattering is analyzed within non-commutative spaces and modified non-commutative geometry frameworks. In this context, two different approaches to non-commutative geometry are studied, and their effects on non-abelian scattering and energy equations are explored. Thompson scattering is formulated at the Lagrangian level using a non-abelian aether framework, resulting in a modified non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law. This modification gives rise to non-Casimir energy, altering previous Casimir energy calculations. An alternative approach to non-commutative geometry is explored, focusing on geometric actions, and its influence on non-abelian scattering and energy equations is examined. In this approach, a non-abelian potential emerges, affecting Thompson scattering and the non-abelian energy equations. The interplay between the two approaches is also concurred, and open questions regarding their connections and quantum particle behaviors are raised. Furthermore, a study on the properties of the Dirac propagator in non-abelian spaces, conducted via the differential approach, reveals that non-abelian spaces possess non-trivial non-commutative properties. This property transfer is examined and compared to the conservative energy shift, given by Casimir energy, and is found to satisfy a non-abelian triangle rule. Additionally, potential applications and connections to non-abelian electrodynamics are explored, and the possibility of detecting non-abelian spaces through Casimir energy is considered. A discussion on the potential connections of this work to string theory is also initiated. The non-abelian version of Thompson scattering reveals that an abelianization of non-abelian spaces is not feasible. This conclusion is further solidified by examining the non-abelian Dirac propagator and Casimir energy via the differential approach, showing that quantum particles cannot be translated from non-abelian to abelian spaces. A comparison to existing non-abelian quantum field theories is made, highlighting the unique characteristics of the non-abelian Thompson scattering. Ultimately, the non-abelian Thompson scattering represents a novel area of research, offering a fresh perspective on the non-abelian space theory. The non-abelian Thompson scattering concept demonstrates a quantum reliability independent of the number of particle states, for instance, the quantum states of an electron. We present a flexible neural framework for modeling syntax and semantics jointly, learning stable, general language patterns. By training this model on extensive datasets consisting of examples from various languages, we investigate its ability to recognize common syntactic and semantic structures across multiple languages, which it does successfully. To support this investigation, we compile a substantial cross-lingual splitable dataset comprising 42 million examples from 6 languages and categorize them into 181 distinct semantic classes. We also demonstrate that this model can accurately predict novel sentence meanings based on modified inputs. Furthermore, we identify unfamiliar words that the model struggles with and discover that word embeddings primarily capture positional information rather than the actual word form. Ultimately, we discover that this model can effectively generate novel, realistic sentences given a given meaning. Our code and data are publicly available for review at https://github.com/davidchai/multilang-semantics.

This methodology was applied to various types of short-lived, radiation-emitting events resulting from the union of compact celestial bodies in the early universe. We studied the prominence of tidal features in a group of 249 early-type galaxies located in the fields of observations conducted with the MaNGA spectrographic instrument. These galaxies have different stellar masses, ranging between 10^10 and 10^11 solar units, and various Hubble types. We found the tidal features to be most common among galaxies with a stellar mass in the middle of this range. We also found the proportion of tidal features to gradually disappear as the stellar mass increased. To study their prominence, we used MaNGA data in three spectral ranges. We then analyzed the tidal features' contribution to the galaxies' light and mass in various luminosity and mass ranges. We found the tidal features' light contribution, relative to the total light of the galaxy, to be highest for less massive galaxies. This contribution, however, decreased as the galaxy's mass increased. Similarly, the tidal features' light contribution, in relation to the total light of the galaxy, decreased as the galaxy's mass increased. We observed the tidal features' mass contribution to be highest at lower masses and decreased as the mass increased. In contrast to previous research, we found the tidal features' mass to be directly related to the galaxy's mass. This relationship showed that the tidal features' mass, in relation to the total mass of the galaxy, decreased as the mass increased. We also found the tidal features to be most extensive in terms of both length and width for less massive galaxies. This decreased as the mass increased. Furthermore, we studied the tidal features' length and width in relation to the galaxy's parameters, finding them to be longest and widest for less massive galaxies. This decreased as the mass increased. We also found the tidal features' length and width to be in relation to the galaxy's radius. This decreased as the mass increased. To study the tidal features' orientation, we used MaNGA data in combination with a technique that corrects for the galaxy's seeing. We found the tidal features' orientation to be most deviant for less massive galaxies. This decreased as the mass increased. We also found the tidal features' isophotal angle to be in relation to the galaxy's mass. This decreased as the mass increased. In conclusion, the tidal features' influence varies depending on the galaxy's mass. This effect can be observed when studying low-level stellar substructure using data conducted with the MaNGA spectrographic instrument. The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation aims to resolve the issues raised by the Radiation Problem in relation to the theoretical aspects of protostar formation and evolution within the context of the Singular Infant Theory of Gravitation. Consequently, ASTG serves as an alternative theory that facilitates the smooth and self-consistent development of massive protostars from uniformly dense, massive, and uniformly expanding singular infanta. Typically, such theories are evaluated in relation to one another, rather than as independent propositions. However, due to the inherent differences and divergent objectives of this review, it is necessary to consider ASTG as a standalone, rather than comparative, theory in this discussion. This analysis commences with a clear and unbiased explanation of ASTG, adhering to the author's original description and interpretation of the theory. It then presents a contrasting assessment of the efficacy and consistency of ASTG, employing established methods of physical evaluation. Ultimately, this review considers the overall validity and consistency of ASTG, distinguish-ing its current status as an untested alternative theory. We have made public the computer code used to generate the plots within this document at https://github.com/astrodog101/AstgCode. Our research focuses on understanding how radio bursts from far-away galaxies emit light across various wavelengths, an aspect largely unexplored until now. To investigate this, we simultaneously observed a distant FRB with optical telescopes. Employing a data analysis method used in particle physics, we found our FRB's flux changed rapidly during its emission, a finding supported by its light curve. This result, obtained through two telescopes' concurrent observations, increased the constraints for models of light emission, an improvement measured as a 3-fold rise in the 'light-curve parameter space' bounds. Given that most galaxies hosting these radio bursts are too distant and obscure to study directly, our method could be used to explore more such galaxies in the future, thus making more precise predictions possible about how these radio bursts emit light across various wavelengths. This, in turn, could facilitate a more thorough understanding of what produces these radio bursts. This study also included a search for unusual astrophysical signals related to the radio burst, a methodological aspect previously untested during the FRB's emission. Before and after this event, our experiment also searched for unusual repeated signals, an indication of nearby, hidden sources of strong radiation. Nonetheless, we found no such repeated signals, a discovery setting a limit on how frequently such radiation changes frequency, an improvement measured as a 50-fold rise in the 'Fourier amplitude constraint'. This research, carried out using the M. D. Geodetti 1.5-m telescope, evaluated a total of 184 nights, an improvement measured as a 50-fold rise in the 'Fourier amplitude constraint'. The data was collected over approximately 3,000 hours. Our proposed Delegated RingCT (DRC) protocol has been designed to improve the efficiency of RingCT transactions in the Silk Road, by switching from a random signature scheme to a fixed delegation model utilizing a secure random number generator. This change allows for fixed selection buffers, enhancing the speed and scalability of RingCT by eliminating the time-consuming process of random selection. Additionally, the traditional RingCT transaction time is further minimized through an integrated merge-and-spend feature facilitated by a blockchain data feed. Our simulation tests demonstrate the effectiveness of DRC in achieving better transaction speed and scalability. Furthermore, the modularity of the DRC protocol makes it easy to integrate into various cryptocurrency networks, such as Zcash, in a seamless manner without affecting existing consensus mechanisms. As such, DRC is suitable for use as a scalable solution in consensual cryptocurrencies. Our research also includes an evaluation of the security level provided by DRC against various forms of breach attempts, including insider threats, network attacks, and parallel mixing attacks, showcasing its ability to offer significant protection against combination attacks due to the substantial difficulty in linking outputs to inputs within the system. In line with its efficiency-enhancing nature, DRC is particularly suitable for use in low-power, low-capability devices such as IoT devices, without the need for extensive computational power. Our contribution to the cryptocurrency community involves the development of DRC, a practical solution that addresses the primary challenge of scalability for direct privacy-enhanced cryptocurrencies like Zcash. This solution not only accelerates transaction execution but also solidifies the security of the RingCT protocol, now widely adopted as a global standard, by reducing reliance on energy-intensive random number generators. Furthermore, the security evaluation of DRC serves as an alternative approach to previous scalability solutions such as Breier et al.'s Linkable Ring Signature v2 and Smart RingCT. Our research corrects the security flaws previously exposed in Breier et al.'s schemes while maintaining the compatibility with v1. As such, the scalability solution we propose is compatible with the current Zappone et al. design, providing an efficient scaling path for Zcash without disrupting existing consensus mechanisms. As such, our research brings forth an innovative solution that is simple yet powerful, scalable yet secure, and suitable for deployment on even the most low-capable devices. To improve the accuracy of beam-beam close orbit measurements, a different method based on beam-beam long range effects has been developed. Since long range beam-beam effects are largely influenced by beam-beam close orbit, this method can determine close orbit precision to about 50 microns. Moreover, long range beam-beam effects are mainly dependent on the beam idiosyncrasies such as beam charge and current, making this method suitable for cases where direct measurement is challenging. Furthermore, this method can also be used to measure and analyze the beam-beam close orbit distortion caused by local dipole magnets, which is beneficial for correcting errors in the beam close orbit during the commissioning phase of a new accelerator. Examples of its application will be given with free electron laser and high energy physics beams. Lastly, this method can be utilized in conjunction with other measurement methods, such as optical kick measurements, to provide more precise close orbit precision measurements. Examples of its application will be given with the Linac Coherent Light Source and the Future Circular Collider Collider. 

Key phrases: beam-beam close orbit measurement, beam-beam long range effects, beam beam kick, precision measurement. 

Note: This method has been tested and proven during a run with the Linac Coherent Light Source in 2010.

This paper addresses the challenge of applying continuation learning to simulate
solid-mechanical phenomena that depend on past histories of loading. To address
this, we've created an innovative form of continuation learning called the
Recurrent ReluDisplacement Autoencoder, or RDA. By leveraging a recurrent deep
learning model that accurately represents material behavior and accounts for its
internal states, we've successfully demonstrated the rapid modeling of various
elastic-brittle and kinematic hardening material models with unprecedented
simplicity. Moreover, our open-source code accelerates simulations by allowing
materials models to be instantly transferred from laboratories to industrial-scale
calculations using standard finite element analysis software. Our model also exhibits
a superior capacity for generalization compared to traditional methods. This work
has significant implications for the modeling of complex phenomena such as the
diffusion of defects, plasticity at small scales, and other subject matters within
the field of solid mechanics. Furthermore, it may also contribute to the further
expansion of deep learning into multi-physics engineering disciplines. By using
existing softwares such as Abaqus through the ODB format, our model can also be
easily implemented in practical industrial environments. The full details of our work
can be found at https://doi.org/10.1017/jnm.20220223.

The charmonium state at approximately 10753 MeV, assigned to $^3D_1^{(2)}$($c\bar c$), appears out of place compared to expectations based on potential model predictions and radial excitations observed in experimental data, leading to the notion that it might be a novel type of charmonium state. A theoretical investigation found that this energy range could be associated with the start of a new charmonium radical series, comprising radial excitations of a novel type of charmonium radical, labeled as $1C_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$). As a result, the experimental observation at approximately 10753 MeV might be attributed to the radical state $1C_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) rather than a conventional bottomonium state. Our team also discovered that the starting point of the $1C_2^{(1)}$ series is accompanied by minima in the charmonium bound state probabilities. The study further revealed that the key properties of the $1C_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) radical state could be estimated using a distinct ratio between the potentials representing the $1C_2^{(1)}$ and $1D_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) states. This novel series begins at a potential strength corresponding to approximately 6.354 times the charm quark mass. Furthermore, the study found that the most likely decay mode for the $1C_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) radical involves the conversion of $1C_2^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) into $1D_1^{(1)}$($c\bar c$) through the emission of a soft charmed meson, with probabilities ranging from 0 to 0.72, depending on the radical's radial order. In conclusion, the experimental observation at approximately 10753 MeV might be associated with the novel charmonium radical state with a probability of around 65\%. Our study suggests that the experimental observation at approximately 10753 MeV is unlikely to be attributed to the conventional bottomonium state $^3D_1^{(2)}$($b\bar b$). The predicted decay modes for the novel series were also presented. Most generative models like Variational Auto-Encoders rely on a pre-defined class set,
often annotated with specific labels. However, class labels aren't always present or easy
to obtain. Therefore, their applications are limited mainly to fields with well-documented classes.
This research introduces a new approach to VAEs, allowing them to generate classless data.
We achieve this by having multiple users simultaneously label the same data with different categories.
This way, our model can identify user-specific labels and the type of object being labeled without being influenced by a particular user's labels.
We experiment with this concept on datasets of new household furniture and medical equipment designed by 'DesignLab' - a collaborative design facility where multiple users generate data through imaging or video. The results show our model is effective in generating data of new categories, as well as refining our generative model to produce more accurate data. We also compared our model to traditional VAEs and other generative models and found our approach outperformed them significantly in generating data of unannotated categories. We further studied our model's capabilities by investigating its performance given limited, annotated data and the impact of varying the number of users contributing to the data. The code for our model is available at https://github.com/amberwangai/VAE-with-multiple-users. This research also highlights the advantage of collaborative design in the field of deep learning. Furthermore, the visualizations generated by our model have the potential to enhance the capabilities of multiple fields including computer vision and machine learning, as well as design and architecture. As the use of generative models increasingly common in designing processes, the need for model applications that don't solely rely on annotated data and can cause self-supervised learning is becoming more pressing. This research fills this gap by revealing new methods to handle data without labels in the generative model field. Ultimately, the research contributes to the further development of designing with AI and increases our understanding of utilizing deep learning in creating visual data. Furthermore, the research causes an investigation in understanding how collaborative design impacts deep learning and vice versa. This research demonstrates that multiple design methodologies including cooperative design and machine learning can enhance each other and result in more advanced applications. We propose the concept of 'design as coding' - a concept in which design and deep learning are highly interdependent and can only function off of one another. Diverging from conventional supervised segmentation techniques that demand extensive labeling, this approach utilizes minimum training data to establish a prior model. Densely annotated scans are initially utilized to build a GP model representing probability distributions over pixel labels. Subsequently, a second GP model is developed using both the original and prior distributions to generate predicted probability maps for unseen subjects. Experimental evaluations on seven benchmark datasets confirm the efficacy of our approach, particularly in identifying cerebral cortex and cerebellum regions. What's more, our segmentation accuracy surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, with remarkable inter-site consistency despite data source diversity. Moreover, our segmentation results lay the groundwork for novel cortical structures' mapping criteria, achieving 75% higher accuracy in detecting unknown regions compared to leading unsupervised methods. By intermingling these concepts with numerical solutions of the non-Hermitian quantum master equation, we explore various parameter regimes to gain a comprehensive understanding. Key aspects of our study include revealing an intricate interplay between dissipation and Floquet heating that leads to significant population growth at late times, identifying a stable correlation time where fluctuations stabilize, and observing the surprising appearance of a dissipative Floquet Bose-Einstein condensation phase when dissipation and Floquet heating are in harmony. This phase is marked by the presence of a conservative Floquet condensate component and a dissipative portion, both of which coexist in a stable, quasi-stationary state. Lastly, we leverage the Bethe lattice to map the complex spectrum of the Floquet system, thus visually illustrating the connection between quasiparticle properties and the eigenvalue spectrum, particularly in the presence of a band of dissipationless modes that contributes to Bose-Einstein condensation. Utilizing these advancements enables simulations of one-dimensional Floquet quantum gases where frequency-dressed states, characterized by their significant population and long survival time, can persist in a stable manner even under moderate interaction forces. Moreover, our results predict the presence of a meta-diffusive regime where the spreading of quasiparticles is decelerated by Floquet effects, observed at intermediate values of interaction-to-dispersion ratio greater than one. This deceleration is caused by the coexistence of Floquet-induced band flattening and Pauli blocking, leading to a quasi-stationary state whose lifespan is independent of the system's dimensionality. Hence, our study provides an in-depth analysis of the non-equilibrium behavior exhibited by cold bath-coupled one-dimensional and higher-dimensional Floquet quantum gases. By leveraging these simulations, we learn to manipulate and optimize thermodynamic properties through the adjustment of cold bath frequencies and strengths, ultimately enabling the attainment of population densities previously unachievable under zero-temperature conditions. In conclusion, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding and practical application of Floquet effects in low-dimensional quantum gases. Moreover, the employed theoretical framework bears significant potential for the simulation of quantum systems coupled to thermal baths, offering an invaluable tool for the investigation and exploration of novel quantum phenomena and materials. We've developed a new type of tensor network code that leverages local tensors to erase and distort data. Each tensor in the network is associated with a random string that serves as a key, used to extract the original tensor from a tensor that has been altered. The circuit simulations reveal that the tensor network behaves as a low-density parity-check code, provided that the initial tensors adhere to a specific restriction: the tensor domain's dimension being smaller than the codeword dimension. In the case of a single-type tensor network, this constraint necessitates that the tensor domain equals 2. The code performance can be analyzed by examining the density of parities within the corresponding bilinear forms' graphs. Furthermore, we've devised an efficient decoding procedure, presented in appendix C, that handles generic instances of these tensor network codes. The paper includes a detailed examination of two specific tensor network code examples, where the underlying tensors constitute linear representations of discrete symmetries in the finite groups $SL_2(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and $\mathbb{F}_q^{\times}\times \mathbb{F}_q$, respectively. In these instances, the associated erasure correction codes possess superior performance levels compared to random parities check codes of equivalent density. The project involves implementations in both Julia and Python programming languages. The former is accessible through the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/PhDMario/Tensor-Code, while the latter is located at https://github.com/PhDMario/Tensor-Code-jp. The implementations demonstrate that the tensor network codes' performance levels closely mirror those predicted parities density models. To optimize the benefits of distributed energy resources (DERs) and cyber security in modern power systems, a new approach is introduced that integrates a robust control method with a secure control method. A parallel computational algorithm is developed to simultaneously address robust and secure control, and its effectiveness is shown through a numerical study to outperform conventional methods. Additionally, the algorithm's complexity is compared to conventional methods to demonstrate its efficiency. The proposed approach offers promise for distributing control signals among power system generators, enhancing the efficiency of DER control and promoting stability, security, and efficiency in modern power systems. Furthermore, this approach can be easily integrated with existing automatic voltage control systems to improve their performance. Overall, this approach represents an innovative solution for optimizing power system performance in the face of disruptions and cyber attacks. Numerical studies in a power system model have shown that integrating secure control within robust control can achieve optimal results with minimal performance loss, and may even improve stability and efficiency compared to conventional control methods, specifically by reducing average power losses by approximately 9.8 percent. These benefits are particularly noticeable in systems vulnerable to cyber attacks, where the proposed approach outperforms conventional methods by a significant margin. Based on these results, it is recommended that power system generators be equipped with intelligent control systems capable of efficiently managing large numbers of DERs and mitigating cyber threats. These advanced control systems could seamlessly integrate with existing power system infrastructure, minimizing disruptions and improving the performance of power systems as a whole. Furthermore, the proposed approach offers potential applications beyond power systems, such as in the integration of energy storage systems (ESS) and other distributed energy sources, and could be the first step in developing advanced control systems capable of mitigating cyber threats and optimizing energy system performance. As such, this approach represents an essential component of a comprehensive cyber security framework for modern energy systems. Numerical analysis of the algorithm's computational requirements has shown that its time complexity is substantially better than conventional methods, opening the possibility for its practical implementation in real-time control systems to optimize power system performance. However, this approach may face challenges in terms of communication reliability during cyber attacks, and further research is needed to address this vulnerability, particularly in systems vulnerable to cyber attacks, where the proposed approach may face significant hurdles in its implementation. As a critical component of a comprehensive cyber security framework, this approach may help stabilize power systems in the event of cyber attacks by reducing stability and efficiency losses, and could potentially be integrated with existing control systems to improve its performance, and could be an essential tool for distributed energy resource management and control.

In multi-armed bandit problems with k options, we've improved regret bounds under common criteria when the best outcome incurs consistent loss or slight time delays. Our optimized loss rates for pulled arms and the top outcome demonstrate enhanced dependability over previously established bounds. Given these optimized loss rates, our regret bounds for smooth regret are superior to what was previously achieved, especially when losses on the best arm are minimal, where our results are exactly optimal. For delay problems, our regret bounds represent significant improvements over prior work, with specific exact optimality in several scenarios. By focusing on optimally handling the top outcome's loss or delay, these advances have been documented through mathematical analysis and simulation. Our representations of loss and delay bandit problems have been successfully generalized to weighted bandit problems, providing additional insight into this area. These theoretical advancements were then applied and demonstrated with a medical study involving device optimization, highlighting the practical value of these findings. Conversely, some scenarios are noted in which current bound representations may offer only theoretical progress at a higher computational cost. These points are briefly discussed within the concluding section. 

Key Contributions: 
- Optimized loss rates for the top outcome in delay bandit problems under general and exponential criteria.
- Most realistic scenarios exhibit improved loss rates when comparing our bounds to what is currently established.
- Representations of the general delay bandit problem have been generalized to the weighted bandit problem, offering additional insight.
- Our findings were applied to a medical study involving device optimization, demonstrating practical value.

- We have successfully extended our findings to the weighted bandit problem, where each arm is assigned a unique weight. This area is explored in greater depth within the background section.

In the realm of dialogue-based text generation, the task is to produce continuous, coherent, and contextually relevant text given the conversational context. Current approaches employing unconditioned generative models pose significant limitations, including an inability to retain context or achieve high conversation depths. In contrast, models incorporating continuing memory or recursive contextual representations still require explicit memory updates after each generated segment, which proves costly and restricts conversation depth. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel framework, the Context-Aware Contextual RNN, designed to facilitate dialogue-based text generation. Building on the architecture of a contextual RNN, the framework incorporates an added layer that monitors and classifies the conversational context, thereby eliminating the need for explicit memory updates. To further enhance conversational depth, the framework incorporates a recursive structure, combining the contextual representations from the top and intermediate layers to produce a comprehensive, hierarchical contextual understanding. We validate the effectiveness of this proposed architecture through thorough experimental evaluation on the Ubuntu forum dataset, which demonstrates that it outperforms current state-of-the-art models by significantly enhancing both conversation depth and overall text generation performance. Notably, the framework's efficiency was found to be superior to existing models, with computer-based calculations indicating a speedup of 3.5 times while maintaining comparable segment accuracy. We anticipate that our proposed architecture will provide valuable insights into dialogue-based text generation and serve as a foundation for the development of more sophisticated conversational systems. All associated code and models have been made publicly available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/jayjaybee/dagcn. Additionally, demo versions of the proposed architecture have been deployed online at http://dagcn-demo.herokuapp.com. Since its inception in 1972, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has served as the foundation for investigating strong-interaction matter. After four decades, extensive research has been conducted, yet a considerable gap remains in our understanding of the strong interactions in matter. The Joint Physics Meeting of the 2012 Quark Matter conference and the 2012 International Conference for Computational Methods in Particle Physics addressed this knowledge gap by bringing together physicists in a multidisciplinary forum. The resulting proceedings feature 33 chapters covering diverse aspects of particle physics, with 9 chapters focused on quantum chromodynamics and nonperturbative aspects, 5 on heavy-ion collisions, 5 on particle physics experiments, 4 on hadron physics, 3 on astrophysics, 3 on theoretical work, 2 on accelerator technology, and 1 on open problems in particle physics. This book provides an overview of the current state of the field and potential avenues for further research in particle physics and the study of matter. The QM2012 JC meeting demonstrated that a diverse array of topics, from quantum chromodynamics to particle physics, cosmology, and the interplay between matter and energy, are interconnected in the field. The resulting proceedings capture this interconnectivity and highlight areas requiring further research. The editors have taken the lead in connecting these areas, with particular focus on theoretical, experimental, and computational aspects in particle physics and the study of matter. The resulting content serves as a starting point for further research in these areas, with the ultimate goal of understanding the nature of strong interactions in matter. The first chapter provides an overview of the current state of the field and potential avenues for further research in quantum chromodynamics and the study of matter. Analyzing data from social media can be achieved by leveraging natural language processing techniques to gain insights into public feelings following a disaster. When utilizing raw, unannotated social data for training machine learning models, the issue of class imbalance frequently arises due to the uneven number of examples across classes. In order to address this problem, two approaches were explored: the first involved utilizing undersampling to reduce the dominant class's examples, while the second involved using generated examples to fill in the underrepresented classes. Considering that social media posts often contain unique vocabulary, words and phrases that are not present in the dataset's training set or its benchmark datasets, word2vec was employed to generate new examples based on the existing dataset's semantics. The goal was to determine whether using generated examples could enhance the accuracy of various supervised learning classifiers in sentiment recognition tasks. The proposed methodology consisted of three phases: the first phase aimed to identify relevant, extended examples using generated word2vec, based on the existing dataset's semantics, to improve model accuracy; the second phase involved using undersampling to rectify class imbalance; the third phase involved evaluating the performance of different machine learning classifiers, including Na\"ive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Maximum likelihood, Neural Network, Recurrent Neural Network and Bagging, on datasets trained with undersampled and generated data. The results showed that using undersampling led to better cross-validation results than using generated data, however when utilizing a Majority Vote RNN classifier, the performance of the model trained with generated data surpassed that of the model trained with undersampled data, resulting in an approximately 5% improvement in its F1 score. The proposed methodology demonstrated efficacy in the context of a disaster application, namely a sentiment recognition task following the 2015 Nepal earthquake. The dataset comprising Twitter posts and raw comments from various sources, including social media, news articles and interviews with affected individuals, covered a range of emotional responses including anger, sadness, disgust, and happiness, and was marked by severe class imbalance. To analyze the dynamics of photo-induced phase transitions in certain materials like perovskite nanocrystals, researchers employ a technique called ultrafast X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. This technique measures changes in the intensity of X-rays absorbed by the material as a function of time following a pulse of light. However, the data from this technique is difficult to interpret because it is heavily influenced by the experimental setup, the material's initial state, the intensity of the X-ray beam, and various experimental inversions. Additionally, the new method must account for the changing experimental conditions over time. Given these challenges, we present a novel approach to analyze these experimental results. This approach involves using time-resolved data from optically pumped rhodamine 123 in solution, where we recover a key measure of the material's electronic dynamics, referred to as the white peak. We initially test our method using simulated data and find that it effectively lifts the constraints imposed by the experimental setup and material conditions. Next, we apply our method to real experimental data collected under two different conditions: in the first case, we introduce more X-ray noise into the data while maintaining the same material response; in the second case, we alter the material's response while preserving the same data and X-ray intensity. We find that our new method accurately identifies the material's response in all scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an additional test by comparing our method's predictions with the results from optically pumping rhodamine 203 in solution. This final test confirms the accuracy of our new inversion technique. We plan to make the code for our new method publicly available at https://github.com/lulius/xanes_inv. We aim to expand the applicability and utility of our new method by investigating a broader range of experimental conditions and materials within the next research project. Autonomous driving may greatly benefit from machine learning-based object tracking and driving scenario recognition. This paper demonstrates how a joint tracking and scene analysis system can improve performance in driving scenarios by analyzing the tracks obtained from a probabilistic data association algorithm. A convolutional neural network is utilized to create a driving scene classifier, which takes vehicle tracks as input. A key challenge in this system is handling noise in the tracks provided by the tracker. We address this issue by modifying a convolutional neural network to classify scenes using weighted vehicle positions. Evaluation of the proposed system utilizing a self-drived dataset indicates its capability to accurately extract driving scenarios from video footage, facilitating autonomous driving on highways. A comparative analysis is conducted between two different truck styles within the dataset. Our results show that the driving scene recognition model effectively identifies both standard and long vehicles in four distinct driving scenes, including solo vehicles, head-on collisions, following vehicles, and pedestrians. Accuracy in driving scene recognition and long vehicle detection reaches 95% in most scenarios. A deeper analysis is also provided by means of confusion matrices. All source code and dataset used in this research can be located on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/Autonome-LLT/JPDA-DRIVEN. A real-time implementation of this system in the vehicle's onboard computer is also described, which relies on open-source software and hardware components for autonomous driving decision-making. A comprehensive discussion is also offered on the design and execution of autonomous driving decision-making functions within the vehicle's systems. A hypothetical use case is presented in which an analysis of driving scenes and vehicle locations can identify and alert the vehicle about pedestrians. A similar application is also offered by analyzing the driving scene and vehicle trajectory data to detect possible accidents in the vicinity. By utilizing the half-space approach, we found the reflected entropy to be $\mathcal{F}(\Delta)=\log\left(1+e^{2\pi\Delta}\right)$ and established its relationship with the Markov gap as $e^{\mathcal{G}_M(\Delta)}=1+e^{2\pi\Delta}$. Furthermore, we derived similar results within the bulk approach, yielding an identical relationship. Subsequently, we explored various boundary scenarios, calculating the Markov gap in integral conformal field theory, general spin conformal field theory, and key compactifications, such as semisimple and $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric gauge theory. Additionally, we investigated the connection between the reflected entropy and partition function in integral conformal field theory. By solving this relationship, we discovered a functional equation governing the 'entanglement gap function' $\mathcal{G}_E(\Delta)$. Interestingly, we found the entropy in 'integral modules' of conformal field theory to be directly related to the level $k$. Lastly, we examined the reflected entropy in string theory, determining the Markov gap in integral modules and Shannon entropy in 'integral modules'. By taking the large $N$ limit, we derived the reflected entropy, Markov gap, and Shannon entropy in terms of $N$, providing significant insights into these phenomena. These findings open the door for investigating similar phenomena in local bulk approaches to these theories and gauge/gravity duality connections. Moreover, we propose an independent method to verify our results via the RT formula. By resolving the Markov gap problem, we established a fundamental concept, allowing comparison of information flow rates across various systems, thereby gaining deeper insights into information transfer. We present an advanced method of channel estimation tailored to Cognitive Radio (CR) and New Radio (NR) systems with limited cyclic prefix and flawed radio hardware, facilitated by Profiling Technology. The proposed technique draws upon the enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM), a sophisticated artificial neural network that accurately predicts channel characteristics. By integrating ELM with the Primary User's (PU) transmitter and receiving antenna, the Cognitive Radio node can acquire precise information on its channel conditions. Simulations indicate that ELM yields superior performance in scenarios with restricted training data, compared to conventional methods such as regularized least square (RLS) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) based ELMs. The improved performance results from the capacity of ELM to leverage its kernel matrix for optimal fitting, whereas RLS and SGD-ELMs rely on limited observation data for fitting purposes. As such, the ELM method offers a reliable solution for CR and NR systems confronted with constrained resources and complex hardware environments. Furthermore, the developed system architecture permits the integration of the artificial neural network (ANN) based channel estimator with other deep learning algorithms, such as extreme learning machine (ELM) assisted detection, to obtain robust data symbols. The ANNs are also capable of modeling the effects of radio frequency (RF) front-end distortions, enabling the PU to compensate for these hardware impairments during data transmission. Overall, the proposed scheme provides a novel solution for estimating channels in CR and NR systems, Scenarios where conventional techniques prove ineffective. The proposed enhanced ELM learning scheme serves as a viable alternative to traditional machine learning channel estimation techniques, offering superior performance characteristics. Lastly, the developed architecture allows for the integration of the ANNs, which can also model and compensate for hardware impairments, providing an additional layer of robustness to the communication system. The advanced ELM learning scheme has the capacity to be generalized and applied to diverse communication systems and testbeds, enabling the PU to efficiently transmit data to the Cognitive Radio node, which is equipped with the capability to accurately detect the PU's data. The radio node is also empowered to compensate for its own hardware impairments, thanks to the developed architecture, which is independent of profiling losses. The scheme has the capacity to be generalized and applied to diverse communication systems and testbeds, enabling the PU to efficiently transmit data to the Cognitive Radio node, which is equipped with the capacity to accurately detect the PU's data. We introduce a novel concept called selective measurement, an approach distinct from traditional projective measurements in quantum theory. Selective measurement is proposed under the assumption that continual measurements on a quantum system, performed by a coherent observer, necessitate a minimum level of projective measurement occurrence. The theory posits that continual measurements may be viewed as an observer adapting to a quantum system based on its state, and then making decisions based on the resulting projected states. Selective measurement's underlying hypothesis suggests that continual measurements may be categorized into two types: those that resemble projective measurements when the quantum system is in a mixed state, and potentially achieving the same outcomes as projective measurements in certain scenarios involving pure quantum states. Specifically, selective measurement's consistency with projective measurements in the Schrödinger-Albert scenario and the quantum harmonic oscillator scenario is explored. Additionally, the concept of selective measurement is demonstrated to be equivalent to projective measurements in certain circumstances such as the post-selected measurement, the anti-selective measurement, the real-time projection measurement, and the continuous von Neumann measurement. Furthermore, the potential implications and limitations of selective measurement are examined. Selective measurement's theoretical framework is comprised of the theory itself, the theory of observer-systems, the theory of adaptability, the theory of observer-relativity, and the theory of observer-backaction. A general framework for characterizing selective measurement is formulated as a quantum process tensor, and the concept is shown to be equivalent to projective measurements in certain circumstances. Selective measurement's theoretical framework proposes that continual measurements may be viewed as an adapted observer-position in an observer-system. The COVID-19 pandemic has hastened the adoption of contact tracing technologies, which have both enhanced public health and presented novel concerns regarding privacy. Tracing apps have predominantly been developed with a focus on data protection, whereas the underlying infrastructure of contact tracing has received less attention. This ignorance regarding contact tracing infrastructure's (CTI) intricacies can lead to misguided perceptions by the public, flawed media reporting, and government officials with ambiguous intentions. Although CTI's are not typically seen as critical infrastructure, their centralization in governments raises concerns of mass surveillance. Furthermore, media reports have shown mixed results in outlining the measures inherent to contact tracing, contributing to an overall lack of transparency. Crucially, citizens' awareness of contact tracing is fundamental to its effectiveness, prompting an examination of the global literature on IoT's, data protection, law enforcement, and the public sector regarding CTI's transparency. Following an analysis of relevant publications utilizing systematic reviews, case studies, and literature reviews, the research concludes with an outline of policy recommendations aimed at prioritizing transparency in contact tracing technologies. These proposed measures include incorporating data protection principles, establishing an independent review board, launching public education initiatives, and fostering collaboration between private and public sectors. Ultimately, the study seeks to contribute to an understanding of the global contact tracing landscape by highlighting the central role of transparency in the context of pandemic management. With the pandemic enduring despite vaccination efforts, the study provides an overview of the current state of contact tracing and highlights remaining challenges regarding CTI's transparency. Furthermore, the research indicates that global contact tracing is dominated by a few prominent systems, such as TraceNZ and Ireland's StopCOVID, emphasizing the need for further discussion regarding CTI's transparency. As distinctions between public and private efforts are becoming increasingly difficult to discern, the study suggests that collaboration and shared reflection are necessary to navigate these complexities. Ultimately, the research indicates that the success of contact tracing heavily relies on the active participation and informed consent of society. By emphasizing transparency as a national requirement, the study suggests that incorporating elements of democratic reflection can bolster trust in contact tracing and enhance their effectiveness. These measures include incorporating elements of democratic reflection such as public forums and national debates to incorporate society's perspectives into CTI's design. Ultimately, the research proposes that the balance between privacy and efficiency in contact tracing is best served by prioritizing transparency. With the endurance of the pandemic despite vaccination efforts, the study suggests that incorporating elements of transparent contact tracing is imperative. These measures include incorporating elements of transparent contact tracing and fostering reflection on the balance between privacy and efficiency

A quantum system composed of multiple interacting subsystems can become entangled as a result of decoherence from internal interactions. (This is in contrast to entropy increase in a classical system.) To study such behavior, we investigate two models where internal interactions cause decoherence, leading to a quantum system being in a highly entangled state. The first model involves random unitary transformations affecting different subsystems, while the second model uses erasure channels with varying degrees of randomness. In both scenarios, we examine the measure of entanglement in the system and demonstrate how it relates to the decoherence effect. Additionally, we show that maximizing this measure to achieve the highest level of entanglement is not always necessary, as introducing additional randomness to the decoherence effect can actually lead to greater entanglement in certain situations. This research provides an in-depth look at the decoherence effect in quantum systems and offers a unique perspective on randomness's role in entanglement formation. Further study of this topic could reveal new insights into the nature of quantum subsystems interacting and interacting independently. Given the differing criteria for subsystem independence in quantum and classical systems, this topic may have significant implications for both. To confirm this, we investigate how the probability distributions related to these two models behave, providing an answer to whether randomness can increase entanglement formation in random unitary transformations. However, our analysis reveals that these probability distributions fail to satisfy the required conditions for subsystem independence in both the unitary and erasure channel models, indicating that subsystems in these models do indeed behave classically. This finding highlights the difference between entanglement formation in quantum systems and the independence requirement for classical subsystems, underscoring the distinct characteristics of these two system types. To answer the question of whether randomness can increase entanglement formation, our analysis shows that yes, randomness can play a beneficial role in decoherence effects leading to entanglement. However, this relationship is complex and varies depending on the specific model being studied. In the case of the unitary model, introducing additional randomness can actually lead to greater entanglement formation, whereas a similar effect is not observed in the erasure channel model. This discrepancy suggests that entertaining different expectations for randomness's role in these two models may be justified. The likelihood that subsystems passing randomness through will become entangled, as opposed to satisfying the requirements for independent subsystems, is an important consideration. be used to calculate $e^+e^-$ lepton polarizations from reconstructed $J/\psi$

are about 0.45 times those of $J/\psi + J/\chi c$ processes, which is important for
producing transversely polarized muons in $e^+e^-$ collisions. This is because the
$\kappa_{\eta c}$ value is lower, suggesting a reduced BOG enhancement for $\eta c$ compared
to $J\chi c$ production. As a result, muon transversity is expected to be magnified for
$J/\psi + \eta c$ events relative to $J/\psi + J/\chi c$ events. This comparison
establishes a reference point within the BOG framework for $\kappa_{\eta c}$ and
$\kappa_{J/\chi c}$ parameter values. The resulting model, referred to as the
$\kappa$-BOG model, offers a standardized framework for determining the polarization
behavior of muons resulting from $e^+e^-$ collisions. Furthermore, this standardization
facilitates the examination of polarization correlations between muons and electrons.

the correlations follow $(\hat{s}/2, \hat{s}/2, \hat{p}_T, \hat{p}_T)$, whereas

\hat{p}_T,-\hat{p}_T)$, showing a symmetry between these two processes.

Users' understanding of the security strengths of identification methods is crucial in determining their security behavior. Despite the escalating adoption of Signal PINs as a primary form of identification on Signal, a secure encrypted messaging platform, there is a lack of research examining the security safeguards of Signal PINs. Our study delves into how regular users perceive the security robustness of Signal PINs in relation to other identification methods, suchishes as fingerprint or PINs from other services. The results from an online survey of 119 participants showed that only 22 users understood the primary purpose of Signal PINs in enhancing end-to-end encryption, with most viewing them as a means of identification rather than true encryption methods. Consequently, this limited understanding led to poorer security practices in relation to Signal PINs, such as using easy-to-guess characters or failing to back up the PIN. The study highlights an urgent need for Signal to educate its users about the security benefits of Signal PINs. Moreover, users should understand the security strengths of their assigned encryption keys by learning about the applied encryption methods. Our study's data contributes to the existing knowledge on the security safeguards of Signal PINs by offering valuable insights to developers designing secure identification methods. The study ultimately advocates for the integration of additional features within Signal to enhance the security safeguards of Signal PINs. These features include integrating optional biometric authentication or multiple choice options for PIN assignment. The associated study can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.02469. The study's data has been made available at https://doi.org/10.21227/M7ykxgM4.signalPINunderstanding. The LSIS 2021 Conference Chair can be reached at g.nakkerud@usn.no. The survey's account managers at Upwork and Clickworker as well as the Norwegian University of Science and Technology's Department of Informatics are also highly appreciated. In conclusion, the primary purpose of this paper is to provide an in-depth examination of the security safeguards of Signal PINs. The survey's findings reveal users' insecurity in the security safeguards of Signal PINs but simultaneously show the scarcity of studies in this area. The study's data highlights that Signal PINs suffer from an inherent security flaw rooted in their design but also indicate the scarcity of studies in this area. The study suggests possible solutions to enhance the security safeguards

I've developed multiple formulas for solar-weighted quadrature, targeting scenarios where direct irradiance is the primary concern. These formulas are applicable when spatial and angular patterns in solar radiation are separable. They offer efficient solutions for simulations involving non-uniform objects that face the sun full-on. These solar-weighted quadrature formulas are particularly beneficial in situations where precise tracking of angular and spatial patterns is not necessary. This technique might experience a resurgence due to increasing demands for precision in solar energy predictions.
