Due to the vast amount of data (approximately 10 to 100 petabytes) and specific requirements such as real-time data transmission or analysis timeframes, direct data assessment becomes impractical using high-performance computing systems. However, significant speedups can be achieved by applying specialized hardware like FPGAs, which we will be exploring in our research. We introduce an efficient data processing technique optimized for processing 223 strain gauge signals with an integrated Fourier transform, highly suitable for handling large-scale data from radio telescopes. To validate the efficacy of our method, we conducted extensive experiments and achieved an impressive acceleration of the data processing rate by up to 65 times compared to standard CPU execution. Notably, our accelerated system is capable of handling 4 million data samples per second, which would take a high-end computer approximately 65 times longer to process. Moreover, our integrated Fourier transform accelerated by up to 3.7 times compared to a specialized GPU implementation. These outstanding acceleration gains make our proposed algorithm highly suitable for hardware integration, particularly where data acquisition and processing occur in tandem, as in the instance of radio telescopes receiving and analyzing signal data in real-time. We argue that the exceptional performance of our algorithm, reinforced by its simplicity, indicates that it has the potential to enhance the efficiency of computing systems used in a broader range of scientific instruments and tools. Moreover, our research illustrates the considerable impact an FPGA accelerator can have when applied to real-world data processing tasks. Calculating a movie's predicted revenue is a problem that has been the focus of intense research in the entertainment industry. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach based on recurrent regression models, aiming to incorporate the temporal aspect of box office sales. Furthermore, we introduce a new method to determine the cultural impact of a movie star through social media analysis and establish a connection between a movie's success and its starring actor's influence. We gather a vast dataset of movie releases, their box office performances, and the power ratings of leading actors, and use conventional evaluation metrics to assess the performance of our model. By taking a predictive approach, our model achieves substantial improvements in forecasting accuracy as the forecast period increases. For example, our model achieves a 31.45% decrease in MAE at t=5.5 weeks ahead compared to the baseline. We also show that our model's performance exceeds that of a baseline that uses historical box office data, demonstrating that incorporating social data can enhance revenue prediction accuracy. Finally, our study highlights the significant contribution of a movie's star to its commercial success, and our method outperforms existing research in this area. We plan to make our code and dataset publicly available to facilitate future research in this domain. As the entertainment industry is increasingly influenced by the internet, our approach provides valuable insights for marketers, producers, and fans. Furthermore, our method may be adapted for applications such as forecasting sports ratings or evaluating the popularity of TV shows and podcasts based on their stars. We hope that our research will lead to the development of more predictive models based on social data. By exploring the relationship between a movie's success and its starring actor's influence, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the movie industry. As the rise of social media continues to grow at a faster rate than the movie industry, our model represents a significant opportunity for revenue enhancement. This work investigates the application of a new approach to stability analysis for power networks in frequency domains, with a focus on its practical application in designing secondary frequency control protocols. Building on the development of a matrix-based frequency response model for power networks, we establish a novel method for calculating the stability of these systems and define a criterion for determining stable operating points. We go on to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by designing an optimal secondary frequency control protocol that meets the desired stability standards across diverse power network configurations. The resulting design not only ensures stability but also provides a means for power system operators to influence voltage dynamics through active management of secondary frequency control. Empirical studies confirm that our approach yields a balanced compromise between stability and tracking accuracy, offering robust performance under a wide range of power demand scenarios. Furthermore, we verify the efficacy of our protocol by comparing it to existing design methods across different power network topologies and secondary frequency control requirements. The research offers a comprehensive and practical solution to the problem of secondary frequency control design, encompassing a range of power network topologies and operation scenarios. Finally, we identify the limitations of conventional power network models when applied to integrated AC/DC power networks, paving the way for future research in this area to address these limitations. However, current light field compression methods typically prioritize a single representation, leading to suboptimal results. In this research, a compression model named LightFLAC is proposed that accurately captures the inherent coherence of these images by employing a hierarchical disparity representation. Furthermore, LightFLAC is an extension of the FLAC image compression model, allowing for the tailored adaptation of coefficients for light fields via the introduction of a disparity-cost model. The formation of planetesimals is thought to occur due to the simultaneous presence of turbulence and density fluctuations in protoplanetary disks.  To better understand how dust grains evolve within these disks, we investigate the simultaneous occurrence of magnetorotational turbulence and density fluctuations using 3D simulations that incorporate the effects of both gravity and the magnetohydrodynamic effect.  This study builds upon previous research by describing dust behavior in protoplanetary disks, particularly how dust sedimentation accelerates in areas away from the disk's center.  Unlike previous research, we discovered that dust sedimentation is slower in the disk's centeral region when compared to its upper layers, due to an increase in turbulence fluctuations occurring on small scales in those regions.  Turbulence fluctuations in areas away from the disk's center are primarily driven by variations in the disk's ionization levels, while those occurring near the disk's center are driven by changes in the disk's net charge.  As a result, dust density fluctuations become more synchronized with pressure fluctuations at higher elevations in the disk.  This trend is reversed for angular momentum fluctuations, as we find that angular momentum fluctuations are more synchronized with pressure fluctuations in the disk's centeral region, yet less synchronized in its upper layers.  Overall, our findings indicate that dust behavior can vary significantly depending on the disk's spatial location and that using average turbulence levels to predict planetesimal formation efficiencies may be insufficient.  Therefore, we recommend using a more comprehensive efficiency formula that takes into account the complex interplay between turbulence and density fluctuations in protoplanetary disks.  Future research should seek to incorporate the effects of this paper's simulations on dust evolution when studying planetesimal formation. We explore the concept of local type spaces within continuous logic and establish a direct correspondence between these spaces and the duality of abelian groups across a fixed scalar field. Our approach involves creating a map that not only preserves logical and model-theoretic properties but also retains isomorphisms between associated Hilbert spaces. This equivalence has far-reaching implications, enabling us to demonstrate that any local continuous logic framework can be mimicked using the Hilbert space duality method developed by Borel. Furthermore, we utilize this equivalence to prove that local continuous logic frameworks are inherently equivalent to standard first-order logic systems. Our research incorporates an extensive collection of model theory theorems, providing a novel foundation for understanding and deriving facts about Hilbert space duality methods. In addition, we extend an existing finite duality theorem for abelian groups to cover scalar fields and establish that the resulting Hilbert space duality method encompasses Araki-Wyler duality. Our work also includes a comprehensive classification of local Hilbert space models, revealing that they can be generated from finite Hilbert space duality methods. Ultimately, we utilize this equivalence to prove that any local continuous logic framework can be reduced to a first-order logic system through a process analogous to Vaught's theorem. This research further expands our knowledge by establishing that local continuous logic frameworks encompass a broad range of other logic frameworks, including continuous logic, Hilbert space logic, and operator algebra logic. Our final achievement involves connecting the concept of local type spaces within continuous logic to the realm of quantum mechanics, highlighting its potential to shed new light on quantum principles through model theory. Additionally, we show that the potential applications of our work extend beyond quantum mechanics, encompassing other areas such as $C^*$-algebra theory and operator topology. Furthermore, we observe some intriguing similarities between the characteristics of our logic framework and features observed in quantum mechanics, such as compactness and positivity. However, our logic framework does not exhibit another typical quantum mechanic property: anticommutativity. Our research aims to explore this connection further, offering insights into what specifically sets quantum mechanics apart from this logic framework. Consequently, our model-theoretic approach may yield significant insights into the underlying principles of quantum mechanics. In the course of our research, we have identified numerous open questions and avenues of exploration that could contribute to a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics. One particular question that arises from our work is whether quantum mechanics can be characterized as a specific sub-classification within our logic framework. This article discusses the integration of ethical considerations into machine learning processes. It explores the role of fairness metrics, the advantages of federated learning for data privacy, and a proposed framework that combines these elements with differential privacy. The system aims to address machine learning's inherent ethical complications, utilizing a movie ratings dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Due to the rising concerns about personal data privacy following recent data breaches, especially those affecting user populations, our research focuses on uncovering the links between data privacy, fairness, and the implementation of machine learning models. Therefore, our study delves into the integration of these essential aspects, revealing that differential privacy can facilitate both data privacy protection and the achievement of fair machine learning models through a proposed deployment on a federated learning platform. Nonetheless, our analysis reveals that leveraging differential privacy to enhance fairness comes with limitations, including reduced model precision and unpredictability in the efficacy of fairness metrics when privacy is strictly enforced. These issues not only reduce the accuracy but also render traditional metrics unreliable under certain privacy settings. This research aspires to contribute to the understanding of the relationships between data privacy, fairness, and the ethical dimensions of machine learning by providing valuable insights into the intersection of these concepts. Moreover, our study aims to highlight the practical complexities and constraints associated with machine learning in an ethical context, specifically regarding the trade-off between achieving fairness, maintaining data privacy, and the overall performance of the model. In addition, our research will explore whether differential privacy can effectively address the privacy concerns of users while fostering a fair machine learning environment. In safe control, pinpointing the optimal action to achieve desired goals while avoiding hazards is of paramount importance. A new method, building on nonlinear programming and neural networks, has been developed to safely address complex dynamical systems. By optimizing control policies within a designated safety area using learned constraint models, the proposed algorithm safely explores the state space. In contrast to other reinforcement learning approaches that prioritize high rewards over safety, our method effectively learns robust control policies that work across a wide range of dynamic scenarios. Moreover, our method exhibits superior performance when faced with limited data, yielding more accurate results. We validated the proposed algorithm using multiple safe control problems, demonstrating its superiority over other reinforcement learning methods. A fascinating finding revealed that the constraint models learned through safe exploration enabled our method to withstand noisy dynamical systems not encountered during training. In a remarkable example, our method successfully adapted to a bunny's dynamics that were abruptly introduced after initial learning, showcasing our approach's robustness and generalizability. Following the success of Generative Adversarial Networks, related architecture variations, and relation-aware designs have been experimented with to enhance their performance. A novel GAN architecture, the RelationGAN, was introduced to achieve high-quality image generation by establishing a new relation between the input vector and generated images through a stable and consistent output value. Experimentation showed that this approach produced highly realistic images and suggested a novel application for relation learning in GANs, while also offering advantages over existing architectures in both low and high resolution image generation tasks. Notably, results showed that RelationGAN produced higher quality images than StyleGAN in a task where subjects identified fabricated facial images from a set. The relation-learning design in the RelationGAN resulted in several benefits, including the elimination of a secondary learning process, the reduction of a significant computation step, and the capability to generate images at high resolution that are unique for each input vector. Overall, the relation-learning design in the RelationGAN offers many benefits. Furthermore, an evaluation of its architecture designs showed that a linear learning approach for the relation module yielded superior outcomes when compared to variations of a degree of freedom. It was also observed that a reduction in a particular computation step led to an improvement in the speed at which the model could translate inputs. Lastly, the results of an evaluation of the generated images revealed that they often received a higher score from a perception model when compared to a network trained using a different state-of-the-art image synthesis method. Quantum communication networks need to identify specific data transmission paths to function efficiently under noisy conditions. Currently, phase-based methods are the primary means of establishing a global phase reference to support quantum key distribution (QKD). We've developed an innovative approach that leverages reference frames to facilitate global phase recovery for twin-field QKD. By analyzing the connection between reference frames and global phases, and proposing a model to quantify the phase estimation process, we show that our method can accurately determine the global phase with high efficiency and minimal reliance on specific data input. Furthermore, the proposed protocol is robust against potential errors and can be used to establish a global phase reference in diverse quantum communication systems. Additionally, we've analyzed the requirements for generating reference frames in practical twin-field QKD implementations and found that they can be satisfied using existing technology. We also explored the potential security flaws in the phase estimation model and proposed ways to counter them. Overall, our study provides valuable insights for the practical application of global phase references in QKD communications. It further examines the invertibility of these operators and their relationship to a parameter-dependent metric on the symbol space. By drawing parallels to a well-known result for the standard Bergman space, the authors prove that a symbol leads to a invertible Toeplitz operator on the p-Fock space, and this operator corresponds to a projection operator on the symbol space. Conversely, the authors also identify necessary conditions for a symbol to support invertible Toeplitz operators on the p-Bergman space, and they propose a conjecture in this regard that is confirmed in the case where p equals 2. Moreover, the authors are able to generalize known results previously obtained by other researchers, and they are also able to generate a list of symbols for which invertible Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space do exist. It is also shown, in the course of this investigation, that a certain set of functions serves as a complete metric invariant for the class of symbols for which invertible Toeplitz operators on the p-Fock space do exist. A common challenge in object detection tasks within computer vision involves obtaining accurate annotations for data samples. While comprehensive annotations including mask information can significantly enhance detector performance, such detailed tasks are time-consuming and may not always be feasible due to limited resources. In this paper, we explore a cost-effective approach to generate pseudo bounding-box annotations based on the concept of compactness, thereby supplementing existing annotation sets. By defining compact regions within an image, we can identify multiple detection candidates within a predefined scale, allowing us to generate pseudo boxes for each detection. Our method for generating these pseudo boxes data (PBD) differs from standard augmentation-based approaches as it involves examining detection variability within distinct spatial contexts. By combining our PBD methodology with standard data augmentation, we can create supplementary data (SD) to complement existing annotation sets. Our research evaluates the effectiveness of this data complement approach on two frameworks: Faster R-CNN and SOLOv2, showcasing notable performance improvements on the MS-COCO dataset when incorporating our proposed supplementary data alongside regular data augmentation. As a result, our approach bridges the gap between existing annotation sets and those lacking mask information via efficient, cost-free data augmentation. Furthermore, our PBD methodology also serves as a novel variant in the family of pseudo labeling techniques. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hi-ml/dynamic-box-data. Overall, our approach delivers superior results when incorporating our proposed supplementary data alongside regular data augmentation, yielding a 2.5% increase in mean average precision (MAP) at 10 recall levels for the COCO 'car' category when compared to standard data augmentation alone. In contrast, the average MAP improvement for various 64x64 object categories under different learning regimes is 1.3%; incorporating our proposed method for these categories yields a notable MAP improvement of 1.9%. Our approach effectively supplements existing annotation sets with multiple instances of varying box annotations. As such, our technique may also find applications in novel domains requiring various box annotations, such as image-to-image translation using box-based contextual information. In image-to-image translation tasks, our method can serve as a powerful regulator in both unsupervised and supervised learning environments. Our findings illustrate the efficacy of our proposed approach, demonstrating a notable increase of 4.04 of the structural Simon-s-Kit dataset's metric of compactness, and a significant improvement of 3.35 of the dataset's metric of variance. These gains in compactness and variance were achieved through a method involving both box translation and regular data augmentation.

Transformers emerged as a promising alternative to traditional convolutional networks by leveraging self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range interactions. Despite their success in machine translation, it remains unclear how well they generalize to other tasks. This work explores the ability of Transformers to excel in the "Super-Glue" chemical reaction prediction task, which is typically addressed using convolual networks. By integrating the essential inductive biases associated with convolutional networks into the Transformer architecture, our results show that it is indeed capable of achieving comparable performance. This outcome implies that the advantages of convolutional networks are largely artifacts of the tasks they were designed for, and that Transformers have the potential to surpass them in a wider range of applications. Additionally, our analysis sheds light on the unique characteristics of the Transformer architecture that allow it to outperform convolual networks when it matters most. These distinguishing features are particularly visible when the goal is to make accurate predictions in cases where the input data may be incomplete or where the focus is on detecting rare occurrences. Moreover, our results show that incorporating the concept of channel attention is essential for teaching the Transformer to adapt to changes in data formats while retaining its ability to compress long-term information in an efficient manner. Finally, our results suggest that the ability of the Transformer to capture long-term interactions is no longer unique once the right inductive biases are incorporated, and that the question of which architecture is superior thus boils down to a matter of interpretation. For instance, under the interpretation that the input should remain unchanged, the Transformer is actually less powerful than convolual networks, whereas when the data is understood to be constant, the benefits of the Transformer become apparent. Overall, our results deliver a decisive verdict in the ongoing debate between convolutional and transformer-based representations: there is no winner: they are simply different. They capture different aspects of the world and fail miserably when forced to conform to the other's inductive biases. They should thus be seen as unique and valuable tools, but a matter of personal taste, rather than a question of who is more superior. Our results are consistent with a vision of AI systems as diverse sensors with distinct capabilities that should be leveraged according to their individual characteristics, rather than a uniform solution applicable in all situations. Our results serve as an inspiration for other AI researchers to question the implicit assumptions behind their choice of representation, to explore its limitations and to see the world from a different perspective. Recent advancements in mortality forecasting have leveraged detailed information and sophisticated statistical techniques, however the inherent structure of mortality data often goes unaccounted for, leading to diminished predictions. This study introduces a novel Bayesian framework incorporating time-varying factor loadings and dynamic common trends to effectively model mortality patterns. We demonstrate that incorporating this information significantly enhances prediction accuracy compared to conventional methods. We also illustrate how the proposed approach effectively captures the impact of significant historical events such as the Ministry of Health's 2019 public health alert in Hong Kong. Furthermore, we derive practical guidelines for effectively utilizing this model as a decision-making tool for mortality-related applications and stakeholders, particularly in the under-resourced public sector. This methodology is developed using a comprehensive dataset of life insurance data but is suitable for any detailed mortality time series. Moreover, with the advent of widespread COVID-19 infections, concern is mounting over its potential long-term effects on human mortality, necessitating the need for sophisticated statistical analysis and modeling to grasp the intricate relationship between mortality and infectious diseases. This research aims to address this pressing issue by applying advanced statistical techniques to better comprehend and predict mortality trends. Additionally, we examine the efficacy of various machine learning methods in predicting COVID-19 incidence and consider the feasibility of leveraging mortality modeling as an inverse problem, where advanced algorithms are used to forecast outcomes from detailed data. This initial exploration paves the way for more intricate analysis and exploration of the link between mortality and infectious diseases, representing an vital area of research for understanding and forecasting the long-term consequences of COVID-19 on human mortality. Interference from previously seen datasets significantly hampers neural architecture search performance. To resolve this challenge, we treat the interference as a low-rank perturbation to validate an optimal solution, then develop two methods for eliminating or reducing the interference: an interference elimination module and a reconstruction module. Through experiments on NAS-Bench-301 and re-designing the generator of a language model to reproduce interference, we discovered that our methods outperform state-of-the-art models like RoBERTa and ELECTRA by 16% to 23% in terms of top-1 accuracy. A translator's performance is often judged based on a quiz that includes both translated text and hidden answers. However, this traditional method has a flaw: the ability to guess the correct translation is high due to most sentences having only one acceptable translation. To address this issue, we've developed a new assessment approach that countering the "guessing advantage" effectively measures translator ability. We've also revised how we score translations to reflect more than just grammatical error in translations, expanding what is considered an acceptable translation. Two new types of reviews are also introduced: a review of complete sentences to evaluate fluency and an analysis of the translator's vocabulary to ensure it is relevant, accurate and sufficient. To compare the efficiency of the new and old assessment methods, we simulated a study using 300 translated and 300 new sentences, evaluating the impact on translator rewards in a crowdsourcing setting. We've found that the elevated level of sentence specificity required for new translations results in slight losses in rewards when considering the quality of translations, but the new evaluation methods yield more precise insights into translator performance, leading to greater rewards consistency. We've seen similar patterns in the actual data from a crowdsourcing platform. Ultimately, the new assessment method excels at identifying skilled translators while yielding slightly less in rewards, however the new evaluation method yields more precise metrics on translator performance, gives more importance to translation quality, and selects more skilled translators. We carry out the large-charge expansion for the Visco-Ferell model, a theoretical model designed to accurately describe the behavior of charge Q, including its interaction with an external magnetic field, in a two-dimensional superconductor. By employing Wilson's exact mapping, we transform the model into a $Z_2$ gauge theory with a complex Higgs field. We then calculate the expectation value of the square of the electric flux in the time direction and analyze its leading behavior as charge Q increases. From this analysis, we derive the leading coefficients of the critical exponents associated with the superconducting phase transition. We compare these findings to Monte-Carlo simulations, noting satisfactory agreement between our theoretical results and the simulations. Additionally, we extend our theoretical model to include the effect of a complex chemical potential, categorizing the resulting phases according to the fundamental degrees of freedom present in the system. We particularly focus on configurations predominantly governed by the $Z_2$ gauge field. By calculating specific critical points in the phase diagram, we determine the corresponding critical exponents. Additionally, our method surpasses recent state-of-the-art domain adaptive techniques that use unlabeled data from a specific domain to achieve better generalization performance. Consequently, our domain adaptive model demonstrates superior performance to baseline supervised models, which require supervision from a particular domain. Within a large interference network, where many transmitters and receivers are scattered across the landscape, we investigate the efficacy of binary power control for each node to minimize the average interference experienced by its partner node, given its geographical position and of the surrounding nodes. Despite being a straightforward method, binary power control surprisingly approaches optimality as the number of nodes grows, as proven through analysis. To further illustrate its performance, numerical simulations demonstrate that it compares favorably to optimal control, yielding similar results, and also outperforms more complex, but suboptimal, methods, such as ant colony optimization and a related binary control technique, in terms of data rates achieved. Moreover, binary power control boasts the advantage of being the fastest method to boot. Finally, considering its simplicity, binary power control's performance gap to optimal control tends to be modest, making it a practically appealing method for use in networks comprising a considerable number of nodes. However, as the number of nodes grows very large, its performance gap to optimality also tends to become more severe. Thus, although binary power control is a viable solution for large networks, it may be less effective when the number of nodes is extremely large. To quantify this, we derive an approximation expressing the relative optimality gap of binary power control in terms of the total number of nodes in the network. As shown, this relative gap is expected to be low for networks comprising a considerable number of nodes, but as the total number of nodes continues to increase, so too does the relative gap, making binary power control less desirable for networks comprising an excessively large number of nodes. As such, additional work may be needed to refine this binary method as the number of nodes in the network continues to grow. To derive mass functions for this paradigm, we developed a natural language processing method based on the semantic orientation technique of sentential similarity. This approach involves creating sentences reflecting the subsets of a set of an accountant's interest and calculating their positive or negative orientation in relation to a universe of financial resources. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining NLP and uncertainty handling for nary financial analysis, an innovative area combining both domains. The FEAM's theoretical foundation offers a sophisticated approach for handling complex financial data involving multiple auditors, while its application in nary financial analysis provides practical insights for decision-makers. Furthermore, the integration of mass functions and FEAM facilitates seamless handling of financial data across accounting periods. In a multitasking environment, successfully managing a continuum of tasks depends on the schedule and sharing strategy. Considering the tendency for task lists to be diverse, we explore a scenario in which the capacity of processors is divided among tasks to maintain uniform waiting times. Varying the ratio of shared processing capacity can significantly impact schedule design. We develop mathematical models, based on an ordinary differential equation, to analyze how task lists evolve in response to varying scheduling approaches. Additionally, by examining task lists through the lens of entropy, we identify optimal task division within a system. We also investigate the strategy of task sequence, focusing on the problem of minimizing waiting times. Drawing upon information theory, we reveal that a greedy algorithm yields the most efficient sequence. Furthermore, we identify a minimal threshold for task division efficiency and discuss its implications. Lastly, we demonstrate that a particular distribution of processing time, characterized by an exponential probability density function with a half-cauchy shape, is ideal for dividing capacity and managing diverse tasks effectively. This optimal distribution provides valuable insight into the efficient multitasking scenario. We validate these findings through numerical examples and computational simulations. In doing so, we reveal the benefits of an adaptive sharing ratio, specifically designed to vary in proportion to the square root of the task count. This ratio is thought to naturally arise from the model, though it can also be intentionally implemented. We explore an implementation idea, suggesting that a dynamic system can regulate the sharing ratio through a control mechanism. Ultimately, we explore the potential for further optimization beyond the waiting time minimization and identify avenues for continuing research. The developed schedule designs hold relevance in a broad range of applications where tasks evolve over time, such as real-time systems, database management systems, the execution of batch jobs, and multiprocessor architecture design. Large-scale Internet of Things (IoT) deployments face numerous challenges when deploying Firmware Updates (FUAs).  To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes Concurrent Transmissions (CT) within a centralized updating system. By enhancing transmission efficiency, our method minimizes update time, increases system scalability, and improves FUA success rate.  Furthermore, CT allows the flexible adaptation of mean time between failures in industrial devices, enabling the immediate recovery of critical equipment.  Extensive simulations utilizing real-world IoT devices have been conducted to validate the efficacy of our approach.  Key outcomes demonstrate that CT substantially boosts FUA rate, significantly decreases update time, and provides industrial-grade reliability.  Moreover, our method outperforms current centralized and distributed updating systems, with CT showing particular efficacy in large-scale IoT environments.  Overall, our solution offers an innovative and efficient solution for updating IoT devices.  As such, it holds great promise for addressing the inherent difficulties associated with FUAs. Radio propagation modeling based on ray tracing techniques is a common approach used in indoor environments where accuracy can be compromised due to low spatial observation density of receivers. Traditional ray tracing requires input on area dimensions and placement, and it often relies on computational intensity to ensure model precision. Recent advancements in radio propagation modeling based on deep neural networks have shown potential, particularly for outdoor environments, due to their ability to learn observed radio signal characteristics. This paper proposes using a deep neural network model adapted from a convolutional autoencoder, termed ProMap, for enhancing radio propagation modeling in indoor settings. By utilizing measured radio signal intensity, the proposed method learns and replicates the radio signal characteristics observed at various locations, thereby reducing modeling errors. Compared to conventional ray tracing methods, the results demonstrate that the proposed ProMap model exhibits comparable accuracy when trained with data obtained through measurements on a single floor levels. The method also appears to be tolerant of modeling data irregularities, such as imperfect modeling of room configurations and radio signal losses, and it can be applied to radio signal strength as well as polarization characteristics. The method has also been tested in scenarios with limited observation densities, demonstrating its ability to generalize to unobserved areas. The method has been shown to achieve a mean absolute error of less than 2 dB when predicting radio signal strength across all observed areas, and this error remains below 4 dB when signal strength is predicted at unobserved locations. The method has also been applied to radio signal polarization with similar accuracy and generalization capabilities. The potential challenges and limitations of this method are also discussed, and this work presents an initial investigation into deep neural network-based radio propagation modeling for indoor settings. The code used to implement this method is available at a publicly accessible repository, and this work presents a prospective outlook for using such models to reduce propagation modeling errors in wireless simulation applications. The proposed method has been shown to enhance radio propagation modeling in indoor scenarios by advancing the state-of-the-art accuracy when compared with established techniques based on machine learning. The study also identifies areas for potential further research in this field. The study presents an initial exploration into the use of deep neural networks for indoor propagation modeling, and it outlines existing obstacles that would need to be addressed in order to implement such models in real-world applications. The database used to train and evaluate the proposed method consists of radio signal characteristics measured at 110 offices located across 34 countries across the globe. The method has been tested using radio signal observations collected at 5-second intervals, and it demonstrates an initial capability to generalize to unobserved areas

For a market with firms hiring skilled workers, we found that when workers rate their options publicly, it leads to less favorable outcomes for all agents, as compared to a scenario where ratings are hidden. This is also observed in a larger class of markets, where a single central entity distributes scarce resources to competing groups. In these cases, public rating systems tend to favor groups with smaller sizes. By extending existing solutions, our work presents a comprehensive analysis of how public rating systems impact stable matchings across various types of markets. It also confirms that in markets with free entry and a limited number of options, public rating systems may not always benefit participants. Only in specific contexts, such as small markets with a large number of options, does the public rating system lead to more favorable outcomes for all agents. Our work also offers guidance on how agents can effectively utilize public rating systems to make informed decisions, by identifying situations in which it is beneficial to enter markets early or opt for smaller groups when possible. SummScore incorporates a new exact match search algorithm called ExactRank, which enhances the connection between a summary and its reference sentence by leveraging a ranking task powered by neural network architecture Transformer. This enables exact match to be paired with high semantic similarity, thereby improving the recall of correct exact matches. In testing SummScore on various datasets, it consistently outperformed existing metrics across diversity and consistency metrics and produced a notable 21-point increase in human-evaluation scores over the top previous metric, further confirming its superiority. By differentiating the flucuating hydrodynamics equations of incompressible fluids, we have derived a wave-like partial differential equation that characterizes the energy dissipation of 3D turbulence. This flucuating equation retains the nonlocal characteristic of its hydraulic counterpart and indicates that energy dissipation is directly proportional to the turbulence's kinetic energy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the deterministic Navier-Stokes equations fail to accurately account for energy dissipation in turbulent flows, particularly at large scales, due to the absence of nonlocal interactions. Instead, the fluid behaves as if it contains an additional, short-wavelength mode that is influenced by fluctuations in the long-wavelength wavepacket, thereby facilitating energy transfer and flow behavior. We have also employed numerical simulations to verify our analytical Navier-Stokes findings. According to these analyses, the energy behavior described by the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equations is significantly more accurate than that predicted by the deterministic model, displaying improved agreement with measurements of 3D turbulence. Finally, we have extended our hydraulic findings to incorporate effects related to compressibility, turbulence scale, and exotic fluid properties like negative binomial distributions. The application of these flucuating equations to describe flow behavior in diverse fluidic systems holds significant practical significance. For instance, in biological systems, the equations can provide insights into the dynamic interactions between solutes, cells, and fluid dynamics, while in engineering contexts, the knowledge gained can inform the design of machines that interact with fluid flows. We anticipate that the incorporation of additional physical effects via renormalization group techniques will further expand the scope of these flucuating hydrodynamics equations. Moreover, our approach may also shed light on the long-standing problem of flow enhancement in superlubricity, by identifying the long-wavelength wavepacket that facilitates energy transfer and flow behavior. This study showcases the versatility of lasers by leveraging thermal gradient imaging. We utilize a laser passed through a He--Ne tube inserted into a hot fluid to observe distinct diffraction patterns, which serve as evidence of spatial intensity fluctuations. The resulting patterns not only demonstrate the ability to visualize thermal gradient distributions in traditional 2D and 3D formats, but also enable real-time, color-coded temperature mapping. The use of a laser in this setup offers an innovative vision for thermal imaging techniques, exploiting an otherwise underutilized aspect of laser technology. Additionally, this approach has the potential to analyze optical phase shifts, thereby enabling precise in-depth temperature measurements. As a means of further experimentation, this study also employs the Mach--Zehnder interferometry method in tandem with the thermal fluid for comparison purposes, and the observed results are discussed in comparison to simulated temperature profiles obtained via numerical calculations based on the Boussinesq approximation. Furthermore, this study further expands on the concept of laser thermal imaging by employing multiple lasers with varying wavelengths to observe predicted intensity modulations according to their wavelength differences. The resulting images illustrate a systematic modification in measured intensity gradients across changing color spectra from red to violet, thus validating the thermal imaging capabilities of the proposed method. Lastly, this study proposes a thermal imaging technique incorporating geometric distortion analysis for compensating thermal phase shift distortions, thereby enhancing the overall precision of temperature measurements. The practical applications of laser thermal gradient imaging are discussed at the end of this study. It is anticipated that this method will contribute to the advancement in the field of thermal imaging technologies. Differently trained AI models can draw various conclusions when answering the same question, which raises concerns about their validity. This issue affects not only machine comprehension but also design - the extraction of design principles and rules from datasets. In design mining, multiple AI models are used to increase conclusion stability and improve the application of design to complex systems. This study employs datasets from two domains, suggesting that higher conclusion stability is linked to a more cross-project consistent set of design rules. Researchers explored multiple techniques to enhance conclusion stability, including training multiple models under human guidance, using natural language generators to present models' views, and combining conclusions from multiple models. They found that guiding AI models during training helps stabilize their conclusions and yields more cross-project consistent design rules when compared to models trained alone. Additionally, discussing conclusions with human designers refined the models' views as perceived by the designers, leading to more consistent designs across projects. These findings have implications for improving design mining transparency and understanding. Lastly, discussing design with human specialists can pave the way for incorporating human-style errors in AI models, which may seem contradictory at first glance but can actually contribute to more reliable design conclusions. This research aims to lay the groundwork for developing new design methods and methods for measuring AI reliability that take into account the role of human specialists in shaping design. It sheds light on the current state of design through AI and steps towards increasing the reliability of design methods. This research conducts an extensive literature review on design through AI, investigating the benefits and drawbacks of different design mining techniques in terms of output quality, transparency, and accountability. It identifies areas of agreement within the research community regarding the benefits of these methods but finds no unified views on their drawbacks. Ultimately, this research aims to increase awareness of the benefits and drawbacks of using AI in design methods, leading to more informed decision-making about design tools and practices. It aims to lay the groundwork for systemic analyses of the benefits and drawbacks of AI-powered design tools and to contribute to ongoing discussions regarding AI use in design. Generally, this research explores how designing with AI alters the relationship between designers and these systems, especially human specialists, and seeks to increase awareness of the ethical implications of designing with AI. It specifically looks at AI as a working tool rather than a replacement for design methods and practices, and as such, raises fundamental questions about the role of AI in design methods and practices. publication trends across decades. To this end, we have gathered a comprehensive
dataset of over 2.6 million publishing records from 1967 to 2019, covering
key metrics like paper titles, authors, and references, as well as venue names
and their categorization. By examining the rise and fall of individual research
fields and the venues associated with them, we have drawn insights from both
quantitative and qualitative analyses. Besides identifying the emergence and
decline of research fields and venues, our dataset also reveals the flow of
ideas across fields, measured by citing relationships. Furthermore, it allows us
to examine how researchers interact through collaboration networks. With these
tools, we can examine the evolution of communities centered around certain
research topics and their spatial dispersion, revealing how geographical and
temporal patterns have shifted over time. By addressing the top research fields
and their associated publication venues, we have drawn conclusions about the
shifts in attention given to software development, data management, and cybersecurity
over the past five decades. In addition, by looking at the publishing records of
individual researchers, we have drawn conclusions about the transient research fields
investigated by prominent scholars. The construction of our dataset, as well as all
associated code and analysis, can be accessed at https://github.com/arsinetr/cs-
evolution. Moreover, a visualization platform with processed data is available at

We introduce a novel class of functorial clustering schemes that address the 'cherry picking' issue in single-linkage clustering, where the result is often dependent on the order of data points. Our approach maintains consistency within a category framework, analogous to concepts in topological space clustering like metric space clustering and persistent homology. It involves adding a category with morphisms reflecting similarity measures and a hierarchy of levels to analyze the clustering at each layer. Furthermore, we develop algorithms to compute such structures and examine the mathematical underpinnings of these algorithms in specific cases. Experiments with a method called nearest-star clustering show that our framework, especially when combined with density estimates, offers precise and detailed analysis of data sets using nested and extended metric spaces. This approach also allows for identifying essential features and estimating data distribution shapes by examining the difference between the original and transformed clustering schemes. As a result, it can facilitate data visualization, highlight significant characteristics, detect anomalies, and establish relationships between data points in metric spaces. Similarly, it can provide insights into the features of data points in hierarchical classification systems by applying a category version of the topological cohomology process, that is, persistent cohomology. A significant challenge in completing a streaming video's missing frames is addressing the changing factor matrices and knowledge growth over time. Previous methods, relying on historical data and assuming stability, have struggled with accuracy when faced with videos containing moving objects. This paper presents a novel, real-time streaming tensor completion algorithm, adapting to the dynamic factors and growing knowledge without any assumptions about the video content. The proposed method accurately reconstructs the missing frames using a model that learns the linear factors based on both the available data in each video segment and the historical information in previous segments. This allows for predicting the missing frames in the current segment. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in precision and visual quality, particularly on videos with moving objects. Additionally, we conducted a thorough parameter sensitivity analysis and demonstrated the real-time capability of the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, we applied this method to restore a real-world video taken during a car ride. Video sequences generated from the reconstructed frames are indistinguishable from the actual video. Specifically, we observed minimal visual disruption in a video of a person holding a mask during COVID-19 lockdown situations. This study's focus on streaming video completion has potential applications in enhancing detection tasks, video editing, feature learning, noise removal, and various computer vision tasks and real-world forensic applications. Inertial wave turbulence within an enclosed two-dimensional space has been experimentally investigated. A specific drive forces the formation of a quasi-steady, anti-symmetric flow structure, which generates and sustains the turbulent inertial waves. Power spectra of the horizontal and vertical velocities were measured and compared across various energy-containing scales. A $k^{-2}$ power spectrum was observed and verified, establishing the presence of pentadic spectrum as initially proposed by Galtier. This experimental verification confirms Galtier's theoretical findings, providing an independent validation. Furthermore, the research shows consistent application of the energy cascade concept across a wide range of the involved frequencies. It also demonstrates that external forces can adjust the turbulent transition process, enabling exploration of the Vortical-Nonturbulent mode transition. In addition to these findings, the research reveals complex interplay between the dominant Galtier spectrum and higher-order spectral components, which can be determined using time-series analysis. It was found that the supporting spectral structures include the initial $k^{-2}$ component as well as lower-order spectral patterns such as the $k^{-4}$ and $k^{-6}$ spectrums. It is observed that the $k^{-2}$ Galtier spectrum dominates while the $k^{-4}$ and $k^{-6}$ spectrums are relatively weaker. A mathematical model based on the assumption that the sum of the higher-order spectral components must be even has also been derived. It was found that the cumulative summation of the $k^{-4}$ and $k^{-6}$ spectrums is indeed even. A similar approach can be applied to determine other higher-order spectral components. It was also found that the Galtier spectrum is associated with fourth-order Coriolis force interactions, which can be explained by the assumption that there are no higher-order interactions. In conclusion, the research explores new applications of the Galtier spectrum, providing valuable insights into inertial turbulence. It also highlights the potential of expanding the spectral analysis techniques used in the research to understand various complex flow dynamics. In addition to these findings, the research reveals that the Galtier spectrum is relevant to a broader range of situations beyond its initial discovery in the context of the sun's convective zone, providing new insights into helioseismology. It also shows that the research can be extended to tackle challenges in the convection problem. However, the research highlights that the spectral analysis techniques must be combined with other methods such as time-series analysis to gain a better understanding of the underlying complex flow

We examine the computational complexity of an iterative graph normalization process, involving the deletion of nodes with the lowest total edge counts, and compare it to existing literature on optimizing similar techniques for removing nodes with minimum maximum edge connections. Normalization by filtering out high-degree nodes is a common approach in data processing and feature engineering. We demonstrate that the iterative process, which solves the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem through successive edge removals, yields equal solutions to the more expensive greedy algorithm that prioritizes high-edge weight nodes. However, the computational time of these methods is directly related to the size of the graphs they are processing. We further show that the iterative process is a suitable candidate for large-scale graph data manipulation due to its efficiency and provision of approximate solutions, which can be crucial in real-world settings. We present experimental evidence of the effectiveness of this iterative method in feature engineering for data classification tasks. We obtained up to a 70 times speedup over the more expensive greedy algorithm while achieving comparable classification performance across various datasets. The algorithms and source code have been made publicly available to facilitate their use in graph and tree data manipulation scenarios. We provide theoretical justification for the effectiveness of node filtering as a general technique, showing that the ordered subsets derived from this process indeed possess lower minimum minimum edge counts than those produced by the more expensive methods. We further established that the ordered subsets derived from node filtering in the context of Markov networks have specific structural characteristics that contribute to their efficiency in optimization problems. These theoretical properties highlight the trade-offs between computational efficiency and solution quality that can be achieved through the use of node filtering as an engineering tool. We obtained empirical evidence of its efficacy in feature engineering for data classification tasks and showed that the ordered subsets produced by node filtering in graph linearized with Markov networks have particular structural characteristics that make them suitable for optimization problems. We evaluated its effectiveness across different dataset sizes, presenting consistent results. The source code has been made publicly available for further research purposes. The M dwarf binary system CR Dra is an optimal target to study the photo-emission from exoplanet host stars using radio telescopes. In 2019, the first comprehensive search for CR Dra's photo-emission was carried out with the LOw Frequency Array (LOFAR) and the Combined Array for Multi-wavelength Astronomy (CAMRA), employing multiple frequencies and a binary model of the source. Despite expecting strong photo-emission signals similar to that of Jupiter's Great Red Spot, the study failed to detect stable radio emissions from CR Dra, with upper limits set at 100-1000 times lower than Jupiter's GR Sot signals. CR Dra's radio emissions, observed sporadically at 10-200 Jy, were highly unpolarized, mobile, and did not align with the physical model of the binary system. These observations left little scope for radio emission enhancement through binarity. Consequently, the study adapted a new radio emission model based on the ALMA telescope's 1.3 mm observations of CR Dra, matching the LOFAR/CAMRA non-detection in the frequency range 10-200 MHz. Additionally, the study explored potential emission patterns in the Lyman-alpha and CO molecular transitions but failed to match the observed non-detection in these spectral bands. Future observations of CR Dra using the next generation radio telescope platform, the square kilometer Array (SKA), are poised to provide significant breakthroughs in understanding photo-emission from exoplanet host stars around binaries similar to CR Dra. Artificial neural networks have surpassed human performance in visual recognition tasks. However, their robustness, or resistance to corrupted input, is not necessarily equivalent to that of humans. This research examines how much visual information must be eliminated or modified for humans and AI models to lose recognition ability, focusing on image categorization. Our studies employ visually identical images with progressively degraded imagery, generated via text prompts. Notably, our findings indicate that both species exhibit remarkably similar robustness levels when using pre-trained Delaunay STN classifiers. Conversely, when using other types of networks, such as those trained by gradient descent on specific image datasets, our results show that humans are more resilient to visual distortions than the networks. Meanwhile, models initialized through contrastive learning, such as NCPC, display superior robustness than their image-prediction-based counterparts. Ultimately, these findings shed light on the visual information processed by artificial and human neural systems, enabling the design of more human-like machine vision architectures in the future. A novel deep learning-based approach for image fusion is developed by integrating multi-spectral and panchromatic images, yielding enhanced performance in land cover classification, particularly favorable for fire detection. Three traditional image fusion methods, GRAY, PCA, and wavelet, are evaluated alongside two deep learning-based techniques, including a high-quality wavelet domain fusion method and a fully learned domain fusion strategy. These five methods are assessed through land cover classification performance, resulting in a clear winner with the GRAY method, however when fire detection capability is the priority a different technique emerges. Utilizing a large multi-year fire dataset from Landsat, researchers find that the deep learning-based image fusion methods exhibit a notable advantage in fire detection accuracy, with false positive rates reduced to ten times that of GRAY. It's observed that GRAY has better fire detection accuracy than deep learning-based methods but suffers from high false positives. In contrast, deep learning-based methods excel at land cover classification and fire detection, but these classes often get conflated with one another. To resolve this, a multi-size patch based analysis is conducted, revealing that smaller patches yield higher accuracy fire detection and larger patches yield higher accuracy land cover classification, pointing to a potential improvement in this area. Ultimately, a fire detection model is constructed by training it with patches of image fusion data that have been previously optimized for that specific task and it demonstrates a notable improvement over baseline methods. This research demonstrates a break-through in fusion algorithms by showcasing their ability to be learned from, rather than solely aperture based, from multiple sources of data. It's observed that the deep learning-based methods are influenced by their training data and to a lesser extent by their approach to fusion, and that techniques such as wavelet are highly consistent across different datasets and to a lesser extent across different fusion algorithms. Additionally, a novel deep learning-based curriculum learning method is developed to teach a network to automatically detect fires from those areas the network is least confident in. This confidence based model is constructed by analyzing the activation of the network's final fully convolutional layer, and by increasing the size of the objects as the network achieves higher confidence it is able to accurately detect fires from those areas the network is least confident in. This research demonstrates a potential improvement in fire detection by using a confidence based approach that can detect fires from those areas the network is least confident in. Ultimately, this research demonstrates a novel deep learning-based approach for image fusion and fire detection, and showcases the potential for deep learning based methods to specifically detect fires from those areas the network is least confident in

The effectiveness of hospitals' and health care institutions' actions in limiting the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, in addition to general lockdown policies, is examined in this study. Focusing primarily on the role of hospitals and related economic losses, we develop a modified SARS-CoV-2 epidemiological model that takes into account the management of occupational health risks, healthcare capacity, and the direct economic impact of the epidemic. By integrating this model with control strategies such as lockdowns and the implementation of hygiene measures, the critical time period for hospital-administered treatments, and the workplace safety protocols, we evaluate the influence of these elements on the epidemic's progression. Ultimately, the cumulative number of infected cases is determined. Our investigation involves simulating scenarios representing the actual epidemic in Italy in 2020, with the aim of identifying crucial factors that contributed to the onset of the epidemic and outlining potential avenues for refinement of our model to inform more effective intervention policies. The evaluation of different intervention scenarios highlights the significance of incorporating measures to reduce infections within hospital settings and the workplace in order to mitigate aerosol-transmitted cases and reduce healthcare system overload during the epidemic. These findings suggest that hospitals and other healthcare institutions should proactively put in place occupational health measures, elevate their official infection control policies, enhance patients' protection strategies, and explore the possibility of introducing rapid, non-invasive testing for SARS-CoV-2 to mitigate transmission risks. Additionally, the economic impact of the epidemic can be minimized through the implementation of economic support strategies that target industries that are most vulnerable to lockdowns and direct government investments in the healthcare sector to reduce hospitalization cases and minimize occupational infections. These measures not only lower the epidemic's peak but also shift the primary channel of transmission from contact to aerosol, thereby lessening the economic devastation caused by the epidemic. The findings of this study emphasize the critical role that hospitals and other healthcare institutions and economic institutions are playing in the fight against SARS-CoV-2 by providing fundamental channels through which pharmacological interventions can help to reduce the epidemic's impact. Consequently, the World Health Organization's call for global cooperation in this field should prioritize integration among the different sectors of society, rather than viewing hospitals and other healthcare institutions and economic institutions as mutually exclusive systems. The essential nature of hospital-administered treatments and the economic significance of the pharmaceutical industry imply that the development and distribution of vaccines and pharmacological interventions against SARS-CoV-2 should prioritize the engagement of hospital administrators, healthcare professionals, and economists in this process. Bass' algorithm developed by Richard Bass and Zhen Quinnyn in 2019, has exhibited robust performance under unpredictable conditions, leveraging state information to optimize outcomes. Building upon this finding, this study extends Bass' algorithm to address unspecified internal dynamics within a networked system. It demonstrates that when all nodes employ Bass' algorithm, the system remains stable and resilient to spillover effects. Furthermore, a decentralized controller utilizing an extended superstability concept and a communication rule based on node importance can achieve stability and optimize performance. It also shows that when all nodes use this controller, the system achieves desired specifications and ensures stable, optimal performance. These results are illustrated through a numerical example. Lastly, this study investigates the conditions for Lyapunov stability in a coupled system and shows that using Bass' algorithm leads to stable convergence among nodes under sufficient conditions. It also presents a condition under which decentralized stability is ensured and offers a pathway towards designing controllers to achieve specified Lyapunov functions in coupled systems. These findings have been formalized into mathematical theorems. It is worth noting that in some cases, decentralized control of coupled systems leads to stable convergence, even when individual system components satisfy only weak stability conditions, as demonstrated through theoretical and numerical examples. It combines his initial dissertation with the work of Deepak Mehta, who contributed the majority of the material, specifically Chapters 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. Our analysis focuses on Automated Market Makers, a broad category of decentralized exchanges that include protocols like Uniswap and Balancer. A fundamental price mechanism, the pricing curve, is inherent in these market makers, representing the maximum amount of tokens a user can buy or sell for a given price. We develop a mathematical framework to quantify the pricing curve's curvature and establish a method for its analysis. We then investigate the effect of token supply and demand on the pricing curve's shape, finding that certain scenarios result in concave curves and two distinct points of highest liquidity. Our findings indicate that higher curvature is associated with reduced arbitrage opportunities and decreased total surplus for traders. Moreover, weresolve a cubic integral in a particular context and demonstrate that, in general, the total surplus is proportional to the square of curvature, while arbitrage opportunities diminish as it increases. Our research provides the first mathematical evidence of a relationship between curvature and total surplus. To confirm the practical impact of our discovery, we conduct a statistical analysis on the curvature of certain cryptocurrencies, revealing that a higher initial curvature is correlated with lower arbitrage opportunities and increased liquidity. Notably, our research highlights the practical significance of our findings, given that Automated Market Making is the dominant form of decentralized market infrastructure. To enhance user trust in these markets, our analysis addresses two key aspects: the first involves developing a new evaluation metric, based on curvature, to gauge the quality of AMM market performance; the second relates to demonstrating that higher initial liquidity is associated with reduced arbitrage opportunities and decreased trading conveniency. This leads to the formulation of three concrete targets for protocol developers, aimed at enhancing user trust in these markets: (i) maintaining pricing curve flatness; (ii) expanding markets to increase trading conveniency; and (iii) enhancing market liquidity to reduce trading time and arbitrage risks. Our research offers valuable insights for AMM protocol developers, operators, and users, providing a framework for gauging the performance of these markets and informing decisions to adapt or improve the underlying design. The misuse of cryptographic functions within programming languages is an ongoing concern.
Our research focuses on assessing the reliability of Python libraries by examining how easy it is to misuse
their API, a task previously completed for Java and C. Through both a online study and an in-lab experiment,
we evaluated the prevalence of misuses among those using the 'crypto' category on PyPI and students
in a in-lab setting, respectively. Our results indicate that Python crypto libraries are nearly three times more
susceptible to misuses compared to those in Java. Notably, we found common traits among the misuses observed,
including the lack of clear error indications, incorrect usage examples, and the ambiguity surrounding function
return values. To address this issue, we developed a set of straightforward heuristics intended to prevent misuses from
occurring. Our final step involves validating the efficiency of our proposed solution through another version of
our in-lab experiment, showing that the integration of these new features significantly lowers the incidence of
misuses. Our research will make the underlying code and data set available for the public. The following link

In large-scale image data analysis, maintaining the high-resolution 3D geometry of models can become extremely costly due to high data volumes. A novel two-step approach is introduced to efficiently recover 3D geometry from large, high-resolution 2D image datasets. First, a comprehensive method for automatic image segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and geometric alignment is developed. This segmentation method leverages a unique geometric framework to identify and separate distinct object groups within images, based on volume and proximity. Secondly, a powerful deep learning technique based on PointNet is developed to rapidly and accurately match reconstructed models to a comprehensive reference model. This approach yields highly accurate results, demonstrating a 94.5% success rate across 886 models, and operates at a remarkably fast processing speed of 0.05 seconds per image. A comprehensive framework incorporating various data sets, codes, and detailed narratives on data preparation, has been made publicly available to the community to support this research. Experimental evaluations show our method to be significantly more efficient than current data-driven approaches, recovering 95.8% of target volume data with a mere 12.3% of original data, and surpassing other state-of-the-art techniques by several fold. Various detailed analysis and results of this research are presented in our accompanying technical report. Furthermore, a remarkable instance of our method applying facial anatomy and physiology to revive ancient personalities through 3D visualization, has been developed and is accessible at https://danielguzman.github.io/3dfrom2d/. This research is aimed at pushing the boundaries of machine learning capabilities to construct highly realistic 3D scenes from mere 2D images, at a speed and accuracy unprecedented in the field. Experimental findings reveal a notable decline in 3D reconstruction accuracy as image volume diminishes, emphasizing the need for rapid and efficient model recovery from large, high-resolution 2D image datasets. A thorough investigation and evaluation of our method, accompanied by several detailed real-world applications and demonstrations, are presented in our research presentation titled "Reviving 3D inanimate objects". A notable 94.5% success rate of our method, along with its ability to tackle problems in the animation industry currently solved by manual crafting, is presented in our research presentation titled "Reviving 3D inanimate objects". A recent update to supplementary materials has been added, featuring additional research findings from our data sets, codes, and detailed narratives on a range of other efficient and efficient 3D geometry recovery methods applicable to a range of diverse domains. In our research, we explore two methods for determining conformal data for quantum spin chains through wavefunction overlaps at low-energy states. We apply these methods to calculate critical exponents in the Ising and XXZ models when the anisotropy parameter is real. We also extend our approach to calculate second magnetic excitations in the XXZ model with complex anisotropy. By utilizing algebraic techniques, we verify the accuracy of our overlap-based results for conformal data. Furthermore, we relate our overlap-based computation to another approach involving Bethe equations, illustrating the reasoning with the analysis of a twisted spin chain. We find that the twist introduces fluctuations in the spin chain but does not impact the solution to the eigenvalue problem derived from the overlap. Consequently, we can compute critical data by resolving two related eigenvalue problems with twisted and untwisted configurations. We observe that one configuration always yields the same results as the non-twisted case, whereas the other configuration depends on the twist angle and may yield different results. We speculate that these results could be connected to exceptional points, a phenomenon found in non-Hermitian systems, and we anticipate this relationship may be more widely applicable across different methods. We believe our simple model offers valuable insights into the behavior of quantum spin chains and may provide a platform for the study of quantum systems in multiple scenarios. The research code used in this research has been made available at https://github.com/julianhomfeld/computing-conformal-data. Additionally, the wavefunctions for the Ising model used in this research have been made publicly available at https://github.com/julianhomfeld/ising-wavefunctions. Furthermore, the wavefunctions for the XXZ model used in this research have been made publicly available at https://github.com/julianhomfeld/xxz-wavefunctions.

Recent research on neural networks has rewritten the principles of part-of-speech tagging. Nevertheless, a significant issue persists when networks encounter unknown words: they tend to assign arbitrary tags, resulting in notably lower precision for words outside the training scope. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel set-valued prediction method, which can effectively handle unknown words, as it produces tags in the form of a probability distribution over a set of possible tags. To accomplish this, we utilize an ensemble of neural networks, each responsible for assigning a tag to a different word, and accumulate the tags assigned by the network corresponding to the given word. The proposed method demonstrates superiority to current techniques on three distinct datasets. Moreover, when combined with existing neural networks, significant performance enhancements were observed across all datasets, and it is observed that the method ensures tags assigned for unknown words are dispersed at the lower end of the probability distribution. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/twprohan/sset_tagging. Moreover, a converted version of the code using the477 dataset can be found at https://github.com/davidchoe/setsupervised_tagging. Finally, a converted version of the code using the WSJ dataset can be found at https://github.com/davidchoe/setsupervised_tagging_wsj. This research introduces a novel concept of convergence for sequences of demand functions with a finite number of goods. The investigation demonstrates that the sequence's pointwise convergence to a limiting demand function $D^*$$\geq$0 retains several desirable properties of the original sequence. Specifically, it remains consistent with the principles of the weak law of large numbers and the portmanteau theorem from empirical process theory. The accompanying theorem establishes that the sequence's convergence to $D^*$ implies the convergence of weighted averages of $D$ with weights drawn from a Dirichlet distribution. The study also provides a method for generating i.i.d. data consistent with a given demand function $D^*$ in the context of the revenue equilibrium model initially introduced by Portnoy and Cesa-Bianchi (2020). The resulting data can be used to estimate the revenue equilibrium as an empirical average of revenue equilibria computed over sequences of i.i.d. demands. The findings are illustrated by a simulation example showing that our method outperforms a common alternative approach based on normal weighting. Furthermore, the study's results are substantiated by two case examples highlighting the merits of utilizing the convergence of demand functions with a finite number of goods. The first example involves the distribution of i.i.d. sales among three goods in a Chinese Township and the second example is a simulated illustration of the model's applicability. The research data and code related to the study are publicly accessible on the GitHub platform.
