The integration of IT systems in monitoring smart cities aims to address the limitations of human-specified requirements, often clouded in subjectivity or a lack of clarity.  This research focuses on a monitoring system for Naples, Italy, designed to enforce objectives formulated as fuzzy logic rules.  Building on the existing system, we developed a new model using formal fuzzy logic rules and established a Petri net representation, expanding the initial system's capabilities.  This Petri net model successfully replicates the original system's behavior and extends the system to model mutual influences between objectives.  The extended Petri net formulation, based on token-ring network structure, enables the determination of worst-case general transitions.  This approach distinguishes our work from other general Petri net models by defining specific transitions and offers a computationally efficient algorithm for determining the worst-case timing of transitions.  To evaluate the system's reliability, we developed an algorithm to calculate the confidence level of objectives.  This is done by examining all possible partitionings of places into positive and negative components, depending on the objectives' fulfillment.  Finally, we conducted an in-depth, detailed case study on the system, targeting objective fulfillment in specific physical spaces.  This research contributed to the development of smart cities by 1) implementing a model for enforcing subjective, fuzzy logical objectives in monitoring systems: 2) designing a Petri net model for achieving mutual influences among objectives in a reliable and efficient manner; 3) developing an algorithm for assessing the confidence level of objective fulfillment; and 4) investigating the dependence of objective fulfillment on time and location within the system.  This research laid the groundwork for integrating subjectivity and fuzziness into smart city monitoring systems, while offering practical applications in monitoring systems, regardless of their underlying modeling approach.  Ultimately, this could facilitate a seamless transition from subjective, low-fidelity planning to precise, high-fidelity computing.  In the context of smart cities, this research explored the implementation of subjective, fuzzy logical objectives in monitoring systems, complementing existing models that enforce strict logical objectives based on Boolean values.  This differentiated our approach from other Petri net models that relied on logical values and offered a novel fusion of fuzzy logic and Petri nets.  Ultimately, this research aimed to enhance smart city living by increasing the confidence level of users.  By addressing the subjectivity of requirements in monitoring systems, this research contributed to the broader field of smart cities.  Yet, in contrast to other smart city applications such as medical imaging, this research focused specifically on urban planning.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a subcategory of some topos, creating a universal cover, with particular properties of preserving chains or regularity in a certain order. This work develops new theorems by adapting existing theorems from topos theory to this subcategory. Due to its universal nature, these theorems remain equivalent to their topos counterparts. As a result, this provides new proofs for the existence of cocartesian images and suprema in specific categories, under specified conditions. This includes proofs for the existence of cocartesian images in categories satisfying particular conditions of preserving chains or regularity in an n-permutable category. Moreover, this provides new proofs for the existence of topological spaces with suprema in categories having a weakly generating set, given certain conditions under lawvere's generalized algebraic theorem. This presents a new method for establishing the existence of suprema in specific categories, creating a connection between topos theory and the field of algebraic geometry. This work further develops an analogy between the existence of certain categories in relation to proper morphisms and the existence of algebraic geometry techniques in relation to flat morphisms. This includes an example of how proper morphisms can replace flat morphisms in certain category exchanges. This provides new theorems on the existence of algebraic geometry techniques in specific categories, under particular conditions. To illustrate this, an example shows how the existence of algebra geometry techniques in the category of schemes under etale topology can be used to exchange the category of schemes under etale topology with the category of schemes under flat topology, given certain conditions under proper morphisms. This presents a new method of exchanging categories, providing a new theorem that corresponds to the existence of algebra geometry techniques in the category of schemes under flat topology when the source and target are etale local isomorphisms. This provides a new proof for the existence of algebra geometry techniques in the category of schemes under flat morphology. This research investigates the joint occurrence of extreme waves and wind conditions
over the North Sea, focusing on non-linear interactions between wind speed and wave height.
Using satellite and buoy data from storms with exceptionally severe wind conditions,
the study reveals a tendency for these events to become spatially correlated within
a distance of approximately 1000 kilometers. Nevertheless, the joint distribution of these
events conditioned on these extreme storms demonstrates a surprisingly rapid decay
in spatial correlation, similar to 1/f behavior, while still maintaining significant
statistical associations. The implications of these findings for predicting extreme
wind conditions in relation to waves in specific geographical locations are discussed. 
Additionally, the paper explores the theoretical foundations of modeling spatial
exceedance of wind conditions, identifying areas where further research is required. 
Finally, the study demonstrates the feasibility of using analogies from wave
theories as a potential method for estimating the occurrence probabilities of severe
wind conditions at high levels of confidence. This method is particularly promising
since computational requirements increase much more slowly with the desired probability
level compared to traditional approaches based on simulation. As a result, the approach
allows for a much more realistic modeling of severe but less probable wind conditions. 
However, there is still a significant research gap in this direction, as evident from
the findings of this study. 
As an additional contribution, the paper provides a detailed evaluation of a
global wind wave model used in this research, identifying a significant discrepancy
between its theoretical and practical performance. 
Furthermore, the study provides estimates for the accuracy of the model used
in this research and examines its consistency with observations from stationary
buoys. As part of this research, the authors also developed software packages that
can be utilized for reproducing the results. These packages, which are available online,
include 'MWWS': a Python module for estimating wave characteristics from satellite
images, as well as 'SWMS': a Python module for stochastic wave modeling. These packages
are listed in the repository https://github.com/joofent/MWWS/tree/main/MWWS
and https://github.com/joofent/SWMS/tree/main/SWMS respectively. 
Lastly, the paper presents a new direction for research based on the findings
in the introduction. As part of this research, the authors also developed a new
method for estimating wind conditions at high levels of confidence based on the

This limitation hinders their performance in image-text learning tasks. To address this issue, this study introduces the concept of using visually-guided texts to refine the cross-modal correlation and enhance feature abstraction. Specifically, it utilizes eye-tracking data to obtain fixation patterns for learning texts, thereby rectifying the discrepancy between specific text commands and images. Moreover, it leverages large-scale eye-tracking data to build a robust recurrent neural network, FCRNN, which demonstrates superior performance compared to existing models. Ultimately, the enhancement of CLIP with VGTs not only accelerates convergence and decreases inference time but also significantly improves the accuracy of cross-modal learning. Extensive experiments validate the strength of the proposed approach in bridging the gap between text and image correlations, especially in challenging scenarios like zero-shot learning and few-shot learning. Our analysis reveals that the method of planet discovery within a microlensing event has a significant impact on detecting planets with lower mass ratios. By comparing the various discovery methods, we've found that the worst case for identifying planets with mass ratios of 0.001 yields a 33% success rate for the critical point formalism, 44% for the circularization method, and 58% for the parallax-relevant formalism. These higher success rates for the latter two methods suggest they are more effective in uncovering planets in microlensing events. Moreover, by utilizing the critical point formalism, we've discovered a planet with a mass ratio of 0.43 times 10^-3 in microlensing event CXCBB-21b, which is particularly challenging to explain using population synthesis models that are less responsive to low mass ratios. In contrast, the critical point formalism, which allows for a more precise prediction of microlensing planets, reveals the presence of a second planet with a mass ratio of 0.23 times 10^-3 that was initially overlooked using this method. Consequently, these discoveries highlight the superiority of using the critical point formalism compared to the other methods in detailed microlensing planet analysis. As a result, we suggest that the critical point formalism should be the standard analysis method when discovering two-plane microlensing systems in the future. Furthermore, by utilizing the critical point formalism, we've discovered a relationship between the microlensing plane's projected distance from its host star and its mass, which can be precisely modeled. Specifically, the analytical expression for the specific microlensing plane mass is 0.89 M_J ± 0.01 M_J. Building on this result, we establish the invariance of orbital integrals across inner forms of reductive groups. Additionally, we extend the principle of orbital stability to these inner forms. Moreover, we adapt the specific orbital integral formula from representative groups to the broader category of inner forms. The relative fundamental lemma can be seen as an extension of the local Shimura correspondence between group schemes and automorphic representations. It serves as a crucial stepping stone for the development of the transfer factor for matching orbits, a concept introduced by Wang and Zhang. Our work ultimately contributes to the creation of a common framework for the relative trace formula across a diverse range of reductive groups, including those of split and non-split type. This research introduces p-value calculations for a range of statistical tests used on bivariate data, extending from correlation and regression analysis coefficients to various other test types. When the actual distribution of data points is unknown, p-values can be estimated by analyzing simulations based on the maximum likelihood estimated covariance structure of a multivariate normal distribution fitted to the given data. We explore the advantages of this method in a case study involving a dataset from environmental science that does not adhere to a bivariate normal distribution. Consequently, p-values are estimated through multivariate normal-based simulations. This approach enables users to easily perform such estimations with software such as R, providing an alternative or supplement to existing data analysis tools. Furthermore, we outline additional techniques to estimate multivariate distribution functions and quantities using this methodology. This work presents a novel framework of distribution-free robust learning. At its core is the idea of using a concept class's inherent properties to establish an upper limit on the nearest neighbor's radius, based on the dimensionality of the data. Within this framework, we have developed several concepts of interest. Firstly, we have adapted existing classes such as Gaussian space, half-spaces, and polytopes for distribution-free robust learning. Additionally, we have defined the concept of $C^{rob}$, which encompasses classes where the nearest neighbor's radius is limited, and demonstrate its applicability using variants of the perceptron. Furthermore, we have established the $\epsilon$-net property for these classes, and use this to derive upper bounds on the sample size required for robust learning across various dimensions. The results demonstrate that distribution-free robust learning can be achieved with a sample size that grows only logarithmically with the dimensionality, provided the query radius is restricted to a certain threshold. The sample size threshold decreases as the query radius approaches its maximum allowed value. The proposed framework also allows for the derivation of robust generalization bounds, under both deterministic and stochastic models. The framework's utility extends to embedding the robust learning problem into the nearest neighbor problem, and using techniques from geometry to derive distribution-free robust learning guarantees. Leveraging this insight, we developed a method to solve optimal transport problems directly using a truncated FS-2 process, bypassing the traditional iterative approach. Our approach utilizes the Goto inequality to accelerate computations by taking advantage of monotonicity. We have experimented with our implementation, known as FS-2 OptT, and found it to consistently outperform existing optimal transport solutions in both time and memory usage. Notably, it offers a significant time advantage for large datasets and scenarios involving sparse transport costs. The code is freely available at https://github.com/libml/mechanism_optimal_transport. Our findings indicate that FS-2 OptT can serve as a reliable alternative to linear programming-based methods, and we encourage future research to further optimize its performance. A new Python library called PyOT for efficient optimal transport computations is also announced and made available. It includes a variety of algorithms with a unified interface for easy experimentation. A comprehensive theoretical analysis of FS-2 OptT is presented in the paper, and we demonstrate its benefits by applying it to a range of data analysis tasks. This research aims to boost the precision of industrial robots in complying with planned trajectories. To achieve this, we suggest an enhanced approach that continuously adjusts the end-effector position based on the actual tracking error. A critical component of this method involves selecting an optimal time-related influence, which maximizes the end-effector's following rate. The proposal incorporates the concept of optimal infinite-dimensional $L_2$ gain scheduling and incorporates a novel feature: it can handle cases where end-effector position, orientation, or velocity is incorrect. To show its effectiveness, we simulate the outcome of this approach through numerical modeling of a KUKA LWR4+ manipulator. The simulation demonstrates that an appropriately designed time-dependent gain can significantly enhance the end-effector's tracking speed, ultimately increasing overall precision. To take the analysis further, we examine the connection between this enhanced technique and a controller that continuously adjusts its action based on the end-effector's displacement. The outcome of this investigation indicates that an optimal time-related influence can significantly lower the end-effector's displacement, thus improving tracking accuracy. Lastly, we examine the properties of the enhanced optimal track-and-follow strategy in an ideal scenario, where no time-related influence is involved. This investigation leads to the discovery that linear time-dependent scheduling can maintain a constant end-effector following rate. Consequently, we have successfully derived an enhanced optimal control law that combines features of track-and-follow and conformant control, offering improved compliance for industrial robots. This research is set to expand our understanding of optimal tracking control, thereby providing a valuable basis for the continuous adjustment of robot movement. The proposed idea holds significant potential for the improvement of robot trajectory accuracy, a characteristic of great importance in industrial applications. To confirm the findings of this study, we have conducted remote presentation at the 2022 IEEE Rachel. This research aims to create a predictive model for the likelihood of myocardial infations within patients who have previously experienced stroke or heart attacks. The study examines whether certain conditions that occur after stroke or heart attacks are more likely to affect certain socio-demographic groups. Using survival analysis, this research predicts the time scale of the events and identifies the factors that influence these predictions. The findings suggest that people who experience certain long-term health conditions after heart attacks or strokes are more likely to die from myocardial infarctions. The study uses Bayesian additive regression trees to analyze data and indicates that certain demographic groups such as men, the over-65s, and those from urban and rural areas of Scotland are at higher risk of myocardial infarctions due to long-term health conditions. Additionally, patients with hypertension, diabetes, and chronic lung disease or respiratory disease are more likely to die from myocardial infarctions. The research suggests that hospitals which provide physical rehabilitation services have lower rates of myocardial infarions compared to those which do not. The study's findings are relevant to long-term condition managers, healthcare professionals and policy makers as they highlight potential gaps in the management of myocardial infarions and heart attacks. We analyze the long-term behavior of a correlated random walk confined to a space with specific geometric restrictions, where movements are influenced by a time-varying memory effect. Specifically, we consider a scenario where a particle can move either along a 2D grid or within a circular domain, with transitions governed by a time-varying correlation coefficient. Our analysis focuses on the asymptotic behavior of this process from the perspective of statistical mechanics. We derive the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix, relating it to the eigenvalues of a related matrix. Additionally, we formulate a detailed expression for the largest eigenvalue of this matrix, thereby determining the exponential decay rate of transient states. Furthermore, we explore analogous findings for correlated random walks in higher-dimensional spaces by generalizing our methods. Moreover, we relate our findings to similar research in statistical mechanics and recent experiments involving confined particle systems. We also show that our expression for the largest eigenvalue generalizes previous results from simpler cases. Our analysis reveals that the time correlation function exhibits an oscillatory behavior, with amplitude diminishing as time increases. However, we identify a specific condition under which these oscillations do not disappear; rather, the time correlation function transitions to a steady-state behavior. We have also computed the asymptotic behavior of the sum over all eigenvalues of the transition probability matrix. According to our findings, this sum grows at an exponential rate, which we have determined analytically. We have also found that, when the dimension of the space increases, this sum grows at an exponential rate, with the inverse of the dimension appearing in the base of this exponential as a consequence of the Pfaffian of a specific commutator matrix growing at an exponential rate. We have expanded our analysis to correlate random walks in higher-dimensional spaces, confining the movement within a rectangular 2D domain with time-dependent correlations across the boundaries. In our study, we discovered that correlates initially decrease at a power greater than one, suggesting that the transient behavior of the correlation function could potentially dominate the behavior over extended periods. We have explored the links between our findings and existing research in correlated random walks, specifically in recent experiments involving confined particle systems. We have used our analysis to establish relationships between physical observables and the transition probability matrix, thereby validating the application of statistical mechanics to correlated random walks. Furthermore, our findings imply that microscopic correlations, which we have quantified as commutators, contribute to the decay of correlations, thereby translating the asymptotic behavior of the correlation function into the pfaffian of a specific commutator

Clock analysis is utilized to establish termination proofs for functional programs by interpreting clock variables as monitoring the progress of reduction transactions. The defining principle of clock analysis is to identify a well-ordering that corresponds to the timing, that is, a relation where being later in time corresponds to being more advanced according to the order. The central hypothesis of clock analysis is the existence of a suitable substitution, which ensures the clock variable minimizes the evaluation depth and consequently simplifies termination proofs. Clock analysis is here reformulated for higher-order functional languages, particularly considering partial functions; this formulation applies the order structure of values to establish the clock order. The study also examines conditions for automatically deriving clock analysis conditions from decidable well-ordering properties of values and shows that, in total functional languages, using minimal function calls simplifies these conditions and enables the application of original clock analysis principles. Conversely, the partial nature of functions raises new challenges when applying clock analysis and renders some clock analysis methods ineffective. The study concludes by demonstrating that clock analysis can be applied to establish termination for partial equational logic programs using the model-based termination method. Additionally, the work demonstrates that clock analysis can be used to prove the bounded model property, which bounds the complexity of evaluation for programs with stable partial functions. The study further showcases its relevance to programming languages by applying clock analysis to the partial subrelation of untyped lambda calculus. The work reveals that clock analysis can be used to establish the bounded model property for both core functional languages such as SPC and SP, as well as the extension of these languages with negation. Finally, the study shows that clock analysis can be used to establish the bounded model property for SP with the inclusion of solvable negation, which can be mapped to first-order logic based on the resolution principle. The study concludes that clock analysis provides an effective method for termination proofing solvable partial functions in the class of functional languages featuring negation. The work further demonstrates its applicability to other logic languages by comparing the termination proofing methods of model completion and clock analysis, showing that clock analysis can be used to establish the bounded model property for the negation extension of first-order logic. Overall, the study provides an extensive analysis of clock analysis for partial functions and its applications across multiple programming paradigms. The work explicitly highlights its relevance to programming languages and shows clock analysis to be an invaluable tool for termination proofing programs with stable partial functions. Several machine learning and data science studies have explored the effectiveness of neural networks in various applications. However, few of these investigations have centered on how the performance of neural networks is influenced by data imbalance, compared to other algorithms. In our research, we investigated the performance of neural networks under different levels of data imbalance, using well-known machine learning algorithms such as K-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machines as points of reference. Our study employed the Imbalanced Learn dataset and implemented two common techniques - oversampling and undersampling - to examine the characteristics of neural networks in relation to data imbalance. Our key findings revealed that neural networks exhibit similar performance issues under data imbalance, similar to K-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machines. However, neural networks are more severely affected by data imbalance than Support Vector Machines. Furthermore, neural networks that utilize oversampling or undersampling exhibit distinct behavior under data imbalance, demonstrating improved performance when using oversampling and reduced performance when using undersampling compared to neural networks that do not employ these techniques. These findings challenge the widespread perception that neural networks are resilient to data imbalance. Our research also highlights the necessity to utilize strategies such as data imbalance oversampling to mitigate the detrimental impact of data imbalance on neural network performance. Overall, our research contributes to the body of knowledge by providing insights into the effect of data imbalance on neural networks, which have not been extensively investigated in previous studies. The findings of our research hold significant practical implications for applications involving data imbalance. In conclusion, our research focuses on data imbalance and neural networks, and aims to stimulate future research in this area. It is our hope that this study will stimulate discussions regarding data imbalance and neural networks, and contribute to the advancement of future research in this field. In addition, the experimental code from this research is accessible via the link to the GitHub repository: https://github.com/julianapb/data-imbalance-neural-networks. In order to promote the reproduction of our results and facilitate future research, our study also includes the visualization of our dataset using Principal Component Analysis, a discussion of the implementation details of our experiments, and a description of the neural network architectures utilized in our research, available at the aforementioned GitHub repository. In summary, our study contributes to the knowledge on the effect of data imbalance on neural networks, and highlights the need for the development of new methods to mitigate the detrimental impact of data imbalance on these algorithms. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of news output related to the COVID-19 pandemic using a large dataset of 4,500 news articles from online sources across the United States and the United Kingdom. The research employs thematic analysis to examine the topic areas covered by news outlets, as well as computational methods to assess news volume, consistency, and variety. The findings reveal that primary school students in the US and UK received an average of 6 hours and 47 minutes of COVID-19 news via BBC News and local TV channels, respectively. Further investigation into the impact of news coverage on local communities involved collecting a 15-day dataset of online news articles from 192 US and 48 UK news sources, including small, private channels. The data shows that news volume was influenced by the severity of the pandemic in a given region, with higher incidence leading to increased news coverage. It was also found that news sources commonly covered the subject of hospital capacity, while other popular topics included government restrictions and the economic impact of the pandemic. The research further demonstrates that news variety was higher in the US compared to the UK, with wider implementation of COVID-related measures in the US contributing to the discovery of more novel topics. The findings also indicate that news sources from private channels covered a greater range of topics, both in the US and the UK, and that approximately 70% of all news articles were comprised of just three topics - the economy, health capacity, and government restrictions. The research finally reveals that news sources from private channels were more likely to cover COVID-19-related topics that were relevant to their local communities. The implications of these findings are that news consumers can benefit from receiving pandemic updates tailored to their local environments through the use of niche news sources and by taking into account the level of incidence in their area. The research also shows the potential for further exploration of the role of news coverage in informing local Incidence. Active research has been devoted to developing improved imitation learning methods to effectively transfer an expert's behavior to a less experienced policy. A limitation of traditional augmented policy cloning techniques arises from their reliance on low-dimensional representations of actions, which are often difficult to obtain for complex systems with high dimensional control inputs. This research presents a novel augmented policy cloning framework to efficiently transfer an expert's behavior to a student policy in such demanding systems. The proposed framework employs a variational autoencoder to produce actionable dimensional action representations that can seamlessly integrate with the student policy's existing network, allowing for seamless action combinations. A critical innovation involves reformulating action combinations as conditional sampling processes that mirror the expert's behavior. The resulting augmented policy cloning framework yields remarkable motion reproduction results and significantly outperforms alternative cloning techniques that require low-dimensional action representations. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the superiority of the proposed framework in comparing it to other action combination methods. The presented framework's efficiency and effectiveness make it a suitable choice for solving complex robotic control problems. A notable application of the proposed framework involves successfully integrating vision-based feedback to steer a difficult-to-control system. We develop a theoretical model of a resonant spin maser with a variable Q factor and conduct a thorough analysis of its noise characteristics in both the radio and microwave frequency ranges. The analysis takes into account the implications of digital signal processing on the maser system's performance, which significantly differs from the outcomes of electrical signal amplification. The integration of digital signal processing leads to a substantial reduction in the spin noise of the maser compared to conventional radio amplifiers. Furthermore, we examine how adjusting the Q factor and resonant frequency affects the noise spectrum and coherence properties of the maser signal, identifying certain criteria that can be optimized for observing Overhauser, nuclear magnetic resonance, or high-resolution spectral features. The theoretical foundations of our model are grounded in earlier research by Gurevich and Shulman and by Anosov, and our analysis builds upon their work by refining the theoretical structure and introducing novel variables to describe the system's noise characteristics. The work presented here is an in-depth expansion of a preliminary findings published as a 1975 Russian-language abstract. The investigation led to the identification of an optimal Q factor of approximately 100, a resonant frequency of 2.5 MHz, and a 40-minute integration time to achieve a frequency stability of ${10^{-17}}$ at the 1-second scale. The analysis also reveals that within a certain maser ring radius range, variations in the spin noise amplitude result in correlations over intervals of a few minutes, mirroring earlier observations made by Shulman and coworkers. The identified correlations, amplitude, and frequency dependencies are consistent with predictions based on the diffusion of magnetic moments in solids, as theorized by Orbach. Consequently, our refined theoretical model offers an enhanced understanding of the physical underpinnings of the observed correlations, complementing the initial structure developed by Gurevich and Shulman. The established methodology enables the calculation of precision clocks by pairing highly coherent maser signals with conventional electric signal amplifiers, thereby achieving levels of precision comparable to but not surpassing optical frequency dipole gratings. The proposed method, however, falls short of achieving the precision required for applications including testing the spatial isotropy of the universe's gravitational field, validating Einstein's equivalence principle, and examining the spatial isotropy of the universe's gravitational field. Yet, our findings indicate that it is feasible to attain precision on the order of $10^{-21}$$\slash$(E) with certain adjustments to the maser setup, though this breakthrough would necessitate further research to achieve this level

Despite significant advancements in NLP, developing language resources for numerous languages remains a major challenge due to their limited use. This study investigates the transfer learning potential between Maltese, an Indo-European language, and other languages with Indo-European roots. We examine the similarities between Maltese and other languages with Indo-European roots and those that are Indo-European family members. Our research reveals that Maltese shares numerous similarities with other languages with Indo-European roots, but exhibits distinct differences on a semantic level. Transfer learning can be beneficial in training Maltese models, but the extent of transfer varies depending on the task at hand. This research aims to develop a method for quantifying the similarity between two random fields observed in distinct operational regimes. To achieve this, we introduce a novel, regime-independent correlation metric based on Tsallis entropy. A comprehensive theoretical analysis is provided, including explicit formulas for the proposed metric and a means of determining the optimal transformation to minimize information dissipation. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations involving samples with varying levels of randomness. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of the method in evaluating the similarity between fields generated by distinct simulation models and contrast it with a similarity quantification method rooted in conditional probability. The outcomes reveal that the new approach offers better fidelity and greater physical validity. Finally, we explore the potential of the method to identify patterns within random fields, offering a new perspective on regime-independent pattern extraction. The approach shows promise for utilising pattern-based similarity measures to merge data from disparate regimes. The research discusses its generalization to multi-dimensional random fields and the challenges associated with its implementation. A detailed guide on implementing the method using the PyTensorBayes platform is provided. The results of the research are further exemplified through three real-world case studies involving turbulence, solar magneto-hydrodynamics, and cuprae, involving simulations conducted via the DeepField, ForwardForge, and ReverseReveal pipelines, respectively. It further eliminates the need for domain decomposition and enables seamless integration of multi-physics problems with little additional coding required. We showcase the performance of the SASK method in solving a variety of time-dependent problems, including highly resolved images created via algorithmic inverse rendering in computer graphics. The objective of this study is to examine the development of entanglement in disordered spin systems with interactions when they're connected to a central qubit or cavity mode. This investigation seeks to determine whether the entanglement in such systems shows an increase or decline over time, and possibly exhibits a sudden rise, similar to the behavior observed in quantum phase transitions. Next, by intentionally raising the trap's electric potential energy, and measuring the resulting increase in the crystal's radial oscillation frequency, one can calculate the average ambient heating rate per unit voltage. 

Ultimately, this rate is converted to a temperature increase per unit time, providing essential climate data for the Coulomb crystal.

In decision-making and learning processes, the preference for averaging reward rates rather than adapting to new information (probability-matching) has long been studied. We explored the role of negative outcomes in this context. Our findings reveal that the tendency to probability-match increases when agents quickly integrate recent losses and the history of those losses. Notably, the apparent conflict between adapting to new information and avoiding negative outcomes can actually arise from the same learning mechanism, which responds to the accumulation of those very outcomes. Furthermore, the rate of exploration, when not a learning parameter itself, can serve as an indicator of how often probability-matching is an acceptable strategy in a given situation. Overall, our results emphasize the importance of considering the specific environment and task when analyzing probability-matching behavior. Moreover, our research implies that the apparent double nature of probability-matching can be resolved if the role of negative information and the agent's learning rate in different environments are properly understood. Our simulations verified these findings in a range of typical learning algorithms, including Q-learning, SARSA, and recursive least squares. The structural commonality between these algorithms means our results likely extend to other adaptive strategies, which can be verified through future research. The source code for these simulations is available online. Our simulation results also show that the rate of learning may influence when probability-matching behaves more like avoiding losses and when more like responding to reward. In the context of reinforcement learning, our results suggest that using negative information may not always have the desired effect if it makes the agent more prone to negative feedback. Conversely, our results also indicate that incorporating a rate of exploration may serve as a useful middle ground between adapting to new information and avoiding negative outcomes. Ultimately, our findings stress the importance of taking into account the specific characteristics of the environment and task in question when analyzing probability-matching behavior. Probability-matching may thus not be a fixed behavioral trait, but rather one that displays considerable context-sensitivity. Our approach transforms a quantum system's linear-algebraic description into a probabilistic model of geometrical nature. Utilizing this framework, we demonstrate the equivalence of nonlocality and contextuality by showing that distinct geometries yield exactly the same predictions. To illustrate this concept, we apply it to various examples. Initially, we establish that introducing a fundamental state to a collection of qubits yields a geometry equivalent to the Melko-Koma lattice. Additionally, we discover that arranging qubits in a unidimensional array generates a geometry analogous to the Braunstein-Caves setup. Lastly, we reveal that clustering qubits in a random division of the array (according to the ER model), is representable within our framework, corresponding to a geometry devoid of contextuality. This last instance highlights how our approach can help in assessing quantum systems. Ultimately, our method enables the transformation of a quantum system from a purely quantum description to a geometric or classical probabilistic model, thereby examining its nonlocality and contextuality properties. Consequently, our method may serve as a valuable tool for investigating quantum systems. Our code for the algorithm is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/adiblockx/geometric-states. Moreover, our approach has potential for expansion to infinite-dimensional quantum systems as shown by the comprehensive discussion in Sec. 5.1.

To investigate this phenomenon, we examined how users respond when robots share part of their code or instructions for a task, discovering that most users become stuck or frustrated if a robot's underlying program is shown, especially if the robot is equipped with voice capabilities. In contrast, users reacted positively when a robot explained its chosen task inputs, such as button presses, and were more likely to achieve the desired task inputs by having the robot demonstrate its chosen inputs, rather than simply providing the code, as highlighting specific steps can make the task input more apparent. This study proposes a novel 2D representation, HiTMap, for agent navigation in complex environments with obstacles. This dynamic map adapts to changing conditions by updating a hierarchical model with multiple beams, each consisting of a range and direction. In comparison to traditional metric maps, HiTMap can streamline navigation by reducing the number of required observations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this representation through navigation experiments in environments with varied dimensions and layouts, where HiTMap successfully led agents to their destinations efficiently, even when the environment was dynamically changed. This was achieved despite the limited visibility of the destination, as HiTMap leveraged the agent's observations to identify suitable paths. Our analysis shows that HiTMap outperforms other topological maps due to its ability to facilitate metric-level navigation. Additionally, HiTMap was found to be more resilient to sensor data noise and imbalances in observation distribution. We compare HiTMap with other representative map types, demonstrating its advantages through comprehensive experiments. Furthermore, HiTMap offers efficient representation, data access, and management of observations. In particular, it allows for the acquisition of both short-range and long-range observations, even in environments with limited visibility. This is achieved through a hierarchical structure where lower-level beams can combine to form high-level beams, providing navigation insights. We illustrate the practical application of HiTMap in real-world robotic scenarios, including autonomous navigation in environments with varying sizes and layouts. Time-series data is often analyzed using charts that show progress over time, 
however these plots can only display two dimensions. Users typically need separate 
visualizations for a complete understanding of their data. We've created TimeLink, 
a system allowing users to link time-based plots with maps, networks, and other 
visualizations using a streamlined interface. This linking capability enables users 
to automatically synchronize related visualizations, effectively creating an 
integrated data analysis platform with actionable insights. We conducted an study 
evaluating the process and results showed that users with experience in data 
analysis could efficiently link visualizations using consistent terminology, 
although this took some time. Untrained users, on the other hand, needed step-by-step 
instructions to learn the process. We used these findings to refine the design of 
the TimeLink interface, resulting in a user-friendly system that efficiently 
facilitates data analysis. This functionality is currently available on various 
data-analysis platforms including OmicsAnalytics, a cancer-data-analysis tool. 
Additionally, we're providing the timelink.js open-source library for developers 
interested in linking their own data visualizations. This research highlights the 
importance of linking disparate visualization components, ultimately saving data 
analysts considerable time. The timelink.js open-source library is available at 
https://github.com/omicsanalytics/timelink.js, with examples of successful linkages 
at https://omicsanalytics.com/app/?project=1&step-timelink. TimeLink is live on 
OmicsAnalytics at https://omicsanalytics.com/.

This paper addresses the challenges of designing an optimal cooperative relay system by developing efficient scheduling and power allocation techniques to minimize energy consumption while ensuring high data rates. By formulating a complex optimization problem in the users, relays, and base station, we leverage a layered optimization framework to decouple the scheduling and power allocation issues and transform the problem into a series of solvable sub-problems. Leveraging these optimized values, we then employ a tool from combinatorial optimization to generate a near-optimal scheduling strategy, and combine this with the previously obtained power values to produce an optimal two-tier cooperation policy that achieves better performance than existing approaches in terms of energy efficiency and spectral efficiency under similar hardware constraints. Simulations confirm the efficacy of our approach. The paper's findings also reveal some counter-intuitive properties of two-tier cooperation. Additionally, we propose an extension of this power allocation technique to systems using adaptive modulation, and demonstrate the potential for minimizing energy consumption while maintaining high data rates. This is achieved through a new power allocation technique that outperforms existing methods, as shown by simulations. Furthermore, we observe that the power loading values modulated by the users are directly proportional to the quality of the wireless link, thereby simplifying the implementation of this technique in systems using adaptive modulation. Moreover, this approach enables the users to adjust their power loading values efficiently according to the channel state, thereby facilitating load balancing among the relays. As a result, the base station can easily identify which relay corresponds to a specific user, and thereby eliminate a major design challenge in multi-user relay systems. All these findings originate from the detailed analysis of the optimization problem and its underlying structure, a task that is taken care of by our framework. Moreover, the framework enables us to generate scheduling and power allocation values for a base station serving a large number of users in just a few seconds, thereby overcoming a major computational hurdle. However, this is challenged when the system uses adaptive modulation, leading to a different type of computational constraint. Upon the presence of magnetic adatoms or dimers within a graphene system that interacts with a superconducting substrate, the spin-dependent density of states exhibits distinct YSR state peaks. The spin-orbit coupling between adatoms significantly influences the positions of YSHC peaks, causing them to shift in response to varying coupling strengths. For magnetic dimer configurations, the spin-orbit coupling leads to the formation of an elliptical ring-shaped structure, resulting in YSHC peaks that appear at points along its periphery, rather than at its center. The spin-orbit coupling has a synergistic effect when considering both adatoms and dimers, broadening the distribution of YSHC peaks in the latter case. This phenomenon can potentially be utilized to analyze local spin-orbit interactions through the examination of de Haas van Hove singularities. Our study provides a theoretical understanding of how spin-orbit coupling affects the YSR state, serving as a basis for future experimental discussions. The results presented serve as recommendations for subsequent research into how to optically detect spin-orbit interactions using magnetic adatoms or dimers. The approach employed allows for a systematic analysis of these systems, and our findings can be applied to a broader range of systems featuring similar magnetic properties. The study further reveals that it is feasible to detect the presence of spin-orbit interactions in local systems through the application of circularly polarized light. The associated methods can be adapted for scanning tunneling spectroscopy to quantify the strength of local interactions, as well as for optical detection in photoluminescence and photodetection to gain a deeper understanding of the unique properties that arise in hybrid systems. The study opens up opportunities for further research on hybrid materials that exhibit unique properties, including spin-valley states in bilayers and the quantum spin Hall effect in monolayers with ferromagnetic insulation. The work also sets the foundation for exploring other unusual states such as the fermionic state in graphene-ferromagnet-superconductor and the bosonic state in graphene-superconductor with spin-valley antiferromagnet. The study identifies that while spin-orbit coupling may lead to the suppression of YSHC peaks, it is theoretically possible to detect these peaks using optical means, particularly in hybrid materials with a large energy gap. The results obtained can be applied to conventional superconductors, where spin-orbit coupling leads to the splitting of YSHC peaks. The study shows that a scanning tunneling spectroscopy based on circularly polarized detectable spin-orbit interactions is feasible.

This study establishes a universal framework for satellite image analysis by employing a deep generative model, and leverages all available meta data from the Universal Machine Learning Artefact registry for transfer learning based on the Universal Adaptive Generative Adversarial Neural machine. This novel UAGAN architecture is a versatile tool for processing satellite images in real-time. Initially, the UAGAN framework is utilized to reconstruct high-resolution satellite images from the WorldView-4 dataset. Adversarial attacks on deep learning models have posed a significant threat. To counter this issue, recent research emphasizes the need for secure systems that can withstand such attacks. This study introduces a unique approach using generative adversarial networks to create noise that deceives adversarial attackers while safeguarding the system's integrity. Experimental results show that our method effectively neutralizes attacks by DeepFOES, a next-generation threat, and outperforms existing techniques. Our method also demonstrates resilience against physiological changes like jitter and noise, and its versatility in enhancing robustness across various data sets, including MNIST and FMNIST. This research proposes a new framework for generating adversarial-resistant noise. To evaluate its efficacy, we compared it against the state-of-the-art approach using transfer learning, and our method emerged superior in terms of accuracy, with a substantial gain of 89% on the MNIST data set. This study's contributions can be categorized into three key areas: first, the development of a unique GAN-based noise generation approach; second, the integration of this approach to counter the DeepFOES attack; third, the adaptability of this approach on diverse data sets to restore model performance under various physiological changes; and fourth, the comparative analysis of this approach against the state-of-the-art approach using transfer learning, showing our method effective on both MNIST and FMNIST data sets. In our approach to recreating the Steiner tree for multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation using a weakly supervised loss function, we find that incorporating experience replay is essential. This method involves periodically collecting and combining previous model outputs, thereby adjusting to more challenging segmentation tasks. Our findings suggest that the enhanced segmentations lead to superior lesion coverage compared to models trained solely on segmentation masks or original images. Additionally, the experience replay technique allows our model to adapt seamlessly to data from different hospitals, producing segments closely akin to those generated by the original training dataset. Importantly, our results indicate that the generated segments contributed significantly to identifying MS lesions that were previously undetected by human observers. Conversely, the segments produced by models trained on alternative objectives showed limited correspondence with clinical expert annotations. Consequently, our experience replay technique represents a valuable strategy for segmenting data from diverse hospital environments. The concept of metric comparison has been explored in various topological spaces, typically equivalent to convergence of Gromov-Wasserstein distances or optimal transport costs. However, these comparisons lack continuity with respect to the domain. We develop a novel metric comparison that demonstrates continuity under certain conditions, specifically when the domain remains unchanged. We also show that its continuity is unaffected by changes in the domain's geometry. The newly introduced comparison is a weighted average of Gromov-Hausdorff distance and optimal transport cost. Our weight parameter allows us to control the influence of either metric, with the former dominant in certain topological scenarios with compact domains. We provide theoretical proofs and numerical examples to support our findings. The talk can be accessed at https://youtu.be/ALp1OoKmRgQ. We explore how learning with partial domain knowledge can enhance the efficiency of training neural networks. We develop a novel framework for combining structured domain data with unstructured data from observations. This hybrid approach yields predictions that are superior to those derived from data alone, while also enabling the incorporation of domain insights without hindering the model's ability to learn from observations. Through experiments on two complex real-world tasks, we demonstrate that this hybrid method achieves better performance with less training data, and that its effectiveness is not compromised by the incomplete nature of its domain knowledge, which can be readily obtained from statistical analyses of the structured domain data. Ultimately, our results indicate that this hybrid strategy is a useful tool for practitioners in the field. The code for our model is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/echen31/ImPerfectNet. This research was supported by the AIR-TP grant from NSERC.

To investigate how massive stellar cores accumulate mass over time, we examined the growth of molecular cores using data collected by the Submillimeter Array. We selected 13 stellar sources located at a significant distance from major stellar disks and were observed in $^{12}$CO(1-0) and $^{12}$CO(2-1) emission lines. By combining these data with data on young stellar object evolution and radial velocity, we calculated the mass of each core when its surrounding envelope had a mass of 0.1 M$_\odot$. We found a direct relationship between core mass and time, described by the equation $M_\mathrm{core}(t) = (5.9 \pm 1.1) \cdot (t^\{1.46 \pm 0.13})^{1.65}$. This growth trend allows massive cores to develop within a few thousand years, laying the groundwork for the formation of massive stars via the collapse of dense filaments. Therefore, such massive cores likely contribute significantly to the production of massive stars, consistent with the predictions of theoretical models. Furthermore, their short formation times may explain why supercritical massive star-forming regions are scarce in the field: if a region takes too long to develop, it will lose its support due to the spreading of infalling material. Additionally, using observed core masses and the initial masses of the resulting stars from our sample, we calculated a scatter of 0.67 and a standard deviation of 0.5 in the relationship between core mass and star mass. This comparison confirms the efficiency of star formation. We also noticed two exceptional cases where the mass of the core exceeded the mass of the resulting star by more than their difference in proportion; further research will be necessary to understand this phenomenon. We assume that these massive cores will eventually develop into massive stars; however, it's also possible that they could remain in a low-mass, high-density, inactive state. Further research, particularly using higher angular resolution observations and mid-infrared imaging, is necessary to clarify this scenario. At any rate, it appears that such massive cores significantly contribute to the production of massive stars. Finally, our sample suggests that the mass of the core grows at a rate comparable to the mass of the resulting star. By comparing these values for 11 sources, we calculated an average "efficiency" of 0.8 $\pm$ 0.9. This comparison confirms the efficiency of star formation. We have conducted in-depth examinations of water's behavior when it freezes in confined spaces with both horizontal and vertical channels, using a series of theoretical models that mimic various types of microfluidic cells. By exploring packing densities ranging from 0.5 to greater than 0.75, we identified two types of frustrated polar ice crystals that can form at high densities. Additionally, we found that horizontal channels lead to the formation of a high-density amorphous phase with an increased tetrahedral coordination, whereas vertical channels lead to the formation of a high-density amorphous phase with a higher number of five-fold coordinated atoms. Our research shows that varying the channel orientation and density influences the type of amorphous phase formed. We validated our results by analyzing dynamic inclusions of larger water molecules within simulations of systems with vertical channels at high densities, confirming that these structures are consistent with our main findings. We observed a transition from non-polar to polar ice at a packing density of approximately 0.65 in systems with vertical channels. Furthermore, we observed a high-density amorphous phase with five-fold coordinated atoms in these systems at even higher densities. Our research also shows that partial substitutions of molecular inclusions with atomic inclusions lead to the formation of a polar ice structure at a lower density. However, this effect is only observable when the molecular inclusions' channels are perpendicular to the polar axis. Our research further explores the relationships between these unique water structures and their potential associations with specific properties of water, such as its boiling point and viscosity. We discovered notable similarities between the unique water structures observed in systems with vertical channels and those found in ice-X, a recently studied form of ice. Our research provides a systematic understanding of water's behavior in diverse confinement conditions. We derive equations to illustrate how pressure and temperature are affected by the unique constraints of microfluidic cells that vary in channel width, height, and temperature. Our research quantitatively demonstrates the unique properties of water in confined spaces and sheds light on the potential connections between these structures and the physical properties of ice-X, paving the way for further studies on this enigmatic form of ice. Ultimately, our research may inspire the development of innovative methods to produce ice-X, as well as other ice forms with unique properties, for use in applications such as cryomedicine, cryotechnology, and climate engineering. Pre-trained language models have become the foundation upon which numerous down-stream tasks build, but a notable shortcoming remains their inability to effectively address negative input examples during fine-tuning. We posit that by modifying the handling of special tokens in these models, this issue can be resolved. This paper introduces two novel pre-trained language models, BERT4Fourier and BERT4Hyper, that incorporate the Fourier transform and the Hypercomplex number system, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, these models represent the first instances of using Fourier transforms and Hypercomplex numbers in NLP model training. During our experiments, we found that the proposed models outperformed the original BERT-DI model on several benchmark datasets, achieving up to an additional 1.3% improvement in the F1 score. We further examined the effects of two distinctive special tokens, <eos> and <pad>, on BERT4Fourier performance and observed significant variations in performance, averaging around 0.5% when these tokens were used at different positions. Conversely, the hypercomplex-based HyperBERT exhibited more robust stability under the insertion of these tokens. Our investigation into the optimal hyperparameter configurations for the Fourier transform in BERT4Fourier revealed that the pre-trained model outperformed its DiE-based counterpart when the top K=5-15 eigenvalues were used. We observed similar stability in the HyperBERT model with the choice of its Hypercomplex representation. We have made the source code available under the terms of the MIT License at https://github.com/Charz Benefiel/HyperBERT. Additionally, our research indicates that the proposed models exhibit an enhanced capacity to recognize negative examples, as evidenced by our observation of a higher DI score within a 90-degree range. We conclude by presenting an insightful representation of the word embeddings resulting from the four HyperBERT models trained using the 4L, 4M, 4L+4M, 4M+4L schedules, demonstrating the model's ability to accurately capture the relationships between the special token <unk> and other words. We have incorporated these results into a new set of four HyperBERT models, namely HyperBERT-4L, HyperBERT-4M, HyperBERT-4L+4M, and HyperBERT-4M+4L, where we found that these models outperformed their closest counterpart, the 4L+4M HyperBERT model. The development of transformer models for natural language inference has been impressive, however they often struggle with nuanced aspects of language that require contextual consideration. Our research aims to improve the contextual analysis capability of these models by incorporating context-dependent negation cues. Three distinct types of negation were examined - lexical, contextual, and sentence-level - each posing different challenges to the model. Our approach enhanced the model's ability to detect context-driven negation by incorporating contextual negation cues via masked language modeling during pre-training. By doing so, the model learned that the negation word's meaning was tied to its surrounding context. Our experiments showed that the revised BERT model was able to correctly identify instances of contextual and sentence-level negation 7% and 8% points higher respectively compared to the original model's performance. Furthermore, the model performed 11% better on a contextual negation-based NLI task and 10% better on the SICK corpus overall. Our analysis also revealed that the model's performance on the test set was linearly correlated with its ability to accurately predict the context-driven negation cues. Our findings suggest that the incorporation of contextual negation cues has the potential to substantially boost the model's performance on NLI tasks with various degrees of negation intensity. Our proposed method can be easily integrated into existing transformer-based models to further refine their performance. Our updated BERT model, referred to as BERT_Neg, can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishjaipur/Contextual-negation-inference. Our research highlights the significance of incorporating a context-driven negation strategy for enhancing the performance and contextual analysis capability of transformer models. Our method may also contribute to the development of a negation bank resource by pinpointing all the contextual negation cues within a given corpus, thereby facilitating easier lookup and reference. Our paper also includes additional experiments and further explores the impact of incorporating various forms of negation cues on the model's performance. Our analysis reveals that the model's performance on the SICK corpus grows in tandem with an increase in the intensity of contextual negation cues. Our method may also aid in the identification of ambiguities in the meaning of negation cues based on their context. Our experiment results quote from our inter-raternal agreement study demonstrate that the model's performance can be substantially enhanced by upper-limit optimisation using contextual negation cues. Our method may also aid in the development of automatic rules for natural language processing by extracting semantic negation cues based on their context. Despite substantial progress in the field of neural machine translation, it remains difficult to effectively model long-distance context, especially in languages with complex morphological features. To address this limitation, we propose a look-ahead attention mechanism that enables a decoder to attend to future segments, as well as incorporate previously unexplored aspects of exponential functions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this mechanism through experiments, revealing that it leads to significant improvements in state-of-the-art models, including Transformer-variant architectures. Notably, when applied to GPT-2, our proposed mechanism achieves a 2.03 BLEU score improvement on the WMT 2014 English-German translation task. Our proposed attention mechanism is compatible with existing models and can be seamlessly integrated into the Transformer architecture. Our research aims to stimulate interest in exploring novel exponential function applications, extending beyond the initial GPT-2 studies. The code and pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/hiick/look-ahead-attention. Furthermore, all translation results can be found at https://fars Matt.github.io/look-ahead-attention/translation-results/. This research develops a novel method for evaluating Asian options of arbitrary types via the Laplace transform technique. Building upon a previous finding that reduced the computational requirements of normal Laplace transforms, we further improve the efficiency of Laplace transforms by investigating series convergence. We demonstrate that our approach enables exact solution of general Asian options with higher operational speed and enhanced memory usage compared to alternative Laplace-based methods. The results display substantial gains over European option pricing methods and are highly effective for options featuring log-normally distributed underlying assets with varying mean values. Due to the exact nature of our transforms, we can precisely calculate convergence thresholds for the Laplace series. Consequently, we devise a straightforward verification procedure for validating the calculated transforms and determining the optimal lap parameter for smooth, error-free solutions. This procedure is incorporated into our software package, LapAsian, which provides a unified environment for pricing Asian options and includes a comprehensive set of predefined option profiles and underlying asset models. The pricing function of the package enables the dynamic calculation of parameters and models, as well as the determination of optimal lap and k values for given accuracy levels. Furthermore, we showcase the effectiveness of our solution for Redd options priced via Laplace transforms by comparing them to alternative pricing methods in a real-world scenario. Specifically, we evaluate a Redd put option with normal underlying assets having a mean of 100 and a covariance of 0.2 as an example of a general Asian option type. In this case, our transforms exhibit optimal convergence when lap equals 0.025. The priced Redd put option value amounts to 16.8725 at normal volatility and 21.5156 at high volatility, surpassing the European option value of 13.9422 at high volatility. The proposed method and its implementation in LapAsian are developed using general Asian option pricing formulas in MATLAB and optimized for operational efficiency. Consequently, we outline a straightforward strategy for converting our solver to a C environment for even greater pricing accuracy. The evaluation of normal Laplace transforms reveals a significant increase in pricing performance at normal underlying assets, advancing from 0.5 seconds per iteration at lap=0.025 to 6 milliseconds per iteration. This advancement at lap=0.1 reduces the pricing time to 11 milliseconds. At higher volatility, the pricing time drops from 13 milliseconds at lap=0.025 to 1 millisecond at lap=0.1. These enhanced pricing speed and accuracy gains are heavily influenced by the exact nature of our transforms, allowing us to determine optimal lap and k values with certainty.

LaViSE utilizes a visual descriptor, implemented as an encoder for a generative adversarial text-converter network, that captures the visual characteristics of the image. Specifically, the researchers examined the reaction of MnGe, a alloy comprised of manganese and germanium, under which a lattice composed of spiral magnetic patterns forms. Experimental data obtained using highly sensitive magnetic detection techniques have confirmed the predictions of the theoretical models regarding the characteristics of the spiral magnetic patterns. This higher internal energy can trigger a shift within the material from its initial spiral magnetic patterns to a more stable uniform magnetic alignment, reveling an additional mechanism for how the material can undergo a phase transition as it is subjected to greater compression by magnetic force.

The interaction between electromagnetic waves in the weakly turbulent plasma is examined through a unified coordinate system that accounts for all possible combinations of wave polarizations and propagating directions. It provides a comprehensive wave-particle interaction model that is applicable in all scenarios. This comprehensive model can be reduced to two distinct limiting models - the quasilinear model when the wave energy is evenly distributed across various modes and the coherent electromagnetic wave (EM) model when the wave energy is primarily held by a single mode. The reduced models retain the key concept of a unified wave-energy framework and are expressed in a coordinate system that considers the relative indices of refraction and polarization. Formulas derived from these models can be used to estimate the rate of electron energy increase, the electron distribution function, the electron temperature, and the electron-ion collision time based on measurements such as the spectral density of the magnetic field, the wave frequency, the plasma density, and the electron scale size. Furthermore, the model allows for predictions about the behavior of other plasma processes such as electron holes, wave instabilities, and particle acceleration. The effectiveness of these models is confirmed by comparing them with simulations and experimental data obtained from various sources, including case studies of the coherent EM model that analyzed the magnetoswitch phenomenon discovered by the Magnetospheric Multiscale mission. Results of the study reveal that these models satisfactorily explain the observed rates of electron energy growth, the distribution of the electron velocity, and the electron temperature, particularly in plasma regions where the plasma frequency and the electron cyclotron frequency are different. They also reveal that the rate of electron energy growth in the EM model lies between the rates predicted by the quasilinear and coherent EM models, particularly at earlier stages of the growth process. The study demonstrates that the coordinate system provides a useful framework for understanding both the spectral composition of the EM modes and the rate of electron energy growth. It offers a versatile concept that is applicable to the study of various EM instabilities activated by the hot electrons in the plasma and the laser-induced plasma created through at least three distinct mechanisms such as plasma interaction with the laser field, thermal effects, and particle collisions. Formulation of the model on an equal basis enables seamless extension of the model to other areas including the interaction of the EM field with other types of particles and the study of other types of particle interactions. Through the AdS/CSDC correspondence, our paper demonstrates that surface defects in 2+1-dimensional spacetimes correspond to boundary conditions of unique one-dimensional conformal field theories.  Meanwhile, specific line defects in these spacetimes are equivalent to operators within the same conformal field theories.  A particular example is offered where a quarter wedge defect in Liouville CFT is linked to a fundamental particle in 1+1-dimensional free fermion theory.  This relationship can be observed in an associated AdS bulk theory with a defect described by a conformal field theory of a particle moving along a circle.  This connection also extends to gauge theories such as QCD where surface defects in 2+1-dimensional QCD are shown to be equivalent to boundary conditions of 1D conformal field theories, including those related to the non-supersymmetric duals of perturbative AdS$_3$ gravity.  This correspondence allows for a connection between gauge-theories and their dual conformal field theories at a level surpassing previous string duals.  Additionally, our work implies the existence of new solutions to quantum gravity featuring fundamental strings as the only degrees of freedom in the bulk.  Finally, the AdS/CFT correspondence for spacetime defects is utilized to investigate the entanglement structure of certain condensed-matter states, including those related to the Jaeger ground state.  This relationship also serves as yet another formulation of the holographic principle outside of the context of local symmetry.  This paper further discusses implications for condensed-matter research, suggesting that the AdS/CFT correspondence could provide a means to understand the entanglement structure of specific condensed-matter states, offering yet another representation of the holographic principle applicable beyond the context of local symmetry.  Ultimately, our work may provide valuable insights into the AdS/CFT correspondence when extended to higher spacetime dimensions.  Additionally, our work may yield useful mathematical structures even in the context of a non-perturbative gravity theory.  Finally, our work may lead to the emergence of new forms of condensed-matter states as a result of the AdS/CFT correspondence.  To facilitate further research, the underlying code used in our work has been made publicly available online at https://github.com/samuel-cutting/adscft-spacetime-defects.  This code includes the specific examples discussed in our work as well as more general tools capable of generating the AdS/CFT correspondence for a given surface defect in any conformal field theory. We describe an enhanced Monte Carlo algorithm for $e^+e^-$ pair production used within the $e^+e^-$ annihilation event generator KKMCee. This new approach expands upon the existing MCREE code by addressing three key improvements: incorporating higher-order QED corrections, accelerating event generation speed, and minimizing computational resource usage. When compared to the original MCREE algorithm, our updated code exhibits a considerable time and efficiency gain, specifically a $\sim$3-fold speedup in event generation and a $\sim$5-fold reduction in memory usage while still providing precise $e^+e^-$ pair cross-section predictions. These advancements benefit the ongoing upgrade of the command-line interface for WPHACT, now in progress, where we intend to integrate an enhanced Monte Carlo event generator capable of utilizing multi-core processors and generating extensive event files for $e^+e^-$ physics research. Furthermore, this improved KKMCee tool also features an upgraded API for user-friendly integration within custom-purpose event generators and their respective software development kits, for instance, in the reimplementation of the Monte Carlo event generator CERES in Fortran 90 and C++. Additionally, KKMCee has been successfully integrated with the Monte Carlo event generator SIXEG, responsible for the majority of simulated events contributing to the world's leading sample of $\gamma\gamma$ collisions, as well as for $e^+e^-$, $\gamma\gamma$, and $B$-meson data at the future electron-positron Higgs-factory. These multi-purpose MC tools are set to serve a diverse array of scientific applications, available for download from the official website: http://www.ph.edm.huberresearch.at/. We anticipate that the advanced features of these Monte Carlo event generators might require some time of exploration and familiarization by the end-user to fully understand their functionality; however, the actual simulation of $\gamma\gamma$, $e^+e^-$, and $B$-meson data would require the utilization of the respective dedicated event generators, like SIXEG and CERES, responsible for the simulation of these three main physics categories. To further verify our results, we performed a comprehensive statistical analysis, demonstrating that our algorithm's outcomes were consistent with those from a different heart rate estimation method. Predicting links in dynamic graphs poses a challenge compared to static structures, where link formation can be more systematically inferred. To tackle this issue, we suggest adjusting the graph autoencoder framework by incorporating a detailed analysis of the network dynamics behind each link, thereby providing essential context for link creation. By recognizing that many dynamic graphs exhibit distinct patterns of growth over time, we modify the standard graph autoencoder framework to include a component that captures temporary trends in link formation, using fewer parameters than a detailed time series analysis. Our proposed approach is compared to other methods for predicting links in both simulated and real-world networks, showing its ability to find a balance between accurately modeling short-term link trends and requiring fewer parameters, thereby shrinking the risk of overfitting on the available data. Overall, our method demonstrates the importance of incorporating network dynamics into link prediction methods, leading to improved performance and a more meaningful understanding of the underlying driving forces behind link formation. The proposed framework is referred to as the Temporal Autoencoder for Link Prediction (TALP). When applied to actual networks, TALP shows its ability to predict links with great success in a number of cases, significantly outperforming other methods for predicting links in both simulated and real-world networks, showing its compatibility with a variety of patterns of growth over time.
