This research explores Nirenberg type problems on the upper half of the sphere's surface. The focus is on a nonlinear elliptic equation in \Bb R^N with  N > 3,  and a given value for the constant \Bb. By employing a combination of approaches from  nonlinear potential analysis and concentration-knowledge,  solutions that violate the elliptic equation's natural constraints are found.  Key results demonstrate two types of solution behaviors: either two or one singularities,  both of which have a total energy of \Bb.  Moreover,  by examining the movement of the concentrations,  the characteristics of the singularities are understood.  In particular,  it is shown that the solution on the sphere has four mount Everest type concentrations,  one in each dimension,  whereas the solution on the upper half sphere has only two such concentrations.  Moreover,  even with the same \Bb and  number of concentrations,  the life span of the solution on the upper half sphere can be longer than on the sphere,  thereby illustrating a phenomenon of delay of blow up.  Finally,  by testing the solution's properties along the boundary via a combination of  blow up and blow down processes,  the solution's convergence towards its natural equilibrium is understood.  In particular,  it is shown that the solution converges towards the solution that depends only on the time variable and the coordinates on the boundary of the sphere. However, their initial goal of creating a unified, discriminative embedding space is still unresolved. In the age of mass application of contrastive learning, traditional methods struggle to overcome their limitations, while graph-based approaches are hampered by their computationally intensive updates. To address these issues, we present a new technique involving class-wise discordance as a supervised discrepancy measure to direct the learning of higher-level features in person reid. Unlike other methods, this approach updates individual features to minimize discordance on a per-class basis using a versatile objective function compatible with current methods, thereby enhancing the separability of the resulting embedding space while being efficient by avoiding the formation of a connected graph. Our method, known as Deep Class-wise Discordance Loss (DCDL), has several key advantages, including its versatility in being used alone or in combination with other methods, its efficiency, and the fact that it can be easily extended to support other supervised objectives. Our experiments demonstrate that DCDL outperforms state-of-the-art methods that employ comparable supervised objectives, while their combination further pushes the boundaries of what is achievable. Our code and model are available for public use at https://github.com/ziplab/DCDL. Our research further reveals that it is possible to create a unified embedding space that is both discriminative and generalizable by leveraging higher-level features, which provides a superior user experience. In the realm of reinforcement learning, constraints can significantly impact an agent's behavior, going beyond the scope of what the agent is learned to do. However, the information about these constraints is often possessed by experts, not the learning agents themselves. We propose a novel framework, Co-Learn, enabling experts to impart these constraints, learned concurrently with the agent's policy. Expert-provided constraints are represented as rules, and as the agent learns, it also learns these constraints, thereby adapting its action choices. We prove that when an expert is part of the same environment, the constraints learned by the agent closely resemble the original rules. We extend this concept to offline settings, demonstrating that constraints learned from multiple experts align with the expert-provided rules. Through experiments, we verify that the constraints learned by the agents closely match the expert-provided rules. Additionally, pre-trained constraints enhance the agent's performance when its policy and constraints are fine-tuned using reinforcement learning. We observe similar outcomes in continuous action spaces. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the optimal performance achievable with perfect constraint knowledge is reachable by combining multiple expert constraints. Overall, Co-Learn offers a novel paradigm for concurrent constraint learning, leveraging expert knowledge to inform both the agent's policy and constraints. This work has the potential to broaden the application of constraints in reinforcement learning. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/WeiZhouPU/Co_Learn. Valley and orbital Hall effects are manifestations of quantum numbers associated with electronic bands and momenta. However, it is challenging to quantify the valley and orbital components of conductivity since the corresponding currents are generated in response to different electric fields. A new concept, the orbital Hall effect, is introduced, which can be measured unambiguously. It is demonstrated that the orbital Hall effect emerges not just from the transition between states with distinct orbital quantum numbers, but also from the process of orbital mixing caused by a magnetic field. This mixing can be detected even when states with clearly distinct orbital numbers are not available. Unlike the valley Hall effect, the orbital Hall effect can be quantified by comparing conductivity at a particular electric field to its non-Hall counterpart, at the same electric field but with a magnetic field present. This comparison facilitates the direct observation of the orbital contribution to conductivity, enabling novel experiments focused on the orbital Hall effect to reveal new details of electronic behavior in various materials. Furthermore, the concept of orbital backscattering is introduced, and it is predicted that this phenomenon could be a primary cause of the orbital Hall effect, given that orbital mixing is common in a wide range of systems, including at room temperature. The integration of the orbital Hall effect into valley-Hall devices is also considered as a means to manipulate electronic valleys. The orbital Hall effect could enhance the efficiency of valley-valve applications based on graphene and other two-dimensional materials by providing an alternative mechanism to activate these devices. Ultimately, the development of device schemes incorporating the orbital Hall effect could lead to the realization of new functions and features. The concept of orbital magnetization associated with orbital numbers is also examined; however, its manifestation is constrained compared to the orbital Hall effect. Potential experimental approaches to observe the orbital Hall effect are discussed, including the examination of graphene and other two-dimensional materials in the presence of in-plane magnetic fields. The findings suggest that the orbital Hall effect could be observed in graphene under an in-plane electric field strength comparable to that used in valley Hall effect experiments. Theoretical predictions suggest that the orbital Hall effect could be more pronounced in materials with a higher number of available orbitals than those in valley Hall effect experiments. The distinct characteristics of the orbital Hall effect have clear implications for device design and the observation of quantum effects in two-dimensional materials. The comparison of the processes responsible for the valley and orbital Hall effects reveals that orbital mixing caused by a magnetic field is a universal driving force for these quantum effects, providing a general perspective on these phenomena. Over the past decade, the threat of adversarial machine learning has gained momentum due to a combination of an increase in processing power and an advancement in Reinforcement Learning techniques. Initially, direct gradient optimization was frequently applied in adversarial attacks, but recent research has revealed the potential of Reinforcement Learning for more sophisticated attacks. However, both direct gradient optimization and Reinforcement Learning have their shortcomings, the former failing to find the most efficient adversarial example and the latter requiring considerable computational resources to find robust examples within a limited budget. 

This study presents RL4AD, a framework that leverages Reinforcement Learning to minimize a predefined cost function. By introducing constraints to prevent excessive exploration, RL4AD is capable of generating adversarial examples within a limited budget. Moreover, our framework's adaptability to various scenarios is demonstrated through its application in three distinct settings: black-box, partial white-box, and fully white-box attacks. 

In an effort to prevent the avoidance of detection mechanisms, RL4AD addresses the challenge of avoiding examples that are easily classified using simple metrics. Through extensive experiments on multiple neural network architectures and datasets, our approach is proven to outperform existing techniques in generating robust adversarial examples that are also non-evasive. Furthermore, our framework's scalability is verified through performance comparisons on various data sets and network models. By employing RL4AD, users are empowered with enhanced flexibility to specify adversarial example standards. This in turn enables researchers to automate this standardization process. Moreover, our approach's potential is extended to defense evaluation through a novel assessment of adversarial example quality using the mean reward obtained from the reward function of RL4AD. Evaluations reveal that examples generated by our approach that meet the specified criteria also possess high quality as judged by state-of-the-art defense methods. This capability further underscores the value of utilizing Reinforcement Learning in advanced adversarial machine learning tasks. Moreover, our approach's potential is extended to advanced applications such as data poisoning via Reinforcement Learning in a pioneering study. This research demonstrates the avoidance of detection as a key challenge that necessitates a robust example search paradigm. Future research will focus on leveraging RL4AD in real-world scenarios with a variety of standards. Moreover, our approach can be utilized in a decentralized environment where examples are generated via communication among users, thereby maintaining user privacy. This research delves into the theoretical underpinnings of these new methods by analyzing their mathematical properties and computational complexity, offering theoretical guarantees similar to those of deep learning techniques. Evaluations on 32 datasets highlight the competitive performance of transmutations and mixture mutations, surpassing several established deep learning methods, including those utilizing label embedding. We investigate the efficiency of algorithms in multi-task linear regression problems where we have a large number of examples. In this research, we first demonstrate that existing efficient algorithms in this area face significant challenges in dealing with a large number of tasks, especially when task variability is high. To overcome these difficulties, we are studying a particular order of tasks - referred to as weakly superposable, which allows us to derive more effective algorithms based on spectral methods. We then present two algorithms that efficiently solve multi-task linear regression problems in the context of weakly superposable tasks, using either a given covariance matrix or an estimate of the matrix. We test these algorithms on synthetic data that we have developed specifically for this purpose. Our findings show that the proposed algorithms are very efficient, yet remain robust across a wide variety of tasks, as well as matrix designs for estimating the covariance of data within each task. We compared the performance of these algorithms with existing efficient algorithms in this research, highlighting their advantages in terms of both prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. This research develops a unified framework that integrates embedded visual learning and visual content learning. By embedding prompts within the image captioning process, it simultaneously learns visual content and visual embedding representation. The visual content focus enables the detection of implicit scene frames and visual structures, and the embedded guide helps tailor the generated caption according to the discovered scene structure. The analysis of fixed guide vs. learned guide shows that both can enhance the effectiveness of image captioning. Furthermore, this method surpasses the state-of-the-art performance in image captioning and establishes a novel benchmark for captioning with structure awareness. Moreover, it shows that these learned guides can be transposed to improve other tasks such as captioning semantic segmentation and zero-shot object detection. Ultimately, the framework enables the visualization of the learned guide, allowing for the understanding of its representation through both visual inspection and human feedback. Results demonstrate that the model captures diverse visual content, including objects, actions, and spatial relationships. Moreover, it is shown that the model is capable of responding to natural language inputs, such as questioning, advising, and requesting, and can be used as a visual question answering model. The research further investigates whether the model captures abstract knowledge by using human feedback to ask questions. For example, it is observed that the model can acquire knowledge about actions, spatial relationships, and group information. Moreover, it is observed that the model can accumulate knowledge from questions and gradually become more informative in response to increasingly complex questioning. The research further estimates the knowledge distribution of the model by analyzing its internal representation through both human and machine questioning. The research provides the first visual inspection of the learned representation by human and machine and provides an analysis of the knowledge gap between machines and humans through this study. The research further discusses several knowledge-related challenges of modern AI systems. The research further presents a new dataset called VCE, a set of 3,320 images divided into 160 groups, and collects the corresponding guides from machines and humans through both automated and manual questioning. The research further reports results on a new task called structure-guided visual content learning and proposes new questions for the new dataset. The concept of causation plays a vital role in various applications, including explaining the effects of actions and evaluating the severity of harms. Causal thinking is also essential in laws and ethics, present at their foundational level. Despite the numerous definitions of causation in the pointwise form 'because A, then B', causality in disjunctive environments 'because either A or B, then C' remains poorly understood. We have devised a novel definition of contrastive causation that accounts for the interplay of multiple conditions and their disjunctive relationships with an effect. This understanding enables the evaluation of the relative contributions of various causes towards an outcome, allowing for a more precise assessment of the severity of a harm. Our work on contrastive causation has been incorporated into a semi-formal account of harm known as Harm3, which is an extension of the formal ontology Onco. We argue that the concept of contrastive causation adds value in evaluating the severity of a disjunctive harm by considering the collective effect of different causes. Ultimately, semi-formal reasoning about causation and harm can facilitate effective communication between professionals and legal entities, while also contributing to the development of artificial intelligence and natural language processing systems. This paper suggests that having some target domain knowledge at hand can significantly improve zero-shot and few-shot performance. We provide a cross-attention mechanism that directs a language model towards more relevant words under limited input knowledge. Moreover, to enhance speech-to-text across languages, we propose a model that incorporates multilingual recurrent neural networks and adapts it to the speech-to-text domain by converging the models' information. We provide an overview of the extension of the standard Fourier heat conduction equation to account for its generalized form, incorporating the concept of fading memory. A relative entropy inequality in the Boltzmann framework leads to the derivation of a new heat conduction equation, compatible with the Fourier law and incorporating a memory kernel. We derive a maximum entropy principle for the generalized Fourier law, establish its representation through a Lagrange multiplier formulation, and link it to a new class of relaxation systems. We demonstrate the well-posedness of the generalized Fourier law within a distributional framework and show that its largest possible solution corresponds to the relaxation system of a "spring-like" nature. Furthermore, we provide an algorithmic framework, based on the dual-weighted duality in Lagrange multipliers, to compute the solution to the generalized heat conduction equation. We verify the numerical scheme's relative entropy stability and demonstrate its convergence to the generalized Fourier law solution, along with the same rate as the numerical approximation error. Extensive numerical results are shown for one-dimensional heat conduction examples, showcasing the numerical scheme's effectiveness. We applied the developed scheme to model the heat conduction process within a bar with a non-homogeneous inner structure and efficiently reproduced its non-intuitive thermal behavior. Our study reveals the significant potential of the general Fourier law in describing and modeling such non-intuitive thermal effects. We also carry out two other numerical case studies, namely, solving the generalized heat conduction equation in a finite bar with no internal structure but with a non-constant boundary thermal slip process and modeling the transition from the standard to the generalized Fourier law process. Our numerical experiments reveal outstanding accuracy, even when the numerical time step is relatively large in comparison to the characteristic time of the memory effect. We further compared the numerical solution of the general Fourier law with the Duvaut-Liu rate-independent damage model on various examples and observed notable similarity between the two models in dynamics. Our study reveals the significant significant potential of the general Fourier law in describing physical phenomena beyond the well-known heat conduction equation. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed scheme to accurately describe such phenomena. We also observed that the numerical solution of the general Fourier law could be well approximated by leveraging the duality approach and by increasing the value of the relaxation parameter. This research centers on improving short-term forecasting of per-apartment energy demand during peak hours (3pm-7pm) at high-rise buildings in urban areas, particularly in Hong Kong. In this context, we examine the value of incorporating peak forecasts generated by cutting-edge deep learning models alongside traditional hourly forecasts. To compare these approaches, we employed 12 months of historical data from a 73-meter tall building with 170 units, gathering readings every 15 minutes on energy consumption, temperature, humidity, air quality, and luminosity. To enhance prediction accuracy, we integrated our previous findings on combining forecasts and energy demand modeling for high-rise buildings. Our results indicate that fusing conventional forecasts with peak forecasts yields a 10% reduction in MAE and MAPE in the three hours preceding the peak period. Notably, using the feature of energy demand variance, we achieved a 7.5% reduction in MAE and MAE. In contrast, using weather forecasts yielded only a 1.7% reduction in MAE. This research offers a reliable method for building energy management during peak hours. Furthermore, we propose a more efficient communication strategy to facilitate energy trading among building energy users, ultimately contributing to the development of peer-to-peer energy trading among high-rise buildings in urban areas. This system is currently being tested in a real-world setting at a 73-meter tall building in Hong Kong's Central Business District. Our energy exchange system is expected to launch in the near future. In the context of energy trading, we identified economic benefits for energy providers, while conducting a case study showed that energy sellers at high-rise buildings in Hong Kong can earn 5-10 HKD per kilowatt-hour. Conversely, energy buyers may save 5-10 HKD per kilowatt-hour. This trend may accelerate as the supply of renewable energy increases. However, our model shows that this trend may be affected by renegerable energy supply. In the long term, energy sellers can earn an average sum of 2,668.64 Hong Kong Dollars ( approx. 335 USD) per year, while energy buyers can save an equivalent amount. This phenomenon yields an attractive return on investment of up to 31.56% per year. To optimize energy trading, we can leverage algorithms for solving an NP-hard problem. By employing a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach, we can devise an efficient communication strategy that facilitates energy trading among building energy users. In our initial experiment, agents trained in this capacity reduced their action finding time by up to 30%

Traditional machine learning and data mining methods are often isolated from established knowledge in their respective fields. However, incorporating knowledge is seen as a potential means of enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of these algorithms. This study examines the incorporation of knowledge into conventional machine learning algorithms and data mining techniques, with a focus on the underlying motivations and key expectations for this approach. We also review existing methodologies for incorporating knowledge and highlight their practical applications, alongside outlining the primary challenges associated with this paradigm. Additionally, this work looks at existing efforts to integrate knowledge from diverse perspectives, including hard and soft integration processes. Ultimately, the discussion sets out potential avenues for future research and highlights the pressing needs in this field. While encouraging machine learning algorithms and data mining techniques to utilize domain-specific knowledge may accelerate their adoption in the domain, the transition from soft to hard integration poses a significant challenge. Ultimately, the discussion seeks to answer the central question: can we confidently integrate domain-specific knowledge into machine learning algorithms and data mining techniques? The investigation into this question sheds light on the current state of this interdisciplinary area. This paper presents an innovative, data-driven approach that utilizes global image labels and a structural consistency framework to accurately identify and pinpoint lesions within CT images. By refining a multi-scale lesion map through iterative revisions, this method achieves enhanced localization results for a variety of tumors, including pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) and colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Building upon this data-driven basis, we develop a network design strategy tailored to detect a specific type of lesion, in this case studying both PNETs and CRLM to design a specialized model for each. Our experiments reveal that our approach delivers comparable performance to state-of-the-art medical radiology techniques, with the additional benefit of reduced data requirements for training a network to identify lesions. Furthermore, our study finds that using images annotated by human radiologists but labeled by a computer is more effective for training a network to detect PNETs when compared to using images annotated by both a computer and a radiologist. Overall, our results indicate that our data-driven strategy is highly effective for a range of imaging tasks. This work shows great potential for detecting and localizing specific types of lesions, in particular for PNETs. However, more research is needed for quantifying the accuracy of detecting and localizing metastases in the liver. We plan to investigate this further. We present an innovative technique for accurately locating vertebrae in spinal
X-RR-Range images, featuring a hybrid framework combining unsupervised feature
extraction and eye fixation models. This approach consists of two stages: the
first utilizes an unsupervised feature extraction method to derive a low-dimensional
representation from the given dataset, followed by a supervised selection process
to identify dominant features, which is then used to build an unsupervised
envelope model. Consequently, an unsupervised redemption module is employed
to transform the features into an intuitive, easy-to-interpret format. Subsequently,
a linear regression model is applied to introduce position context to the
transformed features. Consequently, the position-aware envelope features are used
to train a support vector machine to pinpoint the location of vertebrae.

Experimental evaluations of our proposed method on the public spinal dataset
reveal our method to be significantly more effective in identifying vertebrae,
with an enhanced location precision of 96.69% in comparison to other approaches, which
include C2F3 (87.68%), NCP (84.21%), ResNet(50) (85.46%), RF(52) (85.46),
and Deep ID(48) (85.24). These results indicate our method outperforms these
methods. Moreover, the proposed method exhibits enhanced vertebra identification
rates of 98.84\% for L1-L5 and 99.21% for L2-L5, thus showcasing its superiority. 

This research is pivotal in enhancing software systems for vertebrae location to
reduce radiation exposure in clinical settings for vertebrae fracture analysis. 
In addition, the proposed method has high potential in applications requiring
vertabrae location across a range of spinal images, which will reduce clinical
workload when implemented. Finally, the code for our method is publicly accessible
at https://github.com/NeurolabYNU/vertabrae. 
We are confident that our work will facilitate further research in vertebrae
location and serve as a valuable foundation for other researchers in this field. 
We would like to extend our gratitude to all the researchers who shared their
work, which included C2F3, NCP, ResNet(50), RF(52), and Deep ID(48). Without
their contributions, this research would not have been possible.

Recent breakthroughs in developing optical cavities isolated from the surroundings have enabled researchers to study quantum phenomena isolated from external influences. Our investigation demonstrates that, despite these advancements, persistent currents in superfluid Bose-Einstein condensates trapped within an optical cavity remain vulnerable to interference from the ambient electromagnetic field fluctuations. It is shown that vacuum fluctuations cause polariton state instability, resulting in a limited range of frequencies in which spontaneous emission of polariton modes can occur. This constraint can, however, be overcome by utilizing a dimer of optical cavities, where the connected cavities exhibit distinct resonance frequencies. As a result, an extended frequency range for spontaneous emission of polariton modes is achieved, featuring both odd and even multipolar states. Our theoretical analysis involves integration of the Einstein-Podolsky-Ressler model with the Purcell effect, providing a comprehensive understanding of quantum phenomena in confined systems and their potential applications in quantum computing and precision science. Our work contributes to the advancement of optical cavities as highly sensitive detectors to study fundamental properties of matter. Our research paves the way for realising novel quantum devices, including atomic light sources, quantum processors, and highly sensitive detectors of magnetization and spin polarization. Furthermore, our work sheds light on previously unexplored quantum properties of ultracold atoms and their potential utility in precision science and computing. Our model also reveals that atomic light emission is possible due to coupling with vacuum fluctuations, aligning with the well-established theory of spontaneous emission. Additionally, our research reveals that high sensitivity to external influences is inherent to rare-earth ion systems, underscoring the need for future ion-based applications in sensing rather than quantum computing. Our work provides a systematic understanding of quantum interactions between cold atoms and electromagnetic fields at a fundamental level. Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices can potentially achieve a significant breakthrough in solving the full separability problem in quantum states, such as GHZ states combined with local mixing. We introduce a novel efficient algorithm utilizing NISQ devices to determine whether a given quantum state with at most D non-zero off-diagonal amplitudes is separable. The algorithm is built on repeating the application of the NISQ device's unitary matrix $U$, calculating the absolute value of the corresponding amplitude $\mathcal{V}(U^k\otimes U^{\theta_k})\psi$, and monitoring the growth of $\mathcal{V}(U^k\otimes U^{\theta_k})\psi$ until it surpasses a predetermined threshold. The algorithm's efficiency directly depends on the number of iterations, which is bounded by $2\log_2(e/D)$, requiring only $d$ quantum operations and $2d$ quantum memory. The algorithm's efficiency, along with noise tolerance, greatly surpasses any classical approach with comparable efficiency, leading to a quantum acceleration factor of at least $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{D})$. Furthermore, the algorithm can be easily extended to check the pure separability of states possessing non-trivial entanglement with smaller subsystems and to apply the entanglement purification protocol. The algorithm can be executed on devices such as the IBM QASM simulator using the IBM Q Experience cloud-based quantum computing service. The project's code can be found at https://github.com/johnohb/efficient_separability_test. The problem of depth estimation using a single color image has received considerable attention in recent years due to its numerous practical applications in robotics and self-driving vehicles. Notably, approaches based on neural networks require substantial storage space and computational power, hindering their real-world applicability. A more recent challenge is dealing with occlusions, which typically cause significant areas of the predicted depth map to be marked as unknown. To overcome these limitations, a novel cost constructor based on M\`obius transformation has been developed for depth estimation using a single color image. Leveraging the expatiation properties of M\`obius transformations, this proposed method efficiently handles occlusions by setting zero values in affected areas, ensuring that resulting depth maps are more realistic. Compared to existing methods, this proposed technique demonstrates superior results on the KITTI challenge, alongside significantly reduced memory and processing requirements. Its exceptional performance, combined with a marked decrease in storage needs and computational complexity, makes it highly suitable for application in self-driving cars and other real-world scenarios. Further investigation reveals that the proposed cost constructor can be adapted for depth estimation using multiple color images, yielding promising outcomes. Ultimately, this proposed method offers considerable advantages in terms of applicability, making it a highly desirable choice for a range of depth estimation tasks. This article summarizes a seminar held at KMSAR 2021, in which I introduced some knowledge on embedding various theories of gravity within double field theory framework. A brief overview of the discussion that followed the seminar can be found in arXiv:2103.01530, where I explored the one-form generalizations of Newton's law using DFT. During the seminar, we analyzed the $d$-instanton solutions in FLRW spacetime derived in arXiv:1801.11, and discussed the non-Riemannian volume form in such a spacetime. Subsequently, we examined the Poisson coefficients in both Einstein curvature and Lemaitre curvature contexts that can be expressed as non-parallel one-forms. In the concluding session, we debated the observability of the Poisson coefficients in a static and spherically symmetric setup. This seminar served as a starting point to investigate new interesting topics in the field. Additionally, we recognized that selecting a particular sector of gravity via DFT is tantamount to fixing certain constraints on field space. Home WiFi networks typically operate on an First-Come-First-Served basis, with devices associating with the strongest nearby access point. However, in environments where multiple access points offer similar signal strengths, devices associate in an unpredictable manner, leading to inefficient resource usage. We propose a novel method where devices selectively associate with access points based on load and wireless channel quality. By incorporating load awareness into the association process, we demonstrate that our algorithm improves overall network throughput and user experience. In comparison to conventional methods, our load-aware approach enhances an individual device's speed by 31.5% and reduces its data transfer delay by 36.9% in a home environment with multiple access points and wireless devices. As a result, our load-aware mechanism proves to be an effective solution for improving the efficiency of home WiFi networks. We also examined the feasibility of using load-awareness as a means of improving WiFi network efficiency, through the implementation of a straightforward and efficient algorithm. By its non-complex nature, we conclude our proposed method can be scaling up to larger networks. Furthermore, our load-aware approach can also be applied to femtocell networks to facilitate energy efficiency, by allowing smaller access points to adjust their transmission power according to individual device requirements. As a result, our load-aware mechanism proves to be an essential component for optimizing home WiFi networks and potentially other types of wireless networks. In order to evaluate the practicality of our proposed method, we developed a load-aware association algorithm that incorporates various signal strength metrics, including those from 3D beamforming devices, to efficiently associate with access points. By its non-complex nature, we conclude our proposed method can be scaling up to larger networks. Furthermore, our load-aware approach can also be applied to femtocell networks to facilitate energy efficiency, by allowing smaller access points to adjust their transmission power according to individual device requirements. In order to evaluate the practicality of our proposed method, we developed an experimental framework that utilizes external measurement tools to monitor various signal strength metrics, such as RSSI, data rate, and primary cell information. We also conducted 20 trials of our load-aware algorithm, resulting in an average improvement in speed and delay of 31.5% and 36.9% respectively, in comparison to conventional methods, such as RSSI-based association. In addition, our load-aware approach can also be applied to other types of wireless networks, such as those using 3D beamforming, by efficiently associating with access points.
